author: Mary Shelley
text: A new light seemed to dawn upon my mind, and bounding with joy, I communicated my discovery to my father.
summary: I finally figured something important out and I was so excited I immediately told my dad.

author: Mary Shelley
text: Believe me, Frankenstein, I was benevolent; my soul glowed with love and humanity; but am I not alone, miserably alone? You, my creator, abhor me; what hope can I gather from your fellow creatures, who owe me nothing? They spurn and hate me.
summary: I started out kind and loving but now I feel completely alone because everyone rejects me.

author: Mary Shelley
text: I had often, when at home, thought it hard to remain during my youth cooped up in one place and had longed to enter the world and take my station among other human beings.
summary: I felt trapped at home when I was young and I desperately wanted to get out and live my own life.

author: Mary Shelley
text: My creator, make me happy; let me feel gratitude towards you for one benefit! Let me see that I excite the sympathy of some existing thing; do not deny me my request!”
summary: I am begging for just one good thing so I can feel thankful and know someone actually cares about me.

author: Mary Shelley
text: Young men should be diffident of themselves, you know, M. Clerval: I was myself when young; but that wears out in a very short time.”
summary: I think young guys should stay humble because I was shy once too and it did not last long.

author: Mary Shelley
text: I found myself similar yet at the same time strangely unlike to the beings concerning whom I read and to whose conversation I was a listener.
summary: I feel like other people in some ways but fundamentally different when I watch their lives from outside.

author: Mary Shelley
text: When I found this, I resolved to quit the place that I had hitherto inhabited, to seek for one where the few wants I experienced would be more easily satisfied.
summary: I decided to leave where I was living to find a place where I could meet my basic needs more easily.

author: Mary Shelley
text: Yet I seek not a fellow feeling in my misery. No sympathy may I ever find. When I first sought it, it was the love of virtue, the feelings of happiness and affection with which my whole being overflowed, that I wished to be participated.
summary: I have stopped hoping anyone will understand my pain even though I once only wanted to share love and happiness.

author: Mary Shelley
text: I do break my promise; never will I create another like yourself, equal in deformity and wickedness.”
summary: I am breaking my promise because I refuse to create something that will cause more harm like you have.

author: Mary Shelley
text: Our lives will not be happy, but they will be harmless and free from the misery I now feel.
summary: Our life together will not be joyful but it will be peaceful and free from the pain I feel now.

author: Mary Shelley
text: I wished sometimes to shake off all thought and feeling, but I learned that there was but one means to overcome the sensation of pain, and that was death—a state which I feared yet did not understand.
summary: I sometimes want to shut off all my thoughts and pain, but death scares me because I do not understand it.

author: Mary Shelley
text: Yet even that enemy of God and man had friends and associates in his desolation; I am alone.
summary: Even the worst outcast seems to have company, while I feel completely alone in the world.

author: Mary Shelley
text: I soon found that I had overtaxed my strength and that I must repose before I could continue my journey.
summary: I pushed myself too hard and realized I need to rest before I can keep going.

author: Mary Shelley
text: From my infancy I was imbued with high hopes and a lofty ambition; but how am I sunk! Oh! My friend, if you had known me as I once was, you would not recognise me in this state of degradation.
summary: I once had big dreams and ambition, but now I feel so low you would not recognize me.

author: Mary Shelley
text: But the appearance of my father was to me like that of my good angel, and I gradually recovered my health.
summary: Seeing my dad felt like being saved, and I slowly started to feel healthy again.

author: Mary Shelley
text: Know that, one by one, my friends were snatched away; I was left desolate.
summary: I lost my friends one after another and now I feel completely alone in the world.

author: Mary Shelley
text: I look on the hands which executed the deed; I think on the heart in which the imagination of it was conceived and long for the moment when these hands will meet my eyes, when that imagination will haunt my thoughts no more.
summary: I cannot stop thinking about the terrible thing I did and I just want the guilt to end.

author: Mary Shelley
text: I am an unfortunate and deserted creature, I look around and I have no relation or friend upon earth.
summary: I feel abandoned and alone because I have no family or friends anywhere in my life.

author: Mary Shelley
text: Once commenced, it would quickly be achieved, and I might be restored to my family in peace and happiness.
summary: I believe that if I start this hard task now, I will soon be back home happy with my family.

author: Mary Shelley
text: I had resolved in my own mind that to create another like the fiend I had first made would be an act of the basest and most atrocious selfishness, and I banished from my mind every thought that could lead to a different conclusion.
summary: I decided that making the same harmful mistake again just for myself would be deeply selfish and wrong.

author: Mary Shelley
text: I am full of fears, for if I fail there, I am an outcast in the world for ever.’
summary: I am terrified that if I mess up this chance I will be alone and rejected forever.

author: Mary Shelley
text: Night also closed around; and when I could hardly see the dark mountains, I felt still more gloomily.
summary: I watched the night settle over the dark hills and felt my mood sink even lower.

author: Mary Shelley
text: I felt as if I were placed under a ban—as if I had no right to claim their sympathies—as if never more might I enjoy companionship with them. Yet even thus I loved them to adoration; and to save them, I resolved to dedicate myself to my most abhorred task.
summary: I feel shut out from the people I love yet I adore them enough to do something I hate to protect them.

author: Mary Shelley
text: My trifling occupations take up my time and amuse me, and I am rewarded for any exertions by seeing none but happy, kind faces around me. Since you left us, but one change has taken place in our little household.
summary: I keep busy with small tasks and feel lifted by the happy loving people at home despite missing you.

author: Mary Shelley
text: Our misfortune is doubly hard to us; we have not only lost that lovely darling boy, but this poor girl, whom I sincerely love, is to be torn away by even a worse fate.
summary: We are crushed to have lost a beloved child and now face losing a dear girl to something even worse.

author: Mary Shelley
text: You may deem me romantic, my dear sister, but I bitterly feel the want of a friend.
summary: I know it sounds dramatic but I deeply miss having a close friend in my life right now.

author: Mary Shelley
text: I had been awake the whole of the preceding night, my nerves were agitated, and my eyes inflamed by watching and misery.
summary: I stayed up all night feeling anxious and miserable with burning eyes from lack of sleep.

author: Mary Shelley
text: Darkness then came over me and troubled me, but hardly had I felt this when, by opening my eyes, as I now suppose, the light poured in upon me again.
summary: I felt overwhelmed by darkness and confusion until I opened my eyes and light rushed back in.

author: Mary Shelley
text: I looked upon them as superior beings who would be the arbiters of my future destiny. I formed in my imagination a thousand pictures of presenting myself to them, and their reception of me. I imagined that they would be disgusted, until, by my gentle demeanour and conciliating words, I should first win their favour and afterwards their love.
summary: I built up fantasies about meeting people I admire, fearing rejection but hoping kindness would earn their love.

author: Mary Shelley
text: Peace, peace! Learn my miseries and do not seek to increase your own.”
summary: I want you to listen to my painful story so you do not make the same mistakes I did.

author: Jane Austen
text: I do not mean, however, to assert that we can be justified in devoting too much of our time to music, for there are certainly other things to be attended to.
summary: I think it is fine to enjoy music but I should not let it take over my other responsibilities in life.

author: Jane Austen
text: The recollection of what I then said, of my conduct, my manners, my expressions during the whole of it, is now, and has been many months, inexpressibly painful to me.
summary: I still feel awful months later when I remember how rude and awkward I acted during that conversation.

author: Jane Austen
text: Had I but explained some part of it only--some part of what I learnt, to my own family!
summary: I wish I had warned my family about what I found out instead of keeping it all to myself.

author: Jane Austen
text: A great many changes have happened in the neighbourhood since you went away. Miss Lucas is married and settled: and one of my own daughters. I suppose you have heard of it; indeed, you must have seen it in the papers.
summary: So much has changed since you left, and two women here got married including one of my daughters.

author: Jane Austen
text: You may possibly wonder why all this was not told you last night. But I was not then master enough of myself to know what could or ought to be revealed.
summary: I did not tell you everything yesterday because I was too upset to think clearly about what to share.

author: Jane Austen
text: But when you have had time to think it all over, I hope you will be satisfied with what I have done.
summary: I hope that once you reflect on my choices you will understand and approve of them.

author: Jane Austen
text: There are few people whom I really love, and still fewer of whom I think well.
summary: I truly love very few people and I respect even fewer than that.

author: Jane Austen
text: With these rooms I might have now been familiarly acquainted! Instead of viewing them as a stranger, I might have rejoiced in them as my own, and welcomed to them as visitors my uncle and aunt.
summary: I tour a beautiful home imagining I could have lived there and hosted my family.

author: Jane Austen
text: Society, I own, is necessary to me. I have been a disappointed man, and my spirits will not bear solitude.
summary: I need to be around people because disappointment has left me unable to face being alone.

author: Jane Austen
text: There can be no love in all this. My watchfulness has been effectual; and though I should certainly be a more interesting object to all my acquaintance, were I distractedly in love with him, I cannot say that I regret my comparative insignificance. Importance may sometimes be purchased too dearly. Kitty and Lydia take his defection much more to heart than I do.
summary: I feel relieved I never truly loved him and I do not miss the drama others seem to crave.

author: Jane Austen
text: But I am particularly attached to these young men; and know them to be so much attached to me! They were excessively sorry to go! But so they always are.
summary: I really love having these young guys around and I know they hate leaving me, just like always.

author: Jane Austen
text: But I knew not--I was afraid of doing too much. Wretched, wretched mistake!”
summary: I held back because I feared overstepping, and now I realize that was a terrible mistake.

author: Jane Austen
text: It is, I believe, too little yielding; certainly too little for the convenience of the world. I cannot forget the follies and vices of others so soon as I ought, nor their offences against myself. My feelings are not puffed about with every attempt to move them. My temper would perhaps be called resentful.
summary: I know I hold grudges too long and do not forgive easily when people hurt or disappoint me.

author: Jane Austen
text: I perfectly comprehend your feelings, and have now only to be ashamed of what my own have been.
summary: I finally understand how you feel, and I feel deeply ashamed of how I acted.

author: Jane Austen
text: I was sure you loved your girls too well to neglect such an acquaintance.
summary: I knew you love our daughters too much to pass up introducing them to someone important.

author: Jane Austen
text: You have employed your time much better. No one admitted to the privilege of hearing you can think anything wanting. We neither of us perform to strangers.”
summary: I admire how you use your talent quietly and feel we are alike in avoiding showing off.

author: Jane Austen
text: Do not be afraid of my running into any excess, of my encroaching on your privilege of universal good-will.
summary: I joke that I will not compete with your habit of liking everyone and seeing only good.

author: Jane Austen
text: They always continue to grow sufficiently unlike afterwards to have their share of vexation; and it is better to know as little as possible of the defects of the person with whom you are to pass your life.”
summary: People drift apart after committing and it feels safer not to know a lifelong partner too well beforehand.

author: Jane Austen
text: Is there nothing you could take to give you present relief? A glass of wine; shall I get you one?
summary: I feel worried about you and want to help now by getting you a glass of wine.

author: Jane Austen
text: But nothing can be done; I know very well that nothing can be done. How is such a man to be worked on?
summary: I feel helpless because nothing will change him and I have no idea how to reach him.

author: Jane Austen
text: My father and mother believe the worst, but I cannot think so ill of him.
summary: My parents have given up on him completely, but I still refuse to believe he is that bad.

author: Jane Austen
text: I have been a selfish being all my life, in practice, though not in principle.
summary: I am realizing I have lived selfishly for years even though I always told myself I was a good person.

author: Jane Austen
text: But here, by carrying with me one ceaseless source of regret in my sister’s absence, I may reasonably hope to have all my expectations of pleasure realized.
summary: Honestly my trip will be perfect except I actually miss my sister more than I want to admit right now.

author: Jane Austen
text: Till I have your disposition, your goodness, I never can have your happiness. No, no, let me shift for myself; and, perhaps, if I have very good luck, I may meet with another Mr. Collins in time.”
summary: I admire how kind you are and how happy that makes you, but I will just have to manage alone in love.

author: Jane Austen
text: I wish you had been there, my dear, to have given him one of your set-downs.
summary: I wish you had been there with me to call him out because you always know exactly what to say.

author: Jane Austen
text: Oh that I had been with you! you have had every care and anxiety upon yourself alone.”
summary: I wish I had been there for you instead of letting you handle all the stress alone.

author: Jane Austen
text: And how impossible in others! But why should you wish to persuade me that I feel more than I acknowledge?”
summary: I get frustrated when you insist I have stronger feelings than I am willing to admit.

author: Jane Austen
text: Nor am I ashamed of the feelings I related. They were natural and just. Could you expect me to rejoice in the inferiority of your connections?--to congratulate myself on the hope of relations whose condition in life is so decidedly beneath my own?”
summary: I am not sorry for judging your family background because I honestly believe someone in my position would feel the same.

author: Jane Austen
text: Perhaps I did not always love him so well as I do now; but in such cases as these a good memory is unpardonable. This is the last time I shall ever remember it myself.”
summary: I love him more now than I did before, so I am choosing to forgive his past mistakes and never bring them up again.

author: Jane Austen
text: And with no one to speak to of what I felt, no Jane to comfort me, and say that I had not been so very weak, and vain, and nonsensical, as I knew I had!
summary: I felt ashamed of how foolish and vain I had been, and I had no close friend here to comfort me.

author: Jane Austen
text: What a blessing to young people to be in such hands! Your father and mother seem so totally free from all those ambitious feelings which have led to so much misconduct and misery, both in young and old.
summary: You are lucky to have grounded parents who avoid the ambition that ruins so much.

author: Jane Austen
text: You need not tell me that you had a pleasant evening. I see it in your eye.
summary: I can tell from your face that you had a wonderful time last night.

author: Jane Austen
text: I am every instant hearing something which overpowers me. You sink your voice, but I can distinguish the tones of that voice when they would be lost on others.
summary: I feel overwhelmed because I can pick out your quiet voice anywhere in a crowd.

author: Jane Austen
text: But I too have been thinking over the past, and a question has suggested itself, whether there may not have been one person more my enemy even than that lady? My own self.
summary: I have been reflecting and wondering if I was my own worst enemy all along.

author: Jane Austen
text: Well,” (turning away), “now, where are you bound? Can I go anywhere for you, or with you?
summary: I feel awkward leaving and ask where you are headed and if I can join you.

author: Jane Austen
text: And take it altogether, now that we have been into most of the houses hereabouts and can judge, there is not one that we like better than this. Pray say so, with my compliments.
summary: We have toured a lot of homes around here and honestly yours is still our favorite by far.

author: Jane Austen
text: To begin without knowing that at such a time there will be the means of marrying, I hold to be very unsafe and unwise, and what I think all parents should prevent as far as they can.”
summary: I think starting a relationship without financial stability is reckless and parents should try to stop it.

author: Jane Austen
text: Indeed, I must do ourselves the justice to say, that the few alterations we have made have been all very much for the better.
summary: We have only made a few changes around here but I know they have all improved things.

author: Jane Austen
text: I began to think I should never see you. I am so ill I can hardly speak. I have not seen a creature the whole morning!”
summary: I have been sick and alone all morning waiting for you and I was starting to lose hope.

author: Jane Austen
text: We see nothing of them, and this is really an instance of gross inattention.
summary: We never hear from them anymore and I feel like they are completely ignoring us.

author: Jane Austen
text: For you alone, I think and plan. Have you not seen this? Can you fail to have understood my wishes?
summary: I am only thinking about you and planning our future and I need you to finally see that.

author: Jane Austen
text: With all my soul I wish them happy, and rejoice over every circumstance in favour of it.
summary: I truly want them to be happy together and I feel glad whenever things go well for them.

author: Jane Austen
text: I have loved none but you. Unjust I may have been, weak and resentful I have been, but never inconstant. You alone have brought me to Bath.
summary: I have only ever loved you and I admit I was unfair and weak but I never stopped.

author: Jane Austen
text: To consider it as the certain wish of every being who could hope to influence you!
summary: She feels hurt that everyone around the person she loves tried to turn them against her.

author: Jane Austen
text: To a degree, I could contradict this instantly; but, when I began to reflect that others might have felt the same—her own family, nay, perhaps herself—I was no longer at my own disposal.
summary: I wanted to argue back right away but realizing her family might agree left me feeling powerless.

author: Jane Austen
text: You have difficulties, and privations, and dangers enough to struggle with. You are always labouring and toiling, exposed to every risk and hardship.
summary: You work constantly under risky and exhausting conditions with never enough rest or safety.

author: Jane Austen
text: It was possible that you might retain the feelings of the past, as I did; and one encouragement happened to be mine.
summary: I kept feeling the same as before and hoped you might still feel that way too.

author: Jane Austen
text: I have no reason, from any thing that has fallen within my observation, to do otherwise.
summary: I have seen nothing that gives me any reason to think or act differently.

author: Jane Austen
text: I think differently now; time and sickness and sorrow have given me other notions; but at that period I must own I saw nothing reprehensible in what Mr Elliot was doing.
summary: I see things differently now after illness and grief, though I once saw nothing wrong.

author: Jane Austen
text: I shall be truly glad to have them back again. Our neighbourhood cannot spare such a pleasant family.
summary: I will be so happy when they return because our community really misses that wonderful family.

author: Jane Austen
text: It is a sort of pain, too, which is new to me. I have been used to the gratification of believing myself to earn every blessing that I enjoyed. I have valued myself on honourable toils and just rewards.
summary: I feel a new kind of hurt because I always thought hard work earned me everything good in my life.

author: Jane Austen
text: I am half agony, half hope. Tell me not that I am too late, that such precious feelings are gone for ever.
summary: I feel torn between dread and hope that I have not missed my chance at love forever.

author: Jane Austen
text: It is not that I did not think of it, or desire it, as what could alone crown all my other success; but I was proud, too proud to ask again. I did not understand you. I shut my eyes, and would not understand you, or do you justice. This is a recollection which ought to make me forgive every one sooner than myself.
summary: I let pride stop me from trying again with you, and now I blame myself more than anyone else.

author: Jane Austen
text: We were asked on purpose to be introduced. There was always such a great connexion between the Dalrymples and ourselves.
summary: We were specially invited to meet them because our families have always been closely linked.

author: Jane Austen
text: There was no delay, no waste of time. She was deep in the happiness of such misery, or the misery of such happiness, instantly.
summary: She was overwhelmed right away by a feeling that was painful and joyful at the same time.

author: Jane Austen
text: I always look upon her as able to persuade a person to anything! I am afraid of her, as I have told you before, quite afraid of her, because she is so very clever; but I respect her amazingly, and wish we had such a neighbour at Uppercross.”
summary: I feel intimidated by how smart and persuasive she is, yet I really admire her and wish she lived nearby.

author: Jane Austen
text: Dare not say that man forgets sooner than woman, that his love has an earlier death. I have loved none but you.
summary: I need you to know I have never stopped loving you and never loved anyone else.

author: Jane Austen
text: We cannot help ourselves. We live at home, quiet, confined, and our feelings prey upon us. You are forced on exertion.
summary: I feel stuck at home with nothing to distract me, so my emotions just consume me while you stay busy.

author: Jane Austen
text: I could think of you only as one who had yielded, who had given me up, who had been influenced by any one rather than by me.
summary: I could only see you as someone who gave up on us and let others influence you instead of trusting me.

author: Jane Austen
text: You have always a profession, pursuits, business of some sort or other, to take you back into the world immediately, and continual occupation and change soon weaken impressions.”
summary: You always have your career and daily responsibilities to pull you back out and help you move on quickly.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: It is as well I should ease my mind before I die: what we think little of in health, burdens us at such an hour as the present is to me.
summary: I feel like I need to get this off my chest before I die because it weighs on me now.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: I had a belief she loved me even when she left me: that was an atom of sweet in much bitter. Long as we have been parted, hot tears as I have wept over our separation, I never thought that while I was mourning her, she was loving another! But it is useless grieving.
summary: I held onto thinking she still loved me after we split, and it hurts she moved on while I was still crying.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: I proved it to you in such terms as, I should have thought, would have prevented your ever again alluding to the plan. That you have done so, I regret—for your sake.”
summary: I already told you clearly not to bring up that plan again, and I am disappointed you did.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: I replied, that nothing ailed me save anxiety of mind, which I hoped soon to alleviate.
summary: I told them I was just feeling anxious inside and I hoped I would feel better soon.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: Silence composes the nerves; and as an unbroken hush now reigned again through the whole house, I began to feel the return of slumber. But it was not fated that I should sleep that night.
summary: I was finally calming down in the quiet house and getting sleepy, but I just could not fall asleep that night.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: On sleeping, I continued in dreams the idea of a dark and gusty night.
summary: I fell asleep and kept dreaming about being stuck outside on a dark and stormy night.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: In the midst of my pain of heart and frantic effort of principle, I abhorred myself. I had no solace from self-approbation: none even from self-respect.
summary: I feel heartbroken and hate myself for what I did, finding no comfort in thinking I did the right thing.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: I know I have always loved my own sisters; and I know on what my affection for them is grounded,—respect for their worth and admiration of their talents.
summary: I have always loved my sisters because I deeply respect who they are and admire what they can do.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: I leave no one to regret me much: I have only a father; and he is lately married, and will not miss me. By dying young, I shall escape great sufferings.
summary: I feel like no one will really miss me when I am gone, and dying young would spare me more pain.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: So far I have governed myself thoroughly. I have acted as I inwardly swore I would act; but further might try me beyond my strength.
summary: I have held myself together and kept my promises so far, but I am afraid what comes next will break me.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: And I do not want a stranger—unsympathising, alien, different from me; I want my kindred: those with whom I have full fellow-feeling.
summary: I do not want to be around strangers who do not get me, I want my own people who truly understand me.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: If you have got your feet well warmed, I’ll show you your bedroom. I’ve had the room next to mine prepared for you; it is only a small apartment, but I thought you would like it better than one of the large front chambers: to be sure they have finer furniture, but they are so dreary and solitary, I never sleep in them myself.”
summary: I made up the small cozy room next to mine for you because the big fancy rooms feel too cold and lonely.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: I wish to foster, not to blight—to earn gratitude, not to wring tears of blood—no, nor of brine: my harvest must be in smiles, in endearments, in sweet—That will do. I think I rave in a kind of exquisite delirium.
summary: I want to make you happy and loved, not hurt you, and I feel giddy just thinking about it.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: I have now been married ten years. I know what it is to live entirely for and with what I love best on earth.
summary: I have been married for ten years and I know what it means to live completely for the person I love most.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: Why do I struggle to retain a valueless life? Because I know, or believe, Mr. Rochester is living: and then, to die of want and cold is a fate to which nature cannot submit passively.
summary: I wonder why I keep fighting to survive when I feel worthless, but love makes me refuse to freeze and starve alone.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: I heard you come home that night, Jane, though probably you were not aware that I thought of you or watched for you. The next day I observed you—myself unseen—for half-an-hour, while you played with Adèle in the gallery. It was a snowy day, I recollect, and you could not go out of doors.
summary: I quietly noticed you after you got home and watched you play inside on a snowy day.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: I put out my hand to feel the dark mass before me: I discriminated the rough stones of a low wall—above it, something like palisades, and within, a high and prickly hedge. I groped on.
summary: I felt my way blindly along a stone wall and thorny hedge in the dark.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: Renewing then my courage, and gathering my feeble remains of strength, I pushed on.
summary: I pulled together what little courage and energy I had left and kept going.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: I was at once content and stimulated with what I saw: I liked what I had seen, and wished to see more. Yet, for a long time, I treated you distantly, and sought your company rarely.
summary: I really liked what I saw in you and wanted more, but I acted distant for a while.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: You need not think that because we chanced to be born of the same parents, I shall suffer you to fasten me down by even the feeblest claim: I can tell you this—if the whole human race, ourselves excepted, were swept away, and we two stood alone on the earth, I would leave you in the old world, and betake myself to the new.”
summary: I feel no bond just because we share parents and would leave you behind even if we were alone.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: I hold myself supremely blest—blest beyond what language can express; because I am my husband’s life as fully as he is mine.
summary: I feel incredibly lucky because my partner and I completely belong to each other.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: I felt—yes, idiot that I am—I felt degraded. I doubted I had taken a step which sank instead of raising me in the scale of social existence.
summary: I feel embarrassed and stupid because I worry I made a choice that lowered how others see me.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: I wished you were at home. I came into this room, and the sight of the empty chair and fireless hearth chilled me.
summary: I miss you at home and walking into the empty cold room makes me feel lonely.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: My heart really warmed to the worthy lady as I heard her talk; and I drew my chair a little nearer to her, and expressed my sincere wish that she might find my company as agreeable as she anticipated.
summary: I instantly liked listening to her and moved closer hoping she would enjoy spending time with me.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: Then, too, existence for you must be a scene of continual change and excitement, or else the world is a dungeon: you must be admired, you must be courted, you must be flattered—you must have music, dancing, and society—or you languish, you die away.
summary: You seem to need constant excitement and attention from others or you feel trapped and fade.

author: Emily Brontë
text: Are there any rooms to lodge me in, I wonder? I wish to stay all night.”
summary: I am wondering if there is somewhere I can stay for the night.

author: Emily Brontë
text: Why should you wish to force me to do what I’ll willingly do of myself?”
summary: I feel annoyed that you keep pressuring me to do something I would do anyway.

author: Emily Brontë

summary: I realized that truly loving and grieving one person connects me to everyone else who loves and mourns.

author: Charles Dickens
text: I used to be afraid that I had better have remained your pupil, and almost your child. I used to fear that I was so unsuited to your learning and wisdom.
summary: I often feared I was too immature for you and should have stayed just your student.

author: Charles Dickens
text: I roamed from place to place, carrying my burden with me everywhere. I felt its whole weight now; and I drooped beneath it, and I said in my heart that it could never be lightened.
summary: I keep moving around but I cannot escape this heavy sadness that feels like it will never lift.

author: Charles Dickens
text: I feel my troubles, and they make me contrary. I wish I didn’t feel ‘em, but I do. I wish I could be hardened to ‘em, but I an’t.
summary: I am overwhelmed by my problems and acting cranky, and I wish I could just toughen up and not care.

author: Charles Dickens
text: I was roused by the silent presence of my aunt at my bedside. I felt it in my sleep, as I suppose we all do feel such things.
summary: I woke up sensing someone loving watching over me in bed, the way we all somehow feel that quiet care.

author: Charles Dickens
text: ‘I beg your pardon, sir,’ I faltered. ‘I have never meant to be sullen since I came back.’
summary: I awkwardly apologized for seeming moody since returning and insisted I never meant to act that way.

author: Charles Dickens
text: It’s very gratifying and agreeable to me, I am sure; but don’t you think you could do better? You achieved distinction, you know, when you were with us. You are qualified for many good things.
summary: I told you I appreciate your work but I know you are capable of something greater and better.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: I love to be alone. I never found the companion that was so companionable as solitude.
summary: I really love being alone because no company feels as comforting as my own solitude.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: The light which puts out our eyes is darkness to us. Only that day dawns to which we are awake.
summary: We only truly see and benefit from opportunities when we are awake enough to notice them.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: I left the woods for as good a reason as I went there. Perhaps it seemed to me that I had several more lives to live, and could not spare any more time for that one.
summary: I moved on from a meaningful chapter because I felt I had other lives to explore with my limited time.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: I was as near being resolved into the essence of things as ever I was in my life. I fear my thoughts will not come back to me.
summary: I felt so deeply absorbed in the moment that I worried I might lose my normal way of thinking.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: Let us consider for a moment what most of the trouble and anxiety which I have referred to is about, and how much it is necessary that we be troubled, or, at least, careful.
summary: We should pause and ask ourselves how much of our daily worry is actually necessary or useful.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: I learned this, at least, by my experiment; that if one advances confidently in the direction of his dreams, and endeavors to live the life which he has imagined, he will meet with a success unexpected in common hours.
summary: I learned that chasing my dreams boldly brings surprising success I never expected.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: I did not wish to live what was not life, living is so dear; nor did I wish to practise resignation, unless it was quite necessary.
summary: I do not want to waste my life on empty routines and refuse to just settle.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: I cherish them, I hoe them, early and late I have an eye to them; and this is my day’s work.
summary: I spend my whole day caring for my plants because tending them feels meaningful.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: If the day and the night are such that you greet them with joy, and life emits a fragrance like flowers and sweet-scented herbs, is more elastic, more starry, more immortal,—that is your success. All nature is your congratulation, and you have cause momentarily to bless yourself. The greatest gains and values are farthest from being appreciated. We easily come to doubt if they exist.
summary: True success is waking up joyful each day and feeling deeply connected to the world around you.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: Men frequently say to me, “I should think you would feel lonesome down there, and want to be nearer to folks, rainy and snowy days and nights especially.” I am tempted to reply to such,—This whole earth which we inhabit is but a point in space.
summary: People assume I feel lonely living alone, but I see our vast world very differently.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: Rather than love, than money, than fame, give me truth. I sat at a table where were rich food and wine in abundance, and obsequious attendance, but sincerity and truth were not; and I went away hungry from the inhospitable board.
summary: I would rather have honesty than success, because fancy gatherings without sincerity still leave me feeling empty inside.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: I should not talk so much about myself if there were anybody else whom I knew as well. Unfortunately, I am confined to this theme by the narrowness of my experience.
summary: I only talk about myself so much because I know myself best and my life experience is pretty limited.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: Do not trouble yourself much to get new things, whether clothes or friends. Turn the old; return to them. Things do not change; we change.
summary: I am learning to appreciate what I already have instead of always chasing something new.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: I think that I love society as much as most, and am ready enough to fasten myself like a bloodsucker for the time to any full-blooded man that comes in my way.
summary: I really do enjoy being around people and I will eagerly latch onto anyone interesting who crosses my path.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: I have always been regretting that I was not as wise as the day I was born.
summary: I often feel like I understood life better as a child than I do now as an adult.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: I was actually afraid that I might by that time be doing what is called a good business.
summary: I worry that I will end up trapped in a respectable career I never really wanted.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: You may say the wisest thing you can, old man,—you who have lived seventy years, not without honor of a kind,—I hear an irresistible voice which invites me away from all that. One generation abandons the enterprises of another like stranded vessels.
summary: Even when I respect my elders, I feel pulled to leave their path and start something completely new.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: If I seem to boast more than is becoming, my excuse is that I brag for humanity rather than for myself; and my shortcomings and inconsistencies do not affect the truth of my statement.
summary: If I sound like I am bragging, I am really celebrating what people can do despite my own flaws.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: But to tell the truth, I find myself at present somewhat less particular in these respects.
summary: Honestly, I have started to care less about the standards I used to hold myself to.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: Consider the girls in a factory,—never alone, hardly in their dreams. It would be better if there were but one inhabitant to a square mile, as where I live.
summary: I feel sad for people who are never alone and believe everyone needs much more space and quiet.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: Men who did not know when their visit had terminated, though I went about my business again, answering them from greater and greater remoteness. Men of almost every degree of wit called on me in the migrating season.
summary: I get annoyed when visitors overstay and I have to keep hinting for them to leave.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: I have never felt lonesome, or in the least oppressed by a sense of solitude, but once, and that was a few weeks after I came to the woods, when, for an hour, I doubted if the near neighborhood of man was not essential to a serene and healthy life. To be alone was something unpleasant.
summary: I almost never feel lonely alone, except for one hour when I wondered if I needed people nearby to be okay.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: As I walked on the railroad causeway, I used to wonder at the halo of light around my shadow, and would fain fancy myself one of the elect.
summary: I felt amazed seeing light around my shadow while walking and briefly imagined I was specially chosen.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: My house was not empty though I was gone. It was as if I had left a cheerful housekeeper behind.
summary: I came back to find my empty house still felt warm and cared for, as if someone happy stayed there.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived.
summary: I moved somewhere quiet to focus on what really matters and make sure I actually live before I die.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: While I enjoy the friendship of the seasons I trust that nothing can make life a burden to me. The gentle rain which waters my beans and keeps me in the house to-day is not drear and melancholy, but good for me too.
summary: I feel at peace with the changing seasons and even a rainy day stuck inside feels good to me.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: I do not wish to be any more busy with my hands than is necessary. My head is hands and feet. I feel all my best faculties concentrated in it.
summary: I want to do as little physical work as possible because my real strength is in my thinking.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: I have other affairs to attend to. I came into this world, not chiefly to make this a good place to live in, but to live in it, be it good or bad.
summary: I have my own priorities and I am here to truly live my life, not just fix the world.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: Yet I love to hear their wailing, their doleful responses, trilled along the wood-side; reminding me sometimes of music and singing birds; as if it were the dark and tearful side of music, the regrets and sighs that would fain be sung.
summary: I find comfort in sad distant sounds at night because they feel like beautiful music full of longing.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: They have told me nothing, and probably cannot tell me any thing to the purpose. Here is life, an experiment to a great extent untried by me; but it does not avail me that they have tried it. If I have any experience which I think valuable, I am sure to reflect that this my Mentors said nothing about.
summary: I feel like advice from older people does not help me and I need to learn about life myself.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
I myself but write one or two indicative words for the future,
I but advance a moment only to wheel and hurry back in the darkness.
summary: I feel like I can only leave a small mark for the future before fading back into uncertainty.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
Underneath all is the Expression of love for men and women,
(I swear I have seen enough of mean and impotent modes of expressing
love for men and women,
After this day I take my own modes of expressing love for men and
women.) in myself,
summary: I realize love for other people is underneath everything and I want to show it in my own way.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
Earth! you seem to look for something at my hands,
Say, old top-knot, what do you want?
summary: I feel like the world is waiting on me and I wonder what it actually needs from me.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
I know perfectly well my own egotism,
Know my omnivorous lines and must not write any less,
And would fetch you whoever you are flush with myself.
summary: I know I can be self centered and take up a lot of space, but I want to pull you close to me.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
I resist any thing better than my own diversity,
Breathe the air but leave plenty after me,
And am not stuck up, and am in my place.
summary: I embrace who I am without needing to be better, taking what I need while leaving enough for others.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
Alone I had thought, yet soon a troop gathers around me,
Some walk by my side and some behind, and some embrace my arms or neck,
They the spirits of dear friends dead or alive, thicker they come, a
great crowd, and I in the middle,
summary: I thought I was alone but I feel surrounded by all the friends who love me.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
I ascend to the foretruck,
I take my place late at night in the crow’s-nest,
We sail the arctic sea, it is plenty light enough,
Through the clear atmosphere I stretch around on the wonderful beauty,
summary: I stay up late on a ship taking in the clear bright beauty all around me.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
O past! O happy life! O songs of joy!
In the air, in the woods, over fields,
Loved! loved! loved! loved! loved!
But my mate no more, no more with me!
We two together no more.
summary: I miss the happy days when we were together everywhere and I feel loved and heartbroken now.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
unite with the old ones,
Coming among the new ones myself to be their companion and equal,
coming personally to you now,
Enjoining you to acts, characters, spectacles, with me.
summary: I want to join both old and new friends as an equal and invite you to do things with me.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
time, is provided for in the inherences of things,
I do not think Life provides for all and for Time and Space, but I
believe Heavenly Death provides for all.
summary: I have come to believe that death, not life, is what finally takes care of everything.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
Nations once powerful, now reduced, withdrawn, or desolate,
I dare not proceed till I respectfully credit what you have left
wafted hither,
I have perused it, own it is admirable, (moving awhile among it,)
summary: I pause to honor the great work left behind by those who came before me.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
The night in silence under many a star,
The ocean shore and the husky whispering wave whose voice I know,
And the soul turning to thee O vast and well-veil’d death,
And the body gratefully nestling close to thee.
summary: I stand alone at night by the ocean and feel strangely comforted by the thought of death.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
As the time draws nigh glooming a cloud,
A dread beyond of I know not what darkens me.
summary: I feel a dark dread growing inside me as something unknown gets closer.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
Failing to fetch me at first keep encouraged,
Missing me one place search another,
I stop somewhere waiting for you.
summary: If you cannot find me at first, keep looking because I am waiting for you somewhere.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
That you hide in these shifting forms of life, for reasons, and that
they are mainly for you,
That you beyond them come forth to remain, the real reality,
That behind the mask of materials you patiently wait, no matter how long,
summary: You hide behind everyday changes while your true self waits patiently to emerge.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
Who was to know what should come home to me?
Who knows but I am enjoying this?
Who knows, for all the distance, but I am as good as looking at you
now, for all you cannot see me?
summary: I feel strangely close to you right now even though we are far apart and you cannot see me.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
I do not know what you are for, (I do not know what I am for myself,
nor what any thing is for,)
But I will search carefully for it even in being foil’d,
In defeat, poverty, misconception, imprisonment--for they too are great.
summary: I do not know my purpose yet, but I keep looking for meaning even when life knocks me down.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
Pale, silent, stern, what could I say to that long-accrued retribution?
Could I wish humanity different?
Could I wish the people made of wood and stone?
Or that there be no justice in destiny or time?
summary: I stand speechless before the consequences we earned and wonder if I could ever want people to feel nothing.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
Open mouth of my soul uttering gladness,
Eyes of my soul seeing perfection,
Natural life of me faithfully praising things,
Corroborating forever the triumph of things.
summary: I feel wide open with happiness and see goodness everywhere I look in my everyday life.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
Once I pass’d through a populous city imprinting my brain for future
use with its shows, architecture, customs, traditions,
Yet now of all that city I remember only a woman I casually met
there who detain’d me for love of me,
summary: I visited a busy city once, but all I really remember is a brief loving connection with a stranger.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
O I see now that life cannot exhibit all to me, as the day cannot,
I see that I am to wait for what will be exhibited by death.
summary: I realize life cannot show me everything and I will have to wait until death for the rest.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
Wrench’d and sweaty--calm and cool then my body becomes,
I sleep--I sleep long.
summary: I feel worn out and overheated but finally grow calm and fall into a deep long sleep.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
Felt their arms on my neck as I stood, or the negligent leaning of
their flesh against me as I sat,
Saw many I loved in the street or ferry-boat or public assembly, yet
never told them a word,
summary: I remember feeling close to people I loved in crowds but never finding the courage to speak to them.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
swamp-cedars,
Solitary, singing in the West, I strike up for a New World.
summary: I feel alone yet hopeful as I start singing to welcome a fresh and different future.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
I match my spirit against yours you orbs, growths, mountains, brutes,
Copious as you are I absorb you all in myself, and become the master myself,
America isolated yet embodying all, what is it finally except myself?
These States, what are they except myself?
summary: I feel huge and confident, taking in nature and my whole country as if they all live inside me.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
Offspring of ignorant and poor, boys apprenticed to trades,
Young fellows working on farms and old fellows working on farms,
Sailor-men, merchant-men, coasters, immigrants,
All these I see, but nigher and farther the same I see,
None shall escape me and none shall wish to escape me.
summary: I see workers and newcomers everywhere around me and feel deeply connected to every single one of them.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
That shadow my likeness that goes to and fro seeking a livelihood,
chattering, chaffering,
How often I find myself standing and looking at it where it flits,
How often I question and doubt whether that is really me;
But among my lovers and caroling these songs,
O I never doubt whether that is really me.
summary: I sometimes watch myself hustling for money and wonder if that is really me, but with people I love singing I feel truly myself.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
Perhaps to engage in time in still more dreadful contests, dangers,
Longer campaigns and crises, labors beyond all others,)
Around me I hear that eclat of the world, politics, produce,
The announcements of recognized things, science,
summary: I feel overwhelmed by news of politics and work while bracing for even harder struggles ahead in my life.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
Creeds and schools in abeyance,
Retiring back a while sufficed at what they are, but never forgotten,
I harbor for good or bad, I permit to speak at every hazard,
Nature without check with original energy.
summary: I am setting aside old beliefs for now and letting raw nature and honest energy speak freely through me.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
Spontaneous me, Nature,
The loving day, the mounting sun, the friend I am happy with,
The arm of my friend hanging idly over my shoulder,
The hillside whiten’d with blossoms of the mountain ash,
summary: I am out on a bright day with a close friend beside me, happy and surrounded by blooming hills.

author: Herman Melville
text: What’s all this fuss I have been making about, thought I to myself—the man’s a human being just as I am: he has just as much reason to fear me, as I have to be afraid of him.
summary: I realized my anxiety about a stranger was silly since we are both just human and probably nervous around each other.

author: Herman Melville
text: And much this way it was with me. I said nothing, and tried to think nothing.
summary: I just shut down completely and tried to empty my mind rather than deal with what was happening around me.

author: Herman Melville
text: I have striven to be Thine, more than to be this world’s, or mine own.
summary: I have tried hard to live for something greater than worldly success or my own selfish wants.

author: Herman Melville
text: But my whole clock’s run down; my heart the all-controlling weight, I have no key to lift again.
summary: I feel completely worn out inside, like my energy is gone and I cannot restart myself anymore.

author: Herman Melville
text: And now I’m ordered to make a life-buoy of it. It’s like turning an old coat; going to bring the flesh on the other side now.
summary: I was told to repurpose something grim for survival, flipping its use completely inside out.

author: Herman Melville
text: The path to my fixed purpose is laid with iron rails, whereon my soul is grooved to run. Over unsounded gorges, through the rifled hearts of mountains, under torrents’ beds, unerringly I rush!
summary: I feel locked onto my goal like a train and cannot stop rushing forward no matter what.

author: Herman Melville
text: But that night, in particular, a strange (and ever since inexplicable) thing occurred to me. Starting from a brief standing sleep, I was horribly conscious of something fatally wrong.
summary: I woke up suddenly that night with a horrible feeling that something was terribly wrong.

author: Herman Melville
text: Think of Death and the Judgment then? No! no time to think about Death then.
summary: In a moment of crisis, there is no time to think about death or judgment.

author: Herman Melville
text: Dry heat upon my brow? Oh! time was, when as the sunrise nobly spurred me, so the sunset soothed. No more. This lovely light, it lights not me; all loveliness is anguish to me, since I can ne’er enjoy.
summary: I used to feel energized by mornings and comforted by evenings, but now beauty only hurts because I cannot enjoy it.

author: Herman Melville
text: And somehow, at the time, I felt a sympathy and a sorrow for him, but for I don’t know what, unless it was the cruel loss of his leg.
summary: I felt strange sympathy and sadness for him, probably because of the terrible injury he had suffered.

author: Herman Melville
text: But all remained still as before. I began to grow alarmed. I had allowed him such abundant time; I thought he might have had an apoplectic fit.
summary: I waited too long with no answer and started fearing something terrible had happened to him.

author: Herman Melville
text: A muffled silence reigned, only broken at times by the shrieks of the storm. Each silent worshipper seemed purposely sitting apart from the other, as if each silent grief were insular and incommunicable.
summary: Strangers sit alone together in the storm, each trapped inside private grief.

author: Herman Melville
text: So strongly and metaphysically did I conceive of my situation then, that while earnestly watching his motions, I seemed distinctly to perceive that my own individuality was now merged in a joint stock company of two; that my free will had received a mortal wound; and that another’s mistake or misfortune might plunge innocent me into unmerited disaster and death.
summary: I feel trapped because my life now depends completely on someone else and their mistakes could ruin me.

author: Herman Melville
text: You have got out insurances on our lives and want to murder us all, and pocket the proceeds, do ye?”
summary: I am convinced you bought life insurance on us because you plan to kill us for money.

author: Herman Melville
text: And that’s the reason I never would work for lonely widow old women ashore, when I kept my job-shop in the Vineyard; they might have taken it into their lonely old heads to run off with me.
summary: I avoid working for lonely older women because I joke they would all fall for me.

author: Herman Melville
text: It was a very dubious-looking, nay, a very dark and dismal night, bitingly cold and cheerless. I knew no one in the place.
summary: I am alone in an unfamiliar place on a cold bleak night and feel completely isolated.

author: Herman Melville
text: For my part, I abominate all honorable respectable toils, trials, and tribulations of every kind whatsoever. It is quite as much as I can do to take care of myself, without taking care of ships, barques, brigs, schooners, and what not.
summary: I just want to handle my own life and hate the idea of taking on respectable stressful responsibilities for others.

author: Herman Melville
text: I would be free as air; and I’m down in the whole world’s books. I am so rich, I could have given bid for bid with the wealthiest Prætorians at the auction of the Roman empire (which was the world’s); and yet I owe for the flesh in the tongue I brag with.
summary: I dream of being totally free but feel broke and trapped by debts despite imagining myself as wealthy.

author: Herman Melville
text: Supper over, the company went back to the bar-room, when, knowing not what else to do with myself, I resolved to spend the rest of the evening as a looker on.
summary: I feel awkward and left out tonight so I just sit back and watch everyone else have fun.

author: Herman Melville
text: Peace and satisfaction, thought Flask, have for ever departed from my stomach.
summary: He feels sick and uneasy in his stomach with no peace or comfort left.

author: Herman Melville
text: Though but a point at best; whencesoe’er I came; wheresoe’er I go; yet while I earthly live, the queenly personality lives in me, and feels her royal rights. But war is pain, and hate is woe.
summary: I may be tiny in the universe, but I still feel my own dignity and know fighting only brings pain.

author: Herman Melville
text: What of that? Who’s afraid of black’s afraid of me! I’m quarried out of it!
summary: I am not ashamed of who I am, so if my background scares you then you are scared of me.

author: Herman Melville
text: What then? I’ve part changed my flesh since that time, why not my mind?
summary: My body has changed so much over time, so I wonder why my thoughts should not change too.

author: Herman Melville
text: Methinks my body is but the lees of my better being. In fact take my body who will, take it I say, it is not me.
summary: I feel like my body is just leftover waste and my real self is something separate from it.

author: Herman Melville
text: Only pull, and keep pulling; nothing more. Crack all your backbones, and bite your knives in two—that’s all.
summary: The job is simple and brutal, just keep hauling hard until your body nearly breaks.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I am too much concentrated on myself. My own personality has become a burden to me. I want to escape, to go away, to forget.
summary: I feel trapped inside my own thoughts and just want to get away and forget everything for a while.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I thought how tragic it would be if you were wasted. For there is such a little time that your youth will last—such a little time.
summary: I worry you are wasting your youth because it will be gone before you realize it.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: When I came on to-night, I could not understand how it was that everything had gone from me. I thought that I was going to be wonderful. I found that I could do nothing.
summary: I walked onstage expecting to be amazing but suddenly lost everything and completely froze up.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: The moment I met you I saw that you were quite unconscious of what you really are, of what you really might be.
summary: I saw your hidden potential right away even though you could not see it in yourself yet.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I loved you because you were marvellous, because you had genius and intellect, because you realized the dreams of great poets and gave shape and substance to the shadows of art. You have thrown it all away.
summary: I loved you for your brilliant talent, but now I feel you have wasted everything that made you special.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Some one has killed herself for love of you. I wish that I had ever had such an experience. It would have made me in love with love for the rest of my life. The people who have adored me—there have not been very many, but there have been some—have always insisted on living on, long after I had ceased to care for them, or they to care for me.
summary: I wish someone had loved me so intensely it ruined them, because my own admirers just hung around after the spark died.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I believe my house is somewhere about here, but I don’t feel at all certain about it.
summary: I am wandering around my own neighborhood feeling lost and unsure which house is actually mine.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I was a schoolboy when you knew me. I am a man now. I have new passions, new thoughts, new ideas.
summary: I am not the kid you remember anymore and I have grown into new desires and ways of thinking.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Something seemed to tell me that I was on the verge of a terrible crisis in my life. I had a strange feeling that fate had in store for me exquisite joys and exquisite sorrows. I grew afraid and turned to quit the room.
summary: I suddenly felt I was about to face something huge with intense happiness and pain, so fear made me want to leave.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Be afraid of nothing.... A new Hedonism—that is what our century wants. You might be its visible symbol. With your personality there is nothing you could not do.
summary: Someone tells me to live boldly without fear because I could inspire others and achieve anything.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Live! Live the wonderful life that is in you! Let nothing be lost upon you.
summary: I want to fully embrace my life and not waste any experience or feeling.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: But you were simple, natural, and affectionate then. You were the most unspoiled creature in the whole world. Now, I don’t know what has come over you.
summary: I miss how genuine and kind you used to be because you feel like a different person now.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I want the dead lovers of the world to hear our laughter and grow sad. I want a breath of our passion to stir their dust into consciousness, to wake their ashes into pain.
summary: I want our love to be so joyful and intense that even past lovers would envy us.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I’ll have it off the bunch in a moment. But you don’t think of living up there, sir, and you so comfortable here?”
summary: I am confused why you would want to move when you are already settled and comfortable here.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Good heavens! what a life that is! You have gone from corruption to corruption, and now you have culminated in crime. In doing what I am going to do—what you force me to do—it is not of your life that I am thinking.”
summary: I am horrified by how far you have fallen and feel forced to act for reasons beyond you.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I wanted to have you all to myself. I was only happy when I was with you. When you were away from me, you were still present in my art....
summary: I only feel truly happy when I am with you and I miss you even in my work.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I want you to lead such a life as will make the world respect you. I want you to have a clean name and a fair record. I want you to get rid of the dreadful people you associate with.
summary: I want you to clean up your life and stop hanging out with people who bring you down.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: You are simply jealous and unkind. Ah! I wish you would fall in love. Love makes people good, and what you said was wicked.”
summary: I think you are being jealous and mean and falling in love would make you kinder.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: You filled me with a wild desire to know everything about life. For days after I met you, something seemed to throb in my veins.
summary: I felt intensely alive and curious about everything after meeting you for the first time.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: But I can’t help myself. You are the one man who is able to save me. I am forced to bring you into the matter.
summary: I feel helpless on my own and need you to help me through this serious problem.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: You have everything in the world that a man can want. There is no one who would not be delighted to change places with you.”
summary: You have an amazing life that anyone would envy right now and always.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: What could they know of love such as ours? Take me away, Dorian—take me away with you, where we can be quite alone. I hate the stage. I might mimic a passion that I do not feel, but I cannot mimic one that burns me like fire.
summary: I am so in love that I want to run away together and quit pretending at work.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: When I leave town now I never tell my people where I am going. If I did, I would lose all my pleasure.
summary: I keep my trips secret from family because sneaking off alone makes them more fun.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I wonder what the rest of your life will be. Don’t spoil it by renunciations. At present you are a perfect type. Don’t make yourself incomplete.
summary: I see so much promise in you and I do not want you to waste your future.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: If he is dead, I don’t want to think about him. Death is the only thing that ever terrifies me. I hate it.”
summary: I refuse to think about someone who might have died because death truly frightens me.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: You are not stronger—you are too much afraid of life—but you are better.
summary: You are holding yourself back from life out of fear even though you are a good person.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: The two people who could have described you were dead. I knew nothing of you but the pet name she used to call you. I heard it to-night by chance. Make your peace with God, for to-night you are going to die.”
summary: I finally found you after everyone else is gone and now I am going to kill you tonight.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: And you must not say these extravagant things to me. You don’t know everything about me. I think that if you did, even you would turn from me.
summary: I feel unworthy of your praise and fear you would leave if you knew my real past.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I will work so hard and try to improve. Don’t be cruel to me, because I love you better than anything in the world. After all, it is only once that I have not pleased you. But you are quite right, Dorian.
summary: I am begging you not to be harsh because I love you and promise to do better.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I am nothing of the kind. I know I am not. And yet I must admit that this thing that has happened does not affect me as it should.
summary: I know I am not a bad person but I feel strangely numb about something serious that happened.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Three more months go over and my mother dies. No one knew how deeply I loved and honoured her.
summary: I lost my mom a few months later and nobody realized how much I truly loved and respected her.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: If any love is shown us we should recognise that we are quite unworthy of it. Nobody is worthy to be loved.
summary: I feel like I do not deserve kindness when it comes and that no one really earns love.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I hope to be at least a month with my friends, and to gain peace and balance, and a less troubled heart, and a sweeter mood. I have a strange longing for the great simple primeval things, such as the sea, to me no less of a mother than the Earth.
summary: I want to spend time with friends to heal and I crave simple natural things like the ocean for comfort.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: But to have continued the same life would have been wrong because it would have been limiting. I had to pass on.
summary: I knew staying in my old life would hold me back, so I had to move forward.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I can, at any rate, merely proceed on the lines of my own development, and, accepting all that has happened to me, make myself worthy of it.
summary: I will keep growing as myself and accept my past so I can become worthy of it.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: And so, indeed, I went out, and so I lived. My only mistake was that I confined myself so exclusively to the trees of what seemed to me the sun-lit side of the garden, and shunned the other side for its shadow and its gloom.
summary: I realize I lived only chasing the good times and avoided facing any pain or darkness.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Outside, the day may be blue and gold, but the light that creeps down through the thickly-muffled glass of the small iron-barred window beneath which one sits is grey and niggard. It is always twilight in one's cell, as it is always twilight in one's heart.
summary: Even on a bright day outside, prison makes everything feel dim and sad inside too.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I, and such as I am, have hardly any right to air and sun. Our presence taints the pleasures of others. We are unwelcome when we reappear.
summary: I feel like I do not belong outside anymore and that my presence ruins things for others.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: People must adopt some attitude towards me, and so pass judgment, both on themselves and me.
summary: I know people feel forced to judge me, which says as much about them as me.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: When I say that I am convinced of these things I speak with too much pride.
summary: I admit that even saying I have learned my lesson sounds arrogant and proud.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I see new developments in art and life, each one of which is a fresh mode of perfection. I long to live so that I can explore what is no less than a new world to me.
summary: I feel excited about new possibilities opening up and I want more time to explore this unfamiliar chapter of life.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: And if I then am not ashamed of my punishment, as I hope not to be, I shall be able to think, and walk, and live with freedom.
summary: I hope I can stop feeling ashamed about what I went through and finally live and think freely again.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Now I find hidden somewhere away in my nature something that tells me that nothing in the whole world is meaningless, and suffering least of all.
summary: I am starting to believe that everything has purpose, especially the pain I have been carrying inside me.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I am far more of an individualist than I ever was. Nothing seems to me of the smallest value except what one gets out of oneself. My nature is seeking a fresh mode of self-realisation.
summary: I have become more independent and I only trust what I learn about myself as I search for a new way to grow.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I was a man who stood in symbolic relations to the art and culture of my age. I had realised this for myself at the very dawn of my manhood, and had forced my age to realise it afterwards.
summary: I once believed I represented my generation creatively and I made everyone else finally see that too.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I hope to live long enough and to produce work of such a character that I shall be able at the end of my days to say, 'Yes! this is just where the artistic life leads a man!'
summary: I hope I live long enough to make work that proves my creative life was worth it.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I grew careless of the lives of others. I took pleasure where it pleased me, and passed on. I forgot that every little action of the common day makes or unmakes character, and that therefore what one has done in the secret chamber one has some day to cry aloud on the housetop. I ceased to be lord over myself.
summary: I selfishly chased pleasure and lost self control, forgetting small daily choices shape who I become.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: She will hang the night with stars so that I may walk abroad in the darkness without stumbling, and send the wind over my footprints so that none may track me to my hurt: she will cleanse me in great waters, and with bitter herbs make me whole.
summary: I hope to be protected, forgiven, and healed so I can move forward without fear of my past.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: They loved the trees for the shadow that they cast, and the forest for its silence at noon.
summary: They find comfort in the shade of trees and the quiet stillness of the forest at midday.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: In many ways I had been its enemy, but I found it waiting for me as a friend.
summary: I once fought against something, but it welcomed me back with kindness when I returned.

author: Kate Chopin
text: I’m tired looking after that big house. It never seemed like mine, anyway—like home.
summary: I am exhausted from keeping up this big house that never really felt like my home.

author: Kate Chopin
text: I want my music, my books, my companions. If I had known no other life but this one of privation, I suppose it would be different. If I had to live this life, I should make the best of it.
summary: I miss my music, my books, and my friends, and this stripped-down life feels hard because I know what I am missing.

author: Kate Chopin
text: But I hope you’ll forgive me this once—this very first break. Why, what’s the matter?”
summary: I am apologizing for messing up for the first time and feeling confused about why you are so upset.

author: Kate Chopin
text: I must live another life; the life I lived before. I want to know things that are happening from day to day over the world, and hear them talked about.
summary: I need to get back to my old life where I felt connected to what is happening in the world around me.

author: Kate Chopin
text: I’m not going to be forced into doing things. I don’t want to go abroad. I want to be let alone.
summary: I refuse to be pushed into plans I do not want and just need everyone to leave me alone right now.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I have said of myself that I was one who stood in symbolic relations to the art and culture of my age.
summary: I feel like my life and work really captured what my generation cared about.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: The only people I would care to be with now are artists and people who have suffered: those who know what beauty is, and those who know what sorrow is: nobody else interests me. Nor am I making any demands on life.
summary: I only want to be around creative people and those who have been through pain like I have.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I have given too many to care about them. That side of life is over for me, very fortunately, I dare say.
summary: I am glad that exhausting part of my social life is finally over for good.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Perhaps there may come into my art also, no less than into my life, a still deeper note, one of greater unity of passion, and directness of impulse.
summary: I hope my pain will make my work and my life more honest and passionate going forward.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I had lost my name, my position, my happiness, my freedom, my wealth. I was a prisoner and a pauper.
summary: I have lost my reputation, comfort, and freedom and now feel like I have nothing left.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: And I really shall have no difficulty. When you really want love you will find it waiting for you.
summary: I feel confident that if I truly open myself to love, it will come to me.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Now I am approaching life from a completely new standpoint, and even to conceive happiness is often extremely difficult for me.
summary: I am starting over in life and I can barely even imagine what being happy would look like.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I can be perfectly happy by myself. With freedom, flowers, books, and the moon, who could not be perfectly happy?
summary: I can be completely happy on my own with simple freedom and beautiful small things around me.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I had no idea that it was one of the special things that the Fates had in store for me: that for a whole year of my life, indeed, I was to do little else. But so has my portion been meted out to me; and during the last few months I have, after terrible difficulties and struggles, been able to comprehend some of the lessons hidden in the heart of pain.
summary: I never expected to spend a whole year suffering, but I am finally starting to understand what that pain taught me.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: People used to say of me that I was too individualistic. I must be far more of an individualist than ever I was. I must get far more out of myself than ever I got, and ask far less of the world than ever I asked.
summary: I realize I need to rely more on myself and expect much less from other people going forward.

author: Kate Chopin
text: I never was so exhausted in my life. But it isn’t unpleasant. A thousand emotions have swept through me to-night.
summary: I feel completely drained tonight but in a good way after feeling so much all at once.

author: Kate Chopin
text: I don’t like it. I don’t understand your motive for silence and mystery, never saying a word to me about it this morning.”
summary: I feel hurt and confused that you kept secrets from me instead of telling me this morning.

author: Kate Chopin
text: But some way I can’t convince myself that I am. I must think about it.”
summary: I cannot quite believe something about myself right now and need time to think it through.

author: Kate Chopin
text: I was really not conscious of thinking of anything; but perhaps I can retrace my thoughts.”
summary: I zoned out completely just now and I am trying to remember what was going through my mind.

author: Kate Chopin
text: A certain light was beginning to dawn dimly within her,—the light which, showing the way, forbids it.
summary: She is starting to understand a truth about herself that both guides her and holds her back.

author: Kate Chopin
text: I cannot judge of that myself, but I feel that I have gained in ease and confidence.
