summary: I feel like I am finally becoming more comfortable and confident in myself lately.

author: Kate Chopin
text: I miss the poor fellow myself, my dear. I liked to see him and to hear him about the place—the only Lebrun who is worth a pinch of salt. He comes to see me often in the city.
summary: I really miss having that kind guy around the house and I am glad he still visits me in town.

author: Kate Chopin
text: I know I shall like it, like the feeling of freedom and independence.”
summary: I am excited to live on my own because I know I will love feeling free and independent.

author: Kate Chopin
text: What’s the use? Why should you bother thinking about it when I can tell you what manner of woman you are.”
summary: I feel like telling you exactly who you are instead of letting you figure it out yourself.

author: Kate Chopin
text: One has to think of the children some time or other; the sooner the better.”
summary: Parents cannot ignore their kids forever and need to start putting them first soon.

author: George Eliot
text: If I did anything it would be a little travelling in the tobacco line—or something of that sort, which takes a man into agreeable company. But not without an independence to fall back upon. That’s what I want: I’m not so strong as I was, Nick, though I’ve got more color than you. I want an independence.”
summary: I want a secure backup income so I can do enjoyable social work without worrying as I get older.

author: George Eliot
text: You must remember that you have not done what he thought best for you.
summary: You ignored what someone who cared about you wanted and now live with that disappointment.

author: George Eliot
text: I am no longer sure enough of myself—I mean of what it would be possible for me to do under the changed circumstances of my life.
summary: I feel unsure of myself and what I can still do now that my life has changed so much.

author: George Eliot
text: I have never forgotten any one whom I once knew. My life has never been crowded, and seems not likely to be so.
summary: I remember everyone I have known because my life has always been quiet and lonely.

author: George Eliot
text: I cannot bear to think that any one should die and leave no love behind.”
summary: I am heartbroken by the idea of dying without leaving any love behind me.

author: Kate Chopin
text: I know something of such things. I might help you with a stray suggestion or two.”
summary: I have been through this before and I think I could offer you some helpful advice.

author: Kate Chopin
text: A terrible fear was upon her,—the fear of the world beyond the bayou, the morbid and insane dread she had been under since childhood.
summary: She feels overwhelmed by a lifelong fear of the unfamiliar world outside the small place she knows.

author: Kate Chopin
text: The music filled the room. It floated out upon the night, over the housetops, the crescent of the river, losing itself in the silence of the upper air.
summary: Beautiful music fills the room and drifts out into the night until it fades into silence.

author: Kate Chopin
text: You seem to act without a certain amount of reflection which is necessary in this life.
summary: You act too impulsively without thinking carefully the way adult life requires.

author: Kate Chopin
text: I will let you off this time. It is really too hot to think, especially to think about thinking.”
summary: I am letting you off today because it is too hot and I cannot bother to overthink things.

author: Kate Chopin
text: I feel as if I wanted to be doing something. What do you think of them?
summary: I feel restless and unfulfilled and I am asking someone else what they think I should do.

author: Kate Chopin
text: It was you who awoke me last summer out of a life-long, stupid dream. Oh! you have made me so unhappy with your indifference. Oh! I have suffered, suffered!
summary: I finally woke up last summer because of you, and then your indifference left me suffering and heartbroken.

author: Kate Chopin
text: I’ve been working like a machine, and feeling like a lost soul. There was nothing interesting.”
summary: I have been working nonstop on autopilot and feeling empty because nothing in my life feels meaningful.

author: Kate Chopin
text: It is like a night in a dream. The people about me are like some uncanny, half-human beings.
summary: I feel like I am in a strange dream where everyone around me seems unreal and distant.

author: Kate Chopin
text: There are periods of despondency and suffering which take possession of me. But I don’t want anything but my own way.
summary: I go through dark spells of sadness that overwhelm me, yet I still refuse to live any way but mine.

author: George Eliot
text: But many things have told against me in my practice, and it really just now has ebbed to a low point. I may recover it, but in the mean time we must pull up—we must change our way of living.
summary: My work has really slowed down lately so we need to cut back until things pick up again.

author: George Eliot
text: Remember, you see me in my home, just as it has been since I was a child.
summary: I want you to know this is my childhood home exactly as it has always been.

author: George Eliot
text: I do like to be spoken to as if I had common-sense. I really often feel as if I could understand a little more than I ever hear even from young gentlemen who have been to college.”
summary: I wish people would treat me like I am smart because I know I can understand more than they think.

author: George Eliot
text: These people might not take that high view of you which I have always taken, as an alter ego, a right hand—though I always looked forward to your doing something else.
summary: I have always valued you highly as my closest helper even though I hoped you would move on.

author: George Eliot
text: My father died soon after, and my mother and I were well taken care of.
summary: After my dad passed away, my mom and I were lucky to have people looking out for us.

author: Kate Chopin
text: The night was not a dark one, for the sky was clear and the moon resplendent.
summary: I am outside on a clear bright night with the moon lighting up everything around me.

author: Kate Chopin
text: I didn’t get so deep in their regard. I fear they made more impression on me than I made on them.”
summary: I worry that I cared about these people far more than they ever cared about me.

author: Kate Chopin
text: Do you no longer love me? Have we not been happy together, you and I?”
summary: I am asking my partner whether they still love me after all our happiness together.

author: Kate Chopin
text: I’ve grown used to seeing you, to having you with me all the time, and your action seems unfriendly, even unkind.
summary: I got so used to having you around that your distance now feels cold and hurtful to me.

author: Kate Chopin
text: That is wanting a good deal, of course, when you have to trample upon the lives, the hearts, the prejudices of others—but no matter—still, I shouldn’t want to trample upon the little lives. Oh! I don’t know what I’m saying, Doctor.
summary: I want freedom for myself but I feel guilty about hurting others and I feel totally confused.

author: George Eliot
text: You hearken, missy. It’s three o’clock in the morning, and I’ve got all my faculties as well as ever I had in my life. I know all my property, and where the money’s put out, and everything.
summary: I am wide awake late at night insisting I am still sharp and know exactly where all my money is.

author: George Eliot
text: But I shall not give up my liberty for a dirty annuity. I shall come and go where I like. Perhaps it may suit me to stay away, and correspond with a friend; perhaps not. Have you the money with you?”
summary: I refuse to trade my freedom for money and will live where I want while staying in touch.

author: George Eliot
text: He said you could never think well of him again. But now I have told you, and he cannot reproach me any more.”
summary: I finally told you the painful truth he feared would ruin him so I can stop feeling guilty.

author: George Eliot
text: I know of nothing to make me vacillate. If I changed my mind, it must be because of something important and entirely new to me.”
summary: I feel completely sure of my decision and will only change it for something truly new.

author: George Eliot
text: But it shall not be through me. He has never had any love for me—I know he has not—he has always thought slightly of me.
summary: I feel he has never really loved or respected me and I refuse to take the blame.

author: George Eliot
text: It is my life. I have found it out, and cannot part with it. I have always been finding out my religion since I was a little girl. I used to pray so much—now I hardly ever pray.
summary: I finally figured out what I believe, and even though I rarely pray now I cannot let it go.

author: George Eliot
text: I am not afraid of talking to our old neighbors. But I am really afraid of you.”
summary: I feel comfortable around everyone else, but you intimidate me in a way I cannot hide.

author: George Eliot
text: The more you say anything, the less I shall believe it. The more you want me to do a thing, the more reason I shall have for never doing it.
summary: I push back harder whenever you pressure me, and your convincing only makes me trust you less.

author: George Eliot
text: I used to feel about that, even when I was a little girl; and it always seemed to me that the use I should like to make of my life would be to help some one who did great works, so that his burthen might be lighter.”
summary: Since childhood I have wanted my life to matter by supporting someone doing important work.

author: George Eliot
text: I can only tell you about myself, that I have always been too lax, and have been uneasy in consequence.”
summary: I have to admit I have always been too easy on myself and it leaves me feeling restless.

author: George Eliot
text: I told your father everything, and he was very kind; he treated me as if I were his son.
summary: I finally opened up to your dad and I feel so grateful he welcomed me like family.

author: George Eliot
text: “Yes, yes, I agree with you—I quite take that point of view. I should put it in that light. I should support Grey, you know.
summary: I totally see your point and I am ready to back that side too.

author: George Eliot
text: My own establishment is broken up now my wife’s dead. I’ve no particular attachment to any spot; I would as soon settle hereabout as anywhere.”
summary: Since my wife died my home is gone and I feel rootless enough to live anywhere now.

author: George Eliot
text: I was not quite sure when you first came that you were the same man. I was very glad when I found that you were.
summary: At first I did not recognize you, but I felt so happy realizing you had not changed.

author: George Eliot
text: You always did, and you always will, when you set about doing as you please.
summary: You always do exactly what you want, and I know you will never change that habit.

author: George Eliot
text: It has taken such deep root in me—my gratitude to him for always loving me best, and minding so much if I hurt myself, from the time when we were very little.
summary: I feel deeply thankful for someone who has loved and looked out for me since we were kids.

author: George Eliot
text: I try not to have desires merely for myself, because they may not be good for others, and I have too much already. I only told you, that you might know quite well how my days go at Lowick.”
summary: I try not to want things just for myself and I was just explaining what my daily life is like.

author: George Eliot
text: I thought it would always be part of my life to long for home, and losing that grievance makes me feel rather empty: I suppose it served instead of sense to fill up my mind?”
summary: I always expected to miss home, and now that I do not, I feel empty and directionless.

author: George Eliot
text: I am in no fear of you. Such tales as that will never tempt my tongue.”
summary: I am not afraid of you and I will never be talked into spreading those stories.

author: George Eliot
text: You and I cannot have opposite interests. I cannot part my happiness from yours.
summary: My happiness is completely tied to yours, so we could never want different things.

author: George Eliot
text: It was my father’s dying wish that I should try and get it back again whenever I could; it was in his family for five generations. I promised my father; and besides that, I’m attached to the place. I shall never like any other so well.
summary: I promised my dying dad I would win back our old family home because I still love it.

author: George Eliot
text: But now I must leave you to your own choice. You wish to be independent; you told me so after my father’s death.
summary: I am letting you make your own choice now because you said you want to be independent.

author: George Eliot
text: But I begin to think there can never come much happiness to me from loving; I have always had so much pain mingled with it.
summary: I am starting to feel like love will never really make me happy because it always hurts.

author: George Eliot
text: It is like death. I must part with everything I cared for when I was a child.
summary: I feel like something in me is dying because I have to give up everything from my childhood.

author: George Eliot
text: The new life I have found in caring for your joy and sorrow more than for what is directly my own, has transformed the spirit of rebellious murmuring into that willing endurance which is the birth of strong sympathy.
summary: I feel more at peace now because I focus on supporting you instead of only thinking about myself.

author: George Eliot
text: I think I get worse as I get older, more selfish. That seems very dreadful.”
summary: I worry that I am becoming more selfish as I age and it frightens me.

author: George Eliot
text: The place where you are is the one where my mind must live, wherever I might travel. And remember that I am unchangeably yours,—yours not with selfish wishes, but with a devotion that excludes such wishes.
summary: No matter where I go my thoughts stay with you because I am completely devoted to you.

author: George Eliot
text: I do always think too much of my own feelings, and not enough of others’,—not enough of yours.
summary: I realize I focus too much on my own emotions and do not consider yours enough.

author: George Eliot
text: I have never felt that I was right in giving way about seeing you, though it has been so precious to me in some ways; and now the fear comes upon me strongly again, that it will lead to evil.”
summary: I feel guilty for continuing to see you even though I cherish it because I fear it will end badly.

author: George Eliot
text: Let no self-reproach weigh on you because of me. It is I who should rather reproach myself for having urged my feelings upon you, and hurried you into words that you have felt as fetters.
summary: Please do not blame yourself for my sake since I pushed my feelings on you too fast.

author: George Eliot
text: It’ll give you more importance, and prepare you better for taking some of the anxiety off my shoulders by and by. I’m equal to a good deal o’ work at present, thank God; but I’m getting older,—there’s no denying that.
summary: I am still able to work hard but I know I am aging and want you to step up soon.

author: George Eliot
text: I am so young, so healthy. How shall I have patience and strength? Am I to struggle and fall and repent again?
summary: I feel young and healthy yet I worry I lack the strength to avoid failing again.

author: George Eliot
text: We never thought of being alone together again; it has all been done by others.
summary: We never expected to end up alone together again but other people somehow brought us back.

author: George Eliot
text: She felt lonely, cut off from Philip,—the only person who had ever seemed to love her devotedly, as she had always longed to be loved.
summary: She feels lonely and cut off from the one person whose deep love felt like what she always wanted.

author: George Eliot
text: I want to make amends. I will endure anything. I want to be kept from doing wrong again.”
summary: I want to make up for my mistakes and will suffer anything to avoid hurting anyone again.

author: George Eliot
text: I will add, that personally I have a deep interest in your peace of mind and welfare.”
summary: I want you to know I genuinely care about your happiness and well-being.

author: George Eliot
text: I should have no stay. I should feel like a lonely wanderer, cut off from the past.
summary: I feel like I would be completely lost and alone without my roots anchoring me.

author: George Eliot
text: Of course you are independent of me; you can marry this girl to-morrow, if you like; you are a man of five-and-twenty,—you can go your way, and I can go mine. We need have no more to do with each other.”
summary: I am so angry I am saying go live your own life and cut me out completely.

author: George Eliot
text: Many things are difficult and dark to me; but I see one thing quite clearly,—that I must not, cannot, seek my own happiness by sacrificing others. Love is natural; but surely pity and faithfulness and memory are natural too. And they would live in me still, and punish me if I did not obey them.
summary: I feel confused about a lot, but I know I cannot hurt people I love just to be happy.

author: George Eliot
text: I used to think I could never bear life if it kept on being the same every day, and I must always be doing things of no consequence, and never know anything greater.
summary: I used to fear I could not stand a boring everyday life without any bigger purpose or excitement.

author: George Eliot
text: I kept my eyes and ears open, sir, and I wasn’t too fond of my own back, and I made my master’s interest my own. Why, with only looking into what went on in the mill, I found out how there was a waste of five hundred a-year that might be hindered.
summary: I paid close attention at work and spotted a huge waste of money I could help fix.

author: George Eliot
text: But it isn’t for that that I’m jealous for the dark women,—not because I’m dark myself; it’s because I always care the most about the unhappy people.
summary: I stick up for outsiders not because I am one but because I feel for people who are hurting.

author: George Eliot
text: But I shall soon go away to another situation, and I should like to be friends with him again while I am here.
summary: I am leaving this job soon and I want to fix a friendship before I go.

author: George Eliot
text: I was hoping you would remain among your friends, who are all in this neighbourhood, I believe.”
summary: I hoped you would stay close to your friends here instead of moving away.

author: George Eliot
text: It is very sweet to have people love us. What a wonderful, beautiful thing it seems that God should have made your heart so that you could care about a queer little girl whom you only knew for a few weeks! I remember saying to you that I thought you cared for me more than Tom did.”
summary: I feel so grateful that you loved me after only a few weeks, even more than my own family did.

author: George Eliot
text: And then I shall see you when you’re grown up, and you’ll hardly take any notice of me.”
summary: I worry that when you grow up you will forget about me completely.

author: George Eliot
text: But it has made me restless; it has made me think a great deal about the world; and I have impatient thoughts again,—I get weary of my home; and then it cuts me to the heart afterward, that I should ever have felt weary of my father and mother.
summary: I feel restless and bored at home, then I feel terribly guilty for resenting my parents.

author: George Eliot
text: You’re always in extremes; you have no judgment and self-command; and yet you think you know best, and will not submit to be guided. You know I didn’t wish you to take a situation.
summary: I am angry because you always go to extremes and will not listen to me.

author: George Eliot
text: I don’t think any one ever did such a kind thing for me before. I haven’t many friends who care for me.”
summary: I am so touched by your kindness because I do not have many people who care about me.

author: George Eliot
text: I want you to put aside all grief because of the grief you have caused me. I was nurtured in the sense of privation; I never expected happiness; and in knowing you, in loving you, I have had, and still have, what reconciles me to life.
summary: I forgive you for hurting me because loving you has made my hard life feel worth living.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: What have I to be afraid of? I have done nothing wrong. What is to be, will be! I’ll tell the truth.
summary: I am nervous about facing the consequences but I know I did nothing wrong so I will be honest.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: But I have lived without him, I gave him up for another love, and did not regret the exchange till that love was satisfied.”
summary: I left someone I loved for a new passion and only felt regret once that excitement faded away.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Now I shall understand what the mysterious business is that you are always absorbed in here. No, really, I envy you. What a house, how nice it all is!
summary: I am curious about your work and I admire how cozy and welcoming your home feels to me.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: But we came here early in the spring, lived quite alone, and shall be alone again, and I desire nothing better.
summary: I love our quiet life alone together here and I honestly would not want anything else at all.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Today, after that fright during the storm, I understand how I love him.”
summary: After being so scared during the storm today I finally realized how deeply I love him.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: “What’s done can’t be undone, and you know I never go back on what I’ve done.
summary: I have accepted my past choice and I refuse to second guess myself now.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: What have I to strive and toil for? Why are the children here? What’s so awful is that all at once my heart’s turned, and instead of love and tenderness, I have nothing but hatred for him; yes, hatred. I could kill him.”
summary: I feel exhausted by family life and shocked that my love for my partner has turned into pure hatred.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: And I used to think that, before marriage, life was nothing much, somehow didn’t count, but that after marriage, life began in earnest. And here almost three months have passed, and I have spent my time so idly and unprofitably.
summary: I expected marriage to make my life meaningful, but months later I feel idle and disappointed with myself.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: The chief thing I shouldn’t like would be for people to imagine I want to prove anything. I don’t want to prove anything; I merely want to live, to do no one harm but myself.
summary: I do not want to prove anything to others, I just want to live quietly without hurting anyone but myself.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Haven’t I striven, striven with all my strength, to find something to give meaning to my life?
summary: I have tried so hard to find purpose, yet I still wonder what makes my life meaningful.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: For me now ... everything’s at an end! I’ve made a mess of my life. But this I’ve said, and I say still, that if my share had been given me when I needed it, my whole life would have been different.”
summary: I feel like I have ruined my life completely and keep thinking things would be different if I had gotten help in time.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: “You cannot describe my position as worse than I feel it to be myself; but what are you saying all this for?”
summary: I already know my situation is terrible, so I do not understand why you keep pointing it out to me.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: I have only found out what I knew. I understand the force that in the past gave me life, and now too gives me life.
summary: I finally realized a truth I always knew about what has kept me alive and gives my life purpose.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: What more do I want? I want peace of mind and trust, and I will take the blame on myself.
summary: I just want calm and trust again in my relationship and I am ready to admit I was wrong.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: There was a time when I spoke of your inward attitude, but I am not speaking of that now. Now I speak only of your external attitude.
summary: I am no longer talking about how you feel inside, only about how you are acting toward others right now.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: For me there is one thing, and one thing only—your love. If that’s mine, I feel so exalted, so strong, that nothing can be humiliating to me.
summary: I feel unstoppable and untouchable as long as I know you love me.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Of course, I approved of what you did. But there are ways of doing everything. And I think your action was good in itself, but you didn’t do it quite in the way you ought to have done.”
summary: I agree with what you did, but I wish you had handled it more thoughtfully.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: I’m not speaking of the suffering, I’m not afraid of that. Think only, what are my children to be?
summary: I can handle my own pain, but I am terrified about what will happen to my kids.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: That I’m wasting my life, never having a moment’s peace, either with child, or nursing a child, forever irritable, peevish, wretched myself and worrying others, repulsive to my husband, while the children are growing up unhappy, badly educated, and penniless.
summary: I feel like I am wasting my life exhausted by parenting and failing my husband and kids.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: But suppose that I agree to everything, that I want nothing: what way is there of getting out of our position?”
summary: Even if I give up everything I want, I still see no way out for us.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: I’ve been so busy, I didn’t know when I should be able to tear myself away.
summary: I have been so overwhelmed with work that I cannot figure out when I can finally leave.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: If you knew how I feel on the brink of calamity at this instant, how afraid I am of myself!”
summary: I feel like I am about to ruin everything and I am terrified of what I might do next.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: I went away, you see, because I made up my mind that it could never be, you understand, as a happiness that does not come on earth; but I’ve struggled with myself, I see there’s no living without it.
summary: I tried to walk away because I thought we could never work, but I cannot live without you.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Though I can fancy that, used to town housekeeping as you are, you must feel in the wilds here, and if there’s anything wanted, I’m altogether at your disposal.”
summary: I know you are used to city life and must feel lost here, so let me help with anything.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: I will go alone, when you go back, and then I shall be in no one’s way. And it will be better indeed without you.”
summary: I will travel on my own after you leave so I stop being a burden because you are better off without me.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I’m alone in the world! They would let me in! Do you think they wouldn’t? You’re wrong, I will get in!
summary: I feel completely alone but I keep telling myself people will still accept me if I try.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I know that you don’t believe it, but indeed, life will bring you through. You will live it down in time.
summary: I am trying to reassure you that painful things fade and life gets better with time.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I could rush at him and hug him... weep over him--but I am afraid.... Oh, dear, he’s so strange! He’s talking kindly, but I’m afraid! Why, what am I afraid of?...”
summary: I want to hug someone I care about and cry, but they feel so strange that I feel scared.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I am nothing, no specialty, and sometimes I am positively bored. I really thought you would tell me something new.”
summary: I feel ordinary and bored with myself and disappointed you did not tell me anything exciting.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: Perhaps it will all come back, but now if you love me, give me up... else I shall begin to hate you, I feel it....
summary: I need you to leave me alone for now or I am afraid I will start to resent you.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: I have lived through a long life, and now for the first time I have met what I sought—in you.
summary: After waiting my whole life, I finally found the love I was always looking for in you.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Never! No, everything is over, everything that once made my comfort, the reward of my work, and my sufferings....
summary: I feel like my whole life is finished and everything I worked and suffered for is gone.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Now I’m my real self, all myself. I’m dying now, I know I shall die, ask him. Even now I feel—see here, the weights on my feet, on my hands, on my fingers. My fingers—see how huge they are!
summary: I can feel my body getting heavy and strange as I realize I am actually dying right now.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: “This new feeling has not changed me, has not made me happy and enlightened all of a sudden, as I had dreamed, just like the feeling for my child. There was no surprise in this either.
summary: I expected becoming a parent to transform me instantly, but I feel exactly the same as before.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: I am working here, settled in my own place, and I am happy and contented, and we need nothing more to make us happy.
summary: I feel settled and happy with my work and home, and I honestly do not need anything else.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I am not afraid of anyone, anyone now! Get away from me! I want to be alone, alone, alone!”
summary: I feel defiant and overwhelmed and just need everyone to leave me alone right now.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: At night I had no light, I lay in the dark and I wouldn’t earn money for candles.
summary: I spent my nights lying alone in the dark because I was too broke for light.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I am going at once to give myself up. But I don’t know why I am going to give myself up.”
summary: I feel I should turn myself in right now even though I am not sure why.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I am at least twice as strong as you are and I have nothing to fear, besides.
summary: I feel much stronger than you and I am not worried about anything at all.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I want to live myself, or else better not live at all. I simply couldn’t pass by my mother starving, keeping my rouble in my pocket while I waited for the ‘happiness of all.’ I am putting my little brick into the happiness of all and so my heart is at peace.
summary: I want to truly live by helping my struggling family now instead of waiting for some distant ideal future.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: Stay a little, I won’t talk nonsense, about myself, I mean. I’ll tell you something.
summary: I am asking you to stay a little longer because I have something honest I need to tell you.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I sat in my room like a spider. You’ve been in my den, you’ve seen it....
summary: I hid alone in my messy room for so long that I started feeling like a trapped spider.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I only believe that you have long life before you. I know that you take all my words now for a set speech prepared beforehand, but maybe you will remember them after.
summary: I believe you have a long future ahead and hope you will remember my advice later.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: Why do I hate them now? Yes, I hate them, I feel a physical hatred for them, I can’t bear them near me.... I went up to my mother and kissed her, I remember....
summary: I feel a sudden intense hatred for the people around me even though I remember loving my mother.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: You wanted me to go yourself. Well, now I am going to prison and you’ll have your wish.
summary: I am going to prison now, just like you wanted, so you finally got what you wished for.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: But, you see, I thought I’d made a mess of it, but as I went downstairs a brilliant idea struck me: why should we trouble? Of course if you were in any danger or anything, but why need you care?
summary: I thought I messed everything up, then realized maybe I should just stop worrying about it.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: Leave me, leave me alone. I decided this even before... I’m absolutely resolved on it. Whatever may come to me, whether I come to ruin or not, I want to be alone.
summary: I have made up my mind that I need to be alone, no matter what happens to me next.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I believe my illness is all over. I knew it would be over when I went out.
summary: I finally feel like I am getting better, and just getting outside was what I needed.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: But I am talking too much. It’s because I chatter that I do nothing. Or perhaps it is that I chatter because I do nothing.
summary: I realize I talk too much, and I cannot tell if talking stops me from acting or hides that I do nothing.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I am afraid of death and I dislike its being talked of. Do you know that I am to a certain extent a mystic?”
summary: I am scared of dying and I hate talking about it, even though I think of myself as spiritual.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: Wherever I might go, whatever happened to me, you would remain to look after them. I, so to speak, give them into your keeping, Razumihin. I say this because I know quite well how you love her, and am convinced of the purity of your heart.
summary: I am asking a trusted friend to look after my family no matter what happens to me.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: But that is neither here nor there now. The point is that I have several times watched you. You walk out of your house--holding your head high--twenty paces from home you let it sink, and fold your hands behind your back. You look and evidently see nothing before nor beside you.
summary: I have watched you leave home proudly and then quickly sink into yourself seeing nothing around you.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: We have carried on our trade in that house for years past. We cure and prepare hides, we take work home... most of all I was vexed....”
summary: We have run our small family trade from home for years and I feel frustrated about it.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: For the time I don’t want to speak to anyone about it and I half regret having spoken to you.
summary: I do not want to talk about this right now and I wish I had not mentioned it.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I am putting my little brick into the happiness of all and so my heart is at peace. Ha-ha! Why have you let me slip? I only live once, I too want....
summary: I feel peaceful contributing to collective happiness but I also want to live fully for myself.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: No, life is only given to me once and I shall never have it again; I don’t want to wait for ‘the happiness of all.’ I want to live myself, or else better not live at all.
summary: I only get one life and I want to actually live it now instead of waiting for some future happiness for everyone.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: When I made your acquaintance, I felt attracted by you. Perhaps you will laugh at my saying so. You have a right to.
summary: I felt drawn to you from the moment we met and I feel awkward admitting it in case you laugh.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: There was a time, brother, when I.... Never mind, good-bye. You see, there was a time....
summary: I started to mention how I used to be different but I stopped myself and just said goodbye instead.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I don’t know why I’m afraid of that man. He came here at once after his wife’s funeral. He is very strange, and is determined on doing something.... We must guard Dounia from him... that’s what I wanted to tell you, do you hear?”
summary: I feel uneasy about a strange man who showed up after a funeral and I want to protect my family from him.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: And I was so happy, I did not notice the journey! But what am I saying? I am happy now....
summary: I was so happy on the way here that I barely noticed the trip and I still feel that joy right now.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: But at first, in the beginning, what agonies I endured in that struggle! I did not believe it was the same with other people, and all my life I hid this fact about myself as a secret.
summary: I suffered alone thinking I was the only one like this and hid it my whole life.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I loved to fall into the common rut, and had a whole-hearted terror of any kind of eccentricity in myself. But how could I live up to it?
summary: I desperately wanted to be normal like everyone else and was terrified of standing out, but I could not manage it.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: But how much is your love worth now? You are sold, all of you, body and soul, and there is no need to strive for love when you can have everything without love.
summary: You have sold yourself completely so real love feels worthless when everything can be bought without it.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: But what is to be done if I have taken it into my head that that is not the only object in life, and that if one must live one had better live in a mansion? That is my choice, my desire.
summary: I decided that just surviving is not enough and if I have to live I want real comfort and success.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: Though let me tell you this about it—about your present life, I mean; here though you are young now, attractive, nice, with soul and feeling, yet you know as soon as I came to myself just now I felt at once sick at being here with you!
summary: I woke up feeling suddenly sick and ashamed to be with you even though you are young and kind.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: You declare that you are afraid of nothing and at the same time try to ingratiate yourself in our good opinion.
summary: You say you fear nothing but you still desperately want us to like you.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I grew used to everything, or rather I voluntarily resigned myself to enduring it.
summary: I just got used to putting up with everything and told myself I was choosing to endure it.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: That, however, only happened to me once. As a rule, I was always alone.
summary: Except for one time, I have basically always been on my own in life.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: Why should I not have made up my mind? About that in particular I want to say a few words.
summary: I feel like I had every reason to decide and I need to explain my thinking.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I will push against him just as much as he pushes against me.” At last I made up my mind completely. But my preparations took a great deal of time. To begin with, when I carried out my plan I should need to be looking rather more decent, and so I had to think of my get-up.
summary: I finally decided to stand up to him and spent a long time getting my outfit right for it.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: And how few, how few words, I thought, in passing, were needed; how little of the idyllic (and affectedly, bookishly, artificially idyllic too) had sufficed to turn a whole human life at once according to my will.
summary: I realized just a few romantic words from me completely changed someone else's life direction.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: It was dark; though I tried my best I could not finish dressing quickly. Suddenly I felt a box of matches and a candlestick with a whole candle in it.
summary: I was fumbling to get dressed in the dark when I finally found some matches and a candle.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I frightened him with my passionate affection; I reduced him to tears, to hysterics.
summary: I loved someone so intensely that I scared him and made him break down crying.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: But by then I did not desire their affection: on the contrary, I continually longed for their humiliation. To escape from their derision I purposely began to make all the progress I could with my studies and forced my way to the very top.
summary: I stopped wanting my classmates to like me and worked obsessively to outdo them after they mocked me.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: But I believed that some radical change in my life was coming, and would inevitably come that day.
summary: I felt certain that today was the day my life would completely change for good.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I was always conscious of that weak point of mine, and sometimes very much afraid of it. “I exaggerate everything, that is where I go wrong,” I repeated to myself every hour.
summary: I know I blow everything out of proportion and I worry about that flaw constantly.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: Owing to its rarity, perhaps, any external event, however trivial, always made me feel as though some radical change in my life were at hand.
summary: I overreact to every little thing that happens because my life feels so empty and unchanged.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: Yet there is no work harder or more dreadful in the world or ever has been. One would think that the heart alone would be worn out with tears. And you won’t dare to say a word, not half a word when they drive you away from here; you will go away as though you were to blame. You will change to another house, then to a third, then somewhere else, till you come down at last to the Haymarket.
summary: You endure heartbreaking work in silence and get pushed from place to place until you hit bottom.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I have never in my life been able to imagine any other sort of love, and have nowadays come to the point of sometimes thinking that love really consists in the right—freely given by the beloved object—to tyrannise over her.
summary: I have started to think love just means the other person lets me control and dominate them completely.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: In the first place, by then I was incapable of love, for I repeat, with me loving meant tyrannising and showing my moral superiority.
summary: I realize I was unable to truly love because for me it only meant controlling others and feeling superior.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: There were moments of such positive intoxication, of such happiness, that there was not the faintest trace of irony within me, on my honour. I had faith, hope, love.
summary: I have felt moments of pure happiness where I fully believed in goodness and love.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I felt myself more and more sick and dreary. The images of the previous day began of themselves, apart from my will, flitting through my memory in confusion. I suddenly recalled something I had seen that morning when, full of anxious thoughts, I was hurrying to the office.
summary: I feel sick and gloomy as yesterday keeps replaying in my mind while I anxiously rush to work.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I grew up without a home; and perhaps that’s why I’ve turned so ... unfeeling.”
summary: I grew up without a stable home and I think that made me shut down emotionally.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I made friends with no one and positively avoided talking, and buried myself more and more in my hole.
summary: I avoid talking to anyone and isolate myself more and more from everyone around me.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: On returning home I deferred for a time my desire to embrace all mankind.
summary: I got home and put off my big loving mood to connect with everyone for later.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: Now, I am living out my life in my corner, taunting myself with the spiteful and useless consolation that an intelligent man cannot become anything seriously, and it is only the fool who becomes anything.
summary: I hide in my own corner telling myself smart people never get anywhere and only fools succeed.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: (I have always considered myself cleverer than any of the people surrounding me, and sometimes, would you believe it, have been positively ashamed of it.
summary: I always felt smarter than everyone around me and sometimes felt embarrassed about thinking that way.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: And lo and behold a bright idea dawned upon me! “What,” I thought, “if I meet him and don’t move on one side? What if I don’t move aside on purpose, even if I knock up against him?
summary: I got a stubborn thrill thinking about refusing to step aside and bumping straight into him on purpose.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I wanted her to disappear. I wanted “peace,” to be left alone in my underground world.
summary: I just wanted her gone so I could have peace and hide alone in my own world.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: That is what I want. I want peace; yes, I’d sell the whole world for a farthing, straight off, so long as I was left in peace.
summary: I want peace so badly I would give up everything just to be left completely alone.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I wanted to go to her, but I’d no sooner expressed the wish than she came to me. I knew we should settle everything together—everything.
summary: I wanted to reach out to her and then she showed up, and I felt we could fix everything together.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I seem to be on the right path, don’t I? Yet would you believe it, in the final result I don’t accept this world of God’s, and, although I know it exists, I don’t accept it at all.
summary: I feel like I am doing everything right, yet deep down I just cannot accept the way the world is.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: At night I used to lie sobbing into my pillow in the dark, and I used to brood over it; I used to tear my heart on purpose and gloat over my anger. ‘I’ll pay him out, I’ll pay him out!’ That’s what I used to cry out in the dark.
summary: I used to cry alone at night, feeding my anger on purpose and dreaming about getting revenge.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: Why am I pleased with myself? I’m a scoundrel, but I’m satisfied with myself. And yet I’m tortured by the thought that I’m a scoundrel, but satisfied with myself.
summary: I feel strangely proud of myself even though I know I acted badly, and that contradiction torments me.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: With my memories of home I count, too, my memories of the Bible, which, child as I was, I was very eager to read at home.
summary: I fondly remember being a kid at home, eagerly reading the stories that shaped my childhood.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I am not afraid of it now. I was afraid of it before. Do you know, perhaps I won’t answer at the trial at all.... And I seem to have such strength in me now, that I think I could stand anything, any suffering, only to be able to say and to repeat to myself every moment, ‘I exist.’
summary: I finally feel strong enough to face anything just for the chance to keep being alive.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I feel that perhaps my decision is a terrible one—for me, but I foresee that nothing will induce me to change it—nothing.
summary: I know my choice will hurt me, but I feel completely unable to back out of it.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I know I am dying, but I feel joy and peace for the first time after so many years. There was heaven in my heart from the moment I had done what I had to do.
summary: I feel calm and happy near the end because I finally did what I knew was right.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: We had four, my Nikita and I, and now we’ve no children, our dear ones have all gone. I buried the first three without grieving overmuch, and now I have buried the last I can’t forget him. He seems always standing before me.
summary: I lost all four of my kids and I cannot stop seeing the last one in front of me.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I want to suffer. I will take my punishment and begin to live. You can pass through the world doing wrong, but there’s no turning back. Now I dare not love my neighbor nor even my own children.
summary: I need to face punishment for what I did because my guilt keeps me from loving anyone.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: No, you are not some one apart, you are myself, you are I and nothing more!
summary: I realize the person I am arguing with is really just another part of myself

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: You’re a quiet one, Alyosha, you’re a saint, I know, but the devil only knows what you’ve thought about, and what you know already! You are pure, but you’ve been down into the depths.... I’ve been watching you a long time.
summary: I tell my quiet good friend I know they have seen dark thoughts too despite looking pure

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: But till I am thirty, I know that my youth will triumph over everything—every disillusionment, every disgust with life.
summary: I trust my youth will carry me through every disappointment and disgust until I turn thirty

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I see in that God’s mercy to them. I shall die, and my name will be without a stain for them. And now I feel God near, my heart rejoices as in Heaven ...
summary: I feel at peace facing death knowing my reputation is clean and I feel close to heaven

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I don’t want to live, because I loathe everything! I loathe everything, everything.
summary: I feel like I do not want to keep living because I hate absolutely everything around me

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Another cause succeedeth, and undertakes the work, and in time brings a child (that wonderful effect from such a beginning!) to perfection.
summary: I am amazed how tiny beginnings can slowly grow into something complete and wonderful.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Thus I ever lost my children without solace, and got them amidst fresh grief.....'
summary: I keep losing my children with no comfort and facing each new birth already filled with sorrow.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: I have scrupulously spoken the truth, and have been glad to hear it spoken to me.
summary: I always try to tell the truth myself and I truly appreciate hearing honesty from others.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Yet must thou love them still, for by nature they are thy friends. And the Gods themselves, in those things that they seek from them as matters of great moment, are well content, all manner of ways, as by dreams and oracles, to help them as well as others.
summary: I should keep loving difficult people because we are naturally meant to be friends.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: That I did by times prefer those, by whom I was brought up, to such places and dignities, which they seemed unto me most to desire; and that I did not put them off with hope and expectation, that (since that they were yet but young) I would do the same hereafter.
summary: I helped the people who raised me get the roles they wanted instead of making them wait.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: Such practical ability!... They must appreciate you, they must understand you. If there’s anything I can do, believe me ... oh, I love young people!
summary: I really admire what you can do and I want to help you because I love supporting young people.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: Only now, as you speak, I understand that I was really only seeking your approbation for my sincerity when I told you I could not endure ingratitude. You have revealed me to myself. You have seen through me and explained me to myself!”
summary: I finally see I was just wanting praise for being honest and you helped me understand myself better.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I am alone in the world, and if I die, what will become of all of them? I simply ask you that.
summary: I feel completely alone and I worry constantly about who would take care of everyone if I were gone.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: At your age one can’t know everything that grown-up people know. I’ll come and tell you everything you ought to know.
summary: You are too young to understand adult things yet but I promise I will explain everything to you soon.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: Though I can’t explain it to you, I like to humble myself before them, for I don’t know how to love them enough.
summary: I cannot explain why I put myself down around them except that I wish I could love them more.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If thou shouldst live three thousand, or as many as ten thousands of years, yet remember this, that man can part with no life properly, save with that little part of life, which he now lives: and that which he lives, is no other, than that which at every instant he parts with. That then which is longest of duration, and that which is shortest, come both to one effect.
summary: Whether life is long or short, we only ever lose the present moment we are in.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: I found out many other things which I desired to know, but the only thing I do not desire is that you should be absent from me; that is my chief anxiety.
summary: I have learned a lot of what I wanted, but I feel anxious most about being apart from you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Up and down, from one age to another, go the ordinary things of the world; being still the same.
summary: Generation after generation, everyday life goes up and down but stays basically the same.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: And what do I care for more, if that for which I was born and brought forth into the world (to rule all my desires with reason and discretion) may be?
summary: I do not need much else if I can live my purpose of guiding my wants with clear reason.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: I am weary of an evening, and sleepy in the daylight, and so I don't do much.
summary: I feel tired at night and drowsy during the day, so I end up getting almost nothing done.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I want to live. I love life! You may be sure of that. I love golden-haired Phœbus and his warm light....
summary: I just want to live because I deeply love being alive and feeling the warm sunlight.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: Why do you want to go meddling if your sacrifice is of no use to any one? Because you don’t know yourself why you go! Oh, you’d give a great deal to know yourself why you go! And can you have made up your mind?
summary: You are questioning someone whose pointless sacrifice makes no sense even to themselves.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I don’t know how to put it, but I have often seen it myself. And I feel like that myself, too.
summary: I cannot find the right words but I have seen this before and I feel the same way too.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: You are praying when you light the lamp, and I am praying when I rejoice seeing you.
summary: Your quiet ritual is prayer and my happiness just from seeing you feels like prayer too.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I couldn’t believe myself. Am I so abject? Shall I run to him or not? And I’ve been in such a rage with myself all this month that I am worse than I was five years ago.
summary: I am furious with myself for possibly giving in and feel worse now than I did years ago.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Farewell, Fronto, wherever you are, honey-sweet, my darling, my delight. Why do I want you? I can love you while far away.'
summary: I miss you terribly even though we are apart and I am trying to love you from a distance.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Yet a very little while and I am dead and gone; and all things are at end.
summary: I realize my life will be over very soon and everything I know will end with me.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: XLIV. Is this then a thing of that worth, that for it my soul should suffer, and become worse than it was? as either basely dejected, or disordinately affected, or confounded within itself, or terrified?
summary: I wonder if this problem is really worth the stress and fear it is causing me right now.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: XXXV. To suffer change can be no hurt; as no benefit it is, by change to attain to being. The age and time of the world is as it were a flood and swift current, consisting of the things that are brought to pass in the world.
summary: Change is natural and harmless because life moves forward like a fast river carrying everything along.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Am I then yet unwilling to go about that, for which I myself was born and brought forth into this world?
summary: I question why I still hesitate to do the work I feel I was meant to do.

author: Epictetus
text: But you are afraid lest necessary things should fail you, and are sleepless by night.
summary: You lie awake at night worrying you will not have enough to get by.

author: Epictetus
text: If I have not one, what do you wish me to do? I cannot escape from death.
summary: I feel trapped because there is no way out and I have to face dying someday.

author: Epictetus
text: I accept them: I consider this man a citizen, I accept him as a neighbor, a companion in my voyages.
summary: I choose to welcome others as equals and treat them like trusted companions on my journey.

author: Epictetus
text: Or how are you desirous at the same time to live to old age, and at the same time not to see the death of any person whom you love?
summary: You want a long life but cannot bear the thought of outliving everyone you love.

author: Epictetus
text: Shall I then, if you sail away, sit down and weep, because I have been left alone and solitary?
summary: I wonder if I should just break down crying now that you are leaving me completely alone.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: But before coming to the country-house, we broke our journey at Anagnia, a mile or so from the highroad.
summary: We stopped for a short break just off the main road on our way to the countryside house.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The second point is a strong insistence on the unity of the universe, and on man's duty as part of a great whole.
summary: Everything in the universe is connected and people find purpose by doing their part for the whole.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As for me, this is my joy, if my understanding be right and sound, as neither averse from any man, nor refusing any of those things which as a man I am subject unto; if I can look upon all things in the world meekly and kindly; accept all things and carry myself towards everything according to to true worth of the thing itself.
summary: I feel happy when I stay clearheaded, treat everyone kindly, and accept life as it comes.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: I for my part am in the meantime in possession of as much, as the common nature would have me to possess: and that which mine own nature would have me do, I do.
summary: I have everything I truly need right now and I am doing what I am supposed to do.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: So live as indifferent to the world and all worldly objects, as one who liveth by himself alone upon some desert hill. For whether here, or there, if the whole world be but as one town, it matters not much for the place.
summary: You can live freely anywhere by needing little and treating the whole world as your hometown.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Now what a sunbeam is, thou mayest know if thou observe the light of the sun, when through some narrow hole it pierceth into some room that is dark.
summary: You watch sunlight stream through a small crack into a dark room to understand what light is.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Have I done anything charitably? then am I benefited by it. See that this upon all occasions may present itself unto thy mind, and never cease to think of it. What is thy profession? to be good.
summary: I remind myself that helping others helps me too and that my real job is simply to be good.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Now if you miss me and if you love me, send me your letters often, which is a comfort and consolation to me.
summary: I miss you and your messages comfort me so please write to me often.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: And that I gave over the study of rhetoric and poetry, and of elegant neat language. That I did not use to walk about the house in my long robe, nor to do any such things.
summary: I stopped chasing fancy writing and showing off at home to live more simply and honestly.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: And as for men, towards them as naturally partakers of the same reason, my care is to carry myself sociably.
summary: I try to treat other people with kindness because we all share the same human reason.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: For whatsoever I do either by myself, or with some other, the only thing that I must intend, is, that it be good and expedient for the public.
summary: I want everything I do alone or with others to help the wider community.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Ever maintain thine own purpose and resolution free from all compulsion and necessity.
summary: You should hold onto your own goals without letting pressure or obligation control you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: And my nature is, to be rational in all my actions and as a good, and natural member of a city and commonwealth, towards my fellow members ever to be sociably and kindly disposed and affected.
summary: I try to act thoughtfully and be a kind, supportive part of the community around me.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Neither must thou do it by way of exercise, or ostentation, that they that are by and hear thee, may admire thee: but so always that nobody be privy to it, but himself alone: yea, though there be more present at the same time.
summary: You should do the right thing quietly without performing for praise even when others are watching.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: He that hath not one and the self-same general end always as long as he liveth, cannot possibly be one and the self-same man always.
summary: If I keep changing what I want from life, I cannot stay consistent with myself.

author: Epictetus
text: This is the reason why I also lost my lamp, because in wakefulness the thief was superior to me.
summary: I lost something valuable because someone else was paying closer attention than I was.

author: Epictetus
text: What place then, you say, shall I hold in the city? Whatever you can, if you maintain at the same time your fidelity and modesty.
summary: You can fit in anywhere as long as you stay true to yourself and stay humble.

author: Epictetus
text: Is this power given to you? This only is given to you, to convince yourself; and you have not convinced yourself. Then I ask you, do you attempt to persuade other men? and who has lived so long with you as you with yourself? and who has so much power of convincing you as you have of convincing yourself; and who is better disposed and nearer to you than you are to yourself?
summary: You try to convince everyone else while still failing to believe in yourself after all this time.

author: Epictetus
text: Have I learned nothing else then? I have learned to see that everything which happens, if it be independent of my will, is nothing to me. I may ask, if you have not gained by this.
summary: I finally learned to let go of everything outside my control because it has nothing to do with me.

author: Epictetus
text: I wish I could learn everything before I return; but much labor is necessary, and no one sends me anything, and the baths at Nicopolis are dirty; everything is bad at home, and bad here.
summary: I want to learn so much before going back, but I feel unsupported and everything around me feels miserable.

author: Epictetus
text: Let death and exile and every other thing which appears dreadful be daily before your eyes; but most of all death: and you will never think of anything mean nor will you desire anything extravagantly.
summary: Keeping death in mind each day helps you stop sweating small things and wanting too much.

author: Epictetus
text: If you remember this, you will always maintain your character such as it ought to be. But if you do not, consider that the times of opportunity are perishing, and that whatever pains you take about yourself, you are going to waste them all and overturn them.
summary: If you forget your values now, you will waste all your hard work and lose your chance to change.

author: Epictetus
text: Who wishes to become like you? Who imitates you, as he imitates Socrates? But I can cut off your head.
summary: You mock me as worthless to follow, yet all you have over me is brute power.

author: Epictetus
text: But whether these things are for my interest or whether they are not, I do not intend to ask you.
summary: I will not ask your opinion about whether my choices are good for me or not.

author: Epictetus
text: Shall I then no longer exist? You will not exist, but you will be something else, of which the world now has need; for you also came into existence not when you chose, but when the world had need of you.
summary: I fear disappearing after death, but I remind myself I will become something else the world needs.

author: Epictetus
text: Immediately prescribe some character and some form to yourself, which you shall observe both when you are alone and when you meet with men.
summary: You should decide who you want to be and act that way alone and with others.

author: Epictetus
text: Such is going away from home and a small change: such is death, a greater change, not from the state which now is to that which is not, but to that which is not now. Shall I then no longer exist?
summary: I wonder if leaving home and dying are just changes and whether I will still exist after.

author: Epictetus
text: How then shall I cease to commit them? Formerly I also acted wrong, but now I do not: thanks to God.
summary: I used to keep making the same mistakes but I have finally stopped and I feel thankful for that.

author: Epictetus
text: But how do you act? When you seek what is not your own, you lose that which is your own.
summary: You chase things you cannot control and end up losing the peace and self respect you already have.

author: Epictetus
text: Have I not the notion of it? You have. Do I not adapt it to particulars?
summary: I feel stuck trying to understand why I get the idea but struggle to apply it to real situations.

author: Epictetus
text: If I feel that all these things do not concern me, he does not threaten me at all; but if I fear any of them, it is I whom he threatens.
summary: I realize no one can really threaten me unless I let fear give them power over me.

author: Epictetus
text: If you do not, you will be unfortunate, you will fail in all things, you will be hindered, you will be impeded.
summary: If you ignore what matters, you will feel stuck and fail at everything you try.

author: Epictetus
text: Do you think that freedom is a thing independent and self-governing? Certainly.
summary: You wonder if real freedom truly means being independent and governing yourself.

author: Epictetus
text: And how will you be nobody nowhere, when you ought to be somebody in those things only which are in your power, in which indeed it is permitted to you to be a man of the greatest worth? But your friends will be without assistance!
summary: You feel invisible until you focus on what you can control and become valuable there.

author: Epictetus
text: And for what purpose do you follow them? Slave, is it not that you may be happy, that you may be constant, is it not that you may be in a state conformable to nature and live so?
summary: You are questioning why you chase those rules, hoping they will make you happy and steady.

author: Epictetus
text: When you see a person weeping in sorrow either when a child goes abroad or when he is dead, or when the man has lost his property, take care that the appearance do not hurry you away with it, as if he were suffering in external things.
summary: When you see someone crying over loss, try not to get swept up thinking outside events cause real harm.

author: Epictetus
text: To-morrow, I said, you will find an earthen lamp; for a man only loses that which he has. I have lost my garment.
summary: I lost my jacket and I am telling myself I can only lose what I actually owned anyway.

author: Epictetus
text: Remember this, who gives these things and to whom, and for what purpose. If you cherish yourself in these thoughts, do you still think that it makes any difference where you shall be happy, where you shall please God?
summary: When you remember who provides for you and why, you realize you can find purpose anywhere.

author: Epictetus
text: And do you then, if you wish to be beautiful, young man, labor at this, the acquisition of human excellence? But what is this?
summary: If you want to be truly attractive, you should work on building real character and ask what that means.

author: Epictetus
text: I must go into exile. Does any man then hinder me from going with smiles and cheerfulness and contentment? Tell me the secret which you possess. I will not, for this is in my power.
summary: I have to leave home against my will, but I can still choose to leave with a calm and happy attitude.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: But how shall one who is so weak in his childhood become really strong when he grows older?
summary: I wonder how someone so fragile as a child can ever grow up to be truly strong.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: I can never judge of the same thing exactly in the same way. I cannot judge of my work, while doing it.
summary: I realize my opinion keeps shifting and I cannot fairly judge my own work while I am still making it.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: But at least learn your inability to believe, since reason brings you to this, and yet you cannot believe. Endeavour then to convince yourself, not by increase of proofs of God, but by the abatement of your passions.
summary: I cannot force myself to believe through logic alone, so I need to work on calming my desires instead.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: We are not miserable without feeling it. A ruined house is not miserable.
summary: Misery only exists when I actually feel it, unlike an empty ruined building that feels nothing at all.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: Shall he alone who knows his nature know it only to be miserable? Shall he alone who knows it be alone unhappy?
summary: I wonder if truly understanding myself only brings sadness and leaves me feeling uniquely unhappy and alone.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: Nothing is good but mediocrity. The majority has settled that, and finds fault with him who escapes it at whichever end. I will not oppose it. I quite consent to put myself there, and refuse to be at the lower end, not because it is low, but because it is an end; for I would likewise refuse to be placed at the top.
summary: I am fine staying average because standing out at either extreme just brings criticism.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: True fear is joined to hope, because it is born of faith, and because men hope in the God in whom they believe.
summary: Real fear comes with hope when you deeply trust something greater than yourself.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: Our instinct makes us feel that we must seek our happiness outside ourselves.
summary: I keep looking for happiness in other people and things instead of inside myself.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: Self-will will never be satisfied, though it should have command of all it would; but we are satisfied from the moment we renounce it.
summary: I finally feel at peace when I stop trying to control everything and just let go.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: Time heals griefs and quarrels, for we change and are no longer the same persons.
summary: I got over old hurt and fights because time passed and I became a different person.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: This is what I see and what troubles me. I look on all sides, and I see only darkness everywhere.
summary: I feel lost and overwhelmed because everywhere I look things seem dark and hopeless right now.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: Hence it happens that if any have some interest in being loved by us, they are averse to render us a service which they know to be disagreeable. They treat us as we wish to be treated.
summary: People who want to be liked avoid telling hard truths and just tell others what they want to hear.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: It is false that we are worthy of the love of others; it is unfair that we should desire it. If we were born reasonable and impartial, knowing ourselves and others, we should not give this bias to our will. However, we are born with it; therefore born unjust, for all tends to self.
summary: I realize I am selfish and not truly deserving of love, yet I cannot stop wanting it anyway.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: But I have so often found my right judgment at fault, that at last I have come to distrust myself, and then others.
summary: I have been wrong so many times that I no longer trust my own judgment or anyone else either.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: The whole world now became fervent with love. Princes abandoned their pomp; maidens suffered martyrdom.
summary: Everyone around me suddenly became passionate about a cause, giving up comfort and making huge sacrifices for it.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: He no longer loves the person whom he loved ten years ago. I quite believe it.
summary: I am not surprised that love faded after ten years and he feels different now.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: Let no one say that I have said nothing new; the arrangement of the subject is new.
summary: I may not have invented anything new, but I put things together in my own original way.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: If I lose it, I am undone. I shall not lack accusations, and persecutions.
summary: I am terrified that if I lose what I have, my life will fall apart completely.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: It must give us an explanation of our opposition to God and to our own good. It must teach us the remedies for these infirmities, and the means of obtaining these remedies.
summary: We need to understand why we fight against what is good for us and how to heal.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: Others: This house is of God; for in it there are wrought strange miracles.
summary: People believe this place is holy because amazing unexplained things have happened there.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: Such is my state, full of weakness and uncertainty. And from all this I conclude that I ought to spend all the days of my life without caring to inquire into what must happen to me.
summary: I feel weak and uncertain about everything, so I have decided to stop worrying about what my future holds.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: Thereupon it reasons, and calls this nature, necessity, and can believe nothing else.
summary: People convince themselves that their limited view is just how the world has to work.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: I feel that I might not have been; for the Ego consists in my thoughts.
summary: I sometimes feel like I might not really exist because my self is only made of thoughts.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: How long is necessary? A time commensurate with our vain and paltry life.
summary: I wonder how much time I really need given how short and small my life feels.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: What a happy life, from which we are to free ourselves as from the plague!
summary: I sarcastically call this a happy life when I actually want to escape it like a disease.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: What joy can we find in the expectation of nothing but hopeless misery?
summary: We feel hopeless when we look ahead and see only misery waiting for us.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: I can easily love total darkness; but if God keeps me in a state of semi-darkness, such partial darkness displeases me, and, because I do not see therein the advantage of total darkness, it is unpleasant to me.
summary: I would rather face complete uncertainty than stay stuck halfway without understanding why I am struggling.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: They must lessen our faults, appear to excuse them, intersperse praises and evidence of love and esteem.
summary: I need the people around me to soften my mistakes with kindness and encouragement.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: We are born so averse to this love of God, and it is so necessary that we must be born guilty, or God would be unjust.
summary: We feel broken from the start because we struggle to love what matters most in life.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: This is not the way to cure you of your unrighteousness, which these wise men never knew. I alone can make you understand who you are...."
summary: I know you will not heal this way and only I can show you the truth about yourself.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: This which I think and feel underlay every former state of life and circumstances, as it does underlie my present, and what is called life, and what is called death.
summary: I feel there is a deeper part of me that stays the same through everything, even life and death.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: I do not wish to expiate, but to live. My life is for itself and not for a spectacle.
summary: I want to actually live my own life instead of apologizing or performing for other people.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: I chide society, I embrace solitude, and yet I am not so ungrateful as not to see the wise, the lovely and the noble-minded, as from time to time they pass my gate. Who hears me, who understands me, becomes mine,—a possession for all time.
summary: I prefer being alone over fitting into society, but I deeply treasure the few people who truly understand me.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: I must be myself. I cannot break myself any longer for you, or you. If you can love me for what I am, we shall be the happier.
summary: I need to stop changing myself to please others and hope you can love me as I really am.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: I see its presence to them. I am certified of a common nature; and these other souls, these separated selves, draw me as nothing else can. They stir in me the new emotions we call passion; of love, hatred, fear, admiration, pity; thence come conversation, competition, persuasion, cities and war.
summary: I realize I share something deep with other people, and they pull me in and spark strong feelings in me.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: I fear only that I may lose them receding into the sky in which now they are only a patch of brighter light. Then, though I prize my friends, I cannot afford to talk with them and study their visions, lest I lose my own.
summary: I am afraid that spending too much time on my friends ideas will make me lose my own direction.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: If you leave out their heart, you shall lose your own. The senses would make things of all persons; of women, of children, of the poor.
summary: Seeing people as objects instead of real feeling humans makes life feel empty and cold.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: With every influx of light comes new danger. Has he light? he must bear witness to the light, and always outrun that sympathy which gives him such keen satisfaction, by his fidelity to new revelations of the incessant soul.
summary: Growing in understanding feels risky because staying honest means leaving behind comfortable approval.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
