text: It is to answer for its moderation with its life. For every grain of wit there is a grain of folly. For every thing you have missed, you have gained something else; and for every thing you gain, you lose something.
summary: Every choice in life involves a tradeoff where gaining one thing always means losing something else.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Whilst we converse with what is above us, we do not grow old, but grow young. Infancy, youth, receptive, aspiring, with religious eye looking upward, counts itself nothing and abandons itself to the instruction flowing from all sides.
summary: When we stay open and curious about something bigger, we feel younger instead of growing old.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: But we see them exchange a glance, or betray a deep emotion, and we are no longer strangers. We understand them, and take the warmest interest in the development of the romance. All mankind love a lover.
summary: Watching two strangers fall in love makes me feel connected to them and root for their story.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: As long as all that is said is said against me, I feel a certain assurance of success. But as soon as honeyed words of praise are spoken for me I feel as one that lies unprotected before his enemies.
summary: I feel safer when people criticize me than when they praise me because praise leaves me exposed.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: The sweet of nature is love; yet, if I have a friend I am tormented by my imperfections. The love of me accuses the other party.
summary: I love having close friends but I constantly worry my flaws disappoint them.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Greatness appeals to the future. If I can be firm enough to-day to do right and scorn eyes, I must have done so much right before as to defend me now.
summary: I try to stand up for what is right today trusting my past choices will give me strength.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: A political victory, a rise of rents, the recovery of your sick or the return of your absent friend, or some other favorable event raises your spirits, and you think good days are preparing for you. Do not believe it. Nothing can bring you peace but yourself.
summary: Good news lifts my mood temporarily but lasting peace only comes from within myself.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: But your isolation must not be mechanical, but spiritual, that is, must be elevation. At times the whole world seems to be in conspiracy to importune you with emphatic trifles. Friend, client, child, sickness, fear, want, charity, all knock at once at thy closet door and say,—‘Come out unto us.’
summary: Everyone keeps demanding my attention with small urgent things when I need quiet space to think.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: If I feel overshadowed and outdone by great neighbors, I can yet love; I can still receive; and he that loveth maketh his own the grandeur he loves.
summary: Even when I feel small next to impressive people, I can still admire and learn from what they have.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Nothing. I have been floated into this thought, this hour, this connection of events, by secret currents of might and mind, and my ingenuity and wilfulness have not thwarted, have not aided to an appreciable degree.
summary: I feel like I arrived at this moment through forces I cannot control or explain with my own effort.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Do not set the least value on what I do, or the least discredit on what I do not, as if I pretended to settle any thing as true or false. I unsettle all things.
summary: I am not trying to give final answers, I am trying to question everything I thought I knew.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: There I saw that nothing was changed with me but the place, and said to myself—‘Thou foolish child, hast thou come out hither, over four thousand miles of salt water, to find that which was perfect to thee there at home?’
summary: I traveled far away only to realize I already had what I was searching for back home.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: You are preparing with eagerness to go and render a service to which your talent and your taste invite you, the love of men and the hope of fame. Has it not occurred to you that you have no right to go, unless you are equally willing to be prevented from going?
summary: You are excited to use your talents to help others and be recognized, but you wonder if you could accept being stopped.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: There is a relation between the hours of our life and the centuries of time.
summary: I sense that my small daily moments are connected to something much larger and longer lasting.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: I no longer wish to meet a good I do not earn, for example to find a pot of buried gold, knowing that it brings with it new burdens. I do not wish more external goods,—neither possessions, nor honors, nor powers, nor persons.
summary: I do not want lucky breaks or more stuff anymore because I know they only create extra stress.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: I live in society, with persons who answer to thoughts in my own mind, or express a certain obedience to the great instincts to which I live.
summary: I feel at home among people who share my values and understand how I think about life.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: It is not you, but your radiance. It is that which you know not in yourself and can never know.
summary: You have a light that others can see clearly even though you will never fully see it yourself.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: The new position of the advancing man has all the powers of the old, yet has them all new. It carries in its bosom all the energies of the past, yet is itself an exhalation of the morning. I cast away in this new moment all my once hoarded knowledge, as vacant and vain. Now, for the first time seem I to know any thing rightly.
summary: I feel like I am starting fresh and finally letting go of everything I thought I knew before.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: We walk alone in the world. Friends such as we desire are dreams and fables.
summary: I feel completely alone because the kind of close friendship I want does not seem real.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: The moment we indulge our affections, the earth is metamorphosed; there is no winter and no night; all tragedies, all ennuis vanish,—all duties even; nothing fills the proceeding eternity but the forms all radiant of beloved persons. Let the soul be assured that somewhere in the universe it should rejoin its friend, and it would be content and cheerful alone for a thousand years.
summary: When I let myself love someone, everything feels bright and I could wait forever to be together.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: It respects space and time, climate, want, sleep, the law of polarity, growth and death.
summary: Life has real limits like time, distance, exhaustion, and the natural cycle of growing and dying.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: By persisting in your path, though you forfeit the little you gain the great.
summary: Staying true to your path means giving up small wins to achieve something much greater.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: When aloft, I find myself always alone. No one speaketh unto me; the frost of solitude maketh me tremble.
summary: When I succeed or rise above others, I feel completely alone and shaken by the isolation.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Light am I: ah, that I were night! But it is my lonesomeness to be begirt with light!
summary: I feel painfully exposed and visible all the time and I wish I could disappear into darkness.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: All this went on for a long time, or a short time: for properly speaking, there is NO time on earth for such things—.
summary: Some experiences feel outside of time so you cannot tell if they lasted moments or years.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Meanwhile do I talk to myself as one who hath time. No one telleth me anything new, so I tell myself mine own story.
summary: I talk to myself to pass the time because no one around me says anything new or interesting.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: How I now love every one unto whom I may but speak! Even mine enemies pertain to my bliss.
summary: I feel so grateful just to talk to anyone that even people I disliked now make me happy.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: But my feeling changes suddenly, and breaks out as soon as I enter the modern period, OUR period. Our age KNOWS...”
summary: I feel uneasy and overwhelmed whenever I think about how much our modern world claims to know.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: But a home have I found nowhere: unsettled am I in all cities, and decamping at all gates.
summary: I feel rootless because I have never found a real home in any city I visit.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Fearfully was I terrified thereby: it prostrated me. And I cried with horror as I ne’er cried before.
summary: I was so terrified by what I saw that I collapsed and cried in horror.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: I tell you, your very Self wanteth to die, and turneth away from life.
summary: I see that you have lost the will to live and are turning away.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Whence have gone the tears of mine eye, and the down of my heart? Oh, the lonesomeness of all bestowers!
summary: I feel numb and empty now, and giving so much to others leaves me lonely.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: But how could I be just from the heart! How can I give every one his own! Let this be enough for me: I give unto every one mine own.
summary: I realize I cannot be perfectly fair to everyone so I just offer what I have.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Nothing liveth any longer that I love,—how should I still love myself! Have I still a goal? Where is MY home?”
summary: I feel lost after losing everything I loved and wonder if I still have purpose or belonging.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Now and again I am troubled by the thought: WHAT NEXT? My ‘future’ is the darkest thing in the world to me, but as there still remains a great deal for me to do, I suppose I ought rather to think of doing this than of my future, and leave the rest to THEE and the gods.”
summary: I feel anxious about what comes next so I focus on my work today and trust the future will sort itself.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: I love the great despisers, because they are the great adorers, and arrows of longing for the other shore.
summary: I admire people who reject shallow things because their criticism shows they hunger for something deeper and better.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: To conceal myself and my riches—THAT did I learn down there: for every one did I still find poor in spirit.
summary: I learned to hide my true self and strengths because I felt no one around me could really understand them.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: But I lay enchained to my love for my children: desire spread this snare for me—the desire for love—that I should become the prey of my children, and lose myself in them.
summary: I feel trapped by how much I love my kids and I am losing myself in them.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: For THIS am I from the heart and from the beginning—drawing, hither-drawing, upward-drawing, upbringing; a drawer, a trainer, a training-master, who not in vain counselled himself once on a time: “Become what thou art!”
summary: I have always been someone who lifts others up and helps them become their true selves.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: ‘WHERE is—MY home?’ For it do I ask and seek, and have sought, but have not found it.
summary: I keep asking where I truly belong because I have searched for home and still not found it.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Alone with oneself!—this thought terrifies the modern soul; it is his one anxiety, his one ghastly fear” (English Edition, page 141).
summary: People today are terrified of being alone with themselves and will do anything to avoid it.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Let your love to life be love to your highest hope; and let your highest hope be the highest thought of life!
summary: You should love life by holding onto your greatest hope and highest ideals.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: But I asked once, and suffocated almost with my question: What? is the rabble also NECESSARY for life?
summary: I feel sick wondering if toxic and shallow people are just an unavoidable part of life.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Alone am I again, and like to be so, alone with the pure heaven, and the open sea; and again is the afternoon around me.
summary: I am alone again by the water under the open sky and I love this quiet peace.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Verily, said he unto his disciples, a little while, and there cometh the long twilight. Alas, how shall I preserve my light through it!
summary: I worry about how to keep my inner hope alive through a long dark period ahead.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Thus did time pass with me, and slip by, if time there still was: what do I know thereof!
summary: I lost track of time completely and I am not even sure what time means anymore.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: And, fool that I was, when they misjudged me, I indulged them on that account more than myself, being habitually hard on myself, and often even taking revenge on myself for the indulgence.
summary: I used to excuse people who misunderstood me while blaming myself harshly for being too kind to them.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Nothing liveth any longer that I love,—how should I still love myself?
summary: Since everything I cared about is gone, I do not know how to care about myself anymore.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: I recognise my destiny, said he at last, sadly. Well! I am ready. Now hath my last lonesomeness begun.
summary: I finally accept what is coming and feel ready to face being alone for good.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: And it is not those who lead OUT OF danger that please you best, but those who lead you away from all paths, the misleaders. But if such longing in you be ACTUAL, it seemeth to me nevertheless to be IMPOSSIBLE.
summary: You prefer people who pull you off track rather than keep you safe, but that wish cannot work.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: And I considered a long while, and trembled. At last, however, did I say what I had said at first.
summary: I thought about it for a long time while shaking, then I just repeated what I had said before.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: In your love let there be valour! With your love shall ye assail him who inspireth you with fear!
summary: You should let your love make you brave enough to confront what scares you head on.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: One occasionally embraces some one or other, out of love to mankind (because one cannot embrace all); but this is what one must never confess to the individual.
summary: People sometimes show general kindness through one person without ever admitting the real motive.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Well-being, as you understand it--is certainly not a goal; it seems to us an END; a condition which at once renders man ludicrous and contemptible--and makes his destruction DESIRABLE!
summary: I think chasing only comfort makes people ridiculous and pathetic instead of giving life real purpose.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: It is to be INFERRED that there are countless dark bodies near the sun--such as we shall never see.
summary: We have to accept that many important things near us will always stay completely invisible to us.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Let us at once say again what we have already said a hundred times, for people's ears nowadays are unwilling to hear such truths--OUR truths.
summary: We feel frustrated having to repeat what we know is true because no one today wants to listen.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: For if I had not already decided within myself what it is, by what standard could I determine whether that which is just happening is not perhaps 'willing' or 'feeling'?
summary: I wonder how I can label what I feel inside unless I already decided what those feelings mean.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: To conserve one's three hundred foregrounds; also one's black spectacles: for there are circumstances when nobody must look into our eyes, still less into our "motives."
summary: I keep my guard up and hide my real reasons because I do not want anyone truly seeing me.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Unrestful joy to long, to lurk, to hark! I peer for friends!--am ready day and night, For my new friends.
summary: I feel restless and excited as I wait day and night hoping new friends will finally show up.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: For solitude is a virtue with us, as a sublime bent and bias to purity, which divines that in the contact of man and man--"in society"--it must be unavoidably impure.
summary: I see being alone as cleaner and better because being around other people always feels messy to me.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: My summer's park! Uneaseful joy to look, to lurk, to hark-- I peer for friends, am ready day and night,-- Where linger ye, my friends? The time is right!
summary: I wait anxiously day and night in a happy place, wondering why my friends are taking so long to arrive.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: In the end things must be as they are and have always been--the great things remain for the great, the abysses for the profound, the delicacies and thrills for the refined, and, to sum up shortly, everything rare for the rare.
summary: Some rare and intense experiences in life are only meant for the few people able to truly appreciate them.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Only name it, whatever I have I offer thee! "To refresh me? To refresh me?
summary: I want to give you everything I have but I am confused about what you really need.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: We immortalize what cannot live and fly much longer, things only which are exhausted and mellow!
summary: We only try to preserve things once they are fading and almost gone from our lives.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: To live--is not that just endeavouring to be otherwise than this Nature? Is not living valuing, preferring, being unjust, being limited, endeavouring to be different?
summary: Living means judging and choosing and trying to become something different from nature.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: It is the profound, suspicious fear of an incurable pessimism which compels whole centuries to fasten their teeth into a religious interpretation of existence: the fear of the instinct which divines that truth might be attained TOO soon, before man has become strong enough, hard enough, artist enough....
summary: People cling to religion for centuries because they fear facing a painful truth before they are ready.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Strange am I to Me? Yet from Me sprung? A wrestler, by himself too oft self-wrung? Hindering too oft my own self's potency, Wounded and hampered by self-victory?
summary: I feel like a stranger to myself, constantly fighting myself and getting in my own way.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Love brings to light the noble and hidden qualities of a lover--his rare and exceptional traits: it is thus liable to be deceptive as to his normal character.
summary: Being in love makes someone seem amazing and hides who they really are day to day.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: THE DANGER IN HAPPINESS.--"Everything now turns out best for me, I now love every fate:--who would like to be my fate?"
summary: I feel so lucky right now that I love my life and want to share my good fortune.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Here and there we understand it, and laugh at the way in which precisely the best knowledge seeks most to retain us in this SIMPLIFIED, thoroughly artificial, suitably imagined, and suitably falsified world: at the way in which, whether it will or not, it loves error, because, as living itself, it loves life!
summary: We sometimes laugh realizing even smart ideas keep life simple and false because we love living.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: The great epochs of our life are at the points when we gain courage to rebaptize our badness as the best in us.
summary: I finally feel brave enough to see my worst traits as actually my greatest strengths.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: "I could not have done that," says my pride, and remains inexorable. Eventually--the memory yields.
summary: My pride insists I would never do that, but eventually I have to admit what I did.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Is not life a hundred times too short for us--to bore ourselves? One would have to believe in eternal life in order to...
summary: I feel like life is far too short to waste time boring myself with pointless things.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: It is the business of the very few to be independent; it is a privilege of the strong.
summary: True independence is rare and only the strongest people can really earn and handle it.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: How PERSONAL does a long fear make one, a long watching of enemies, of possible enemies!
summary: Living in fear for a long time while watching for enemies makes you turn deeply inward.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: There must be a sort of repugnance in me to BELIEVE anything definite about myself.--Is there perhaps some enigma therein? Probably; but fortunately nothing for my own teeth.--Perhaps it betrays the species to which I belong?--but not to myself, as is sufficiently agreeable to me."
summary: I resist defining myself clearly and I wonder what that avoidance says about the kind of person I am.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Love to one only is a barbarity, for it is exercised at the expense of all others. Love to God also!
summary: Loving only one person or god feels cruel because it rejects and devalues everyone else.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Not to cleave to any person, be it even the dearest--every person is a prison and also a recess.
summary: Even the closest relationship can feel like a trap that limits personal freedom.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: HOW necessary, HOW logical, even HOW humanely desirable this was, let us consider for ourselves!
summary: I am trying to understand why something that happened felt necessary and right at the time.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: The maturity of man--that means, to have reacquired the seriousness that one had as a child at play.
summary: Growing up well means recovering the focused and wholehearted seriousness children bring to play.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: And have people around you who are as a garden--or as music on the waters at eventide, when already the day becomes a memory. Choose the GOOD solitude, the free, wanton, lightsome solitude, which also gives you the right still to remain good in any sense whatsoever!
summary: Choosing calming friends and healthy alone time helps a person stay kind and grounded.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: The main thing about them is NOT that they wish to go "back," but that they wish to get AWAY therefrom.
summary: Some people are not really nostalgic for the past but simply desperate to escape the present.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
I'm nobody!  Who are you?
Are you nobody, too?
Then there 's a pair of us -- don't tell!
They 'd banish us, you know.
summary: I feel invisible to the world but secretly happy to find someone else who feels the same way too.

author: Emily Dickinson
summary: I am overwhelmed with childlike delight by something beautiful glowing in the night around me.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
Of life? 'T were odd I fear a thing
That comprehendeth me
In one or more existences
At Deity's decree.
summary: I find it strange to be afraid of life when it already holds me completely by design.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
Stare vacant into mine
And ask my business there.
My business, -- just a life I left,
Was such still dwelling there?
summary: I return to a place from my past and wonder why part of me still lingers there.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
I lived on dread; to those who know
The stimulus there is
In danger, other impetus
Is numb and vital-less.
summary: I got so used to living in fear that normal safe life started to feel dull and lifeless.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
I hide myself within my flower,
That, fading from your vase,
You, unsuspecting, feel for me
Almost a loneliness.
summary: I hide a part of myself in something I give you so you will miss me when it fades.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
The sweeping up the heart,
And putting love away
We shall not want to use again
Until eternity.
summary: I am carefully putting my love away because I do not expect to need it again for a very long time.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
But this sort grieved myself, and so
I thought how it would be
When just this time, some perfect year,
Themselves should come to me.
summary: I felt hurt by being left out, so I imagined how wonderful it would feel when I am finally included.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
A thought went up my mind to-day
That I have had before,
But did not finish, -- some way back,
I could not fix the year,
summary: I keep having the same unfinished thought today but I cannot remember when I first started thinking it.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
Success is counted sweetest
By those who ne'er succeed.
To comprehend a nectar
Requires sorest need.
summary: People who never succeed understand success best because wanting something badly teaches its true value.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
Love is anterior to life,
Posterior to death,
Initial of creation, and
The exponent of breath.
summary: Love feels bigger than my life itself, existing before I was born and lasting after I am gone.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
Nor had I time to love; but since
Some industry must be,
The little toil of love, I thought,
Was large enough for me.
summary: I have been too busy for much else, so I decided that simply loving people is enough meaningful work for me.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
I meant to have but modest needs,
Such as content, and heaven;
Within my income these could lie,
And life and I keep even.
summary: I only wanted a simple life with enough happiness to get by and stay at peace with myself.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
Musicians wrestle everywhere:
All day, among the crowded air,
I hear the silver strife;
And -- waking long before the dawn --
Such transport breaks upon the town
I think it that "new life!"
summary: I wake early to beautiful music filling the air and feel overwhelmed like the whole world is starting fresh.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
anything to be elsewhere found,--flashes of wholly original and
profound insight into nature and life; words and phrases exhibiting
an extraordinary vividness of descriptive and imaginative power, yet
often set in a seemingly whimsical or even rugged frame. They are
summary: Her writing has brilliant and original insights about life, even though her style can seem strange and rough.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
So satisfied to go
Where none of us should be,
Immediately, that anguish stooped
Almost to jealousy.
summary: I feel strangely jealous of someone who seemed peaceful leaving a place the rest of us fear to face.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
And were you saved,
And I condemned to be
Where you were not,
That self were hell to me.
summary: I would rather suffer anywhere than be in paradise without the person I love beside me.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
How well I knew the light before!
I could not see it now.
'T is dying, I am doing; but
I'm not afraid to know.
summary: I can feel the light I once knew so well fading, and I am facing that loss without fear.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
Time is a test of trouble,
But not a remedy.
If such it prove, it prove too
There was no malady.
summary: Time only reveals whether pain was real, because real hurt does not simply disappear with waiting.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
There's been a death in the opposite house
As lately as to-day.
I know it by the numb look
Such houses have alway.
summary: I can tell someone died in the house across the street today by its cold and empty stillness.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
Afraid? Of whom am I afraid?
Not death; for who is he?
The porter of my father's lodge
As much abasheth me.
summary: I am not scared of death because it feels like just walking through a door to go home.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
I heard a fly buzz when I died;
The stillness round my form
Was like the stillness in the air
Between the heaves of storm.
summary: I remember lying still at the very end while everything went quiet except for a small buzzing sound.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
A fan, perhaps, a friend's regret,
And certainly that one
No color in the rainbow
Perceives when you are gone.
summary: After death there is nothing left to see, only maybe a fan and friends feeling sad for a while.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
An anguish at the mention,
Which, when to patience grown,
I 've known permission given
To rejoin its own.
summary: I have felt sharp pain when reminded of loss that slowly softened until I could finally let it rest.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
I said I gained it, --
This was all.
Look, how I clutch it,
Lest it fall,
And I a pauper go;
Unfitted by an instant's grace
For the contented beggar's face
I wore an hour ago.
summary: I finally got something good and now I hold it tightly because I am terrified of losing it again.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
'T is so much joy! 'T is so much joy!
If I should fail, what poverty!
And yet, as poor as I
Have ventured all upon a throw;
Have gained! Yes! Hesitated so
This side the victory!
summary: I risked everything I had on one chance and I am overwhelmed with joy that it actually paid off.

author: Emily Dickinson
summary: I feel a deep warm friendship with the animals and plants around me because we truly recognize each other.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
The grass does not appear afraid;
I often wonder he
Can stand so close and look so bold
At what is dread to me.
summary: I feel scared of something scary nearby and I admire how calm and brave the grass looks facing it.

author: Emily Dickinson
text:
I wonder if the sepulchre
Is not a lonesome way,
When men and boys, and larks and June
Go down the fields to hay!
summary: I wonder if being dead feels lonely while everyone else enjoys warm summer days working outside together.

author: Emily Dickinson
summary: I am saying goodbye to my old life and familiar world because I finally feel ready to leave.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
Love is a babe, then might I not say so,
To give full growth to that which still doth grow?
summary: I wonder if I should call my love young because it keeps growing stronger every day.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
Blessed are you whose worthiness gives scope,
Being had, to triumph; being lacked, to hope.
summary: Loving someone amazing feels like winning when together and hopeful when apart.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
This silence for my sin you did impute,
Which shall be most my glory being dumb;
For I impair not beauty being mute,
When others would give life, and bring a tomb.
summary: I stay quiet about my mistake because my silence protects what I love instead of harming it.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
Let no unkind ‘No’ fair beseechers kill;
Think all but one, and me in that one ‘Will.’
summary: I beg you not to reject me and to count me among those you accept.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
Have I not seen dwellers on form and favour
Lose all and more by paying too much rent
For compound sweet; forgoing simple savour,
Pitiful thrivers, in their gazing spent?
summary: I have watched people obsessed with looks and status lose everything chasing what does not last.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
Then need I not to fear the worst of wrongs,
When in the least of them my life hath end.
I see a better state to me belongs
Than that which on thy humour doth depend:
summary: I no longer fear your worst behavior because I have found a steadier life beyond your moods.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
Herein lives wisdom, beauty, and increase;
Without this folly, age, and cold decay:
If all were minded so, the times should cease
And threescore year would make the world away.
summary: Choosing to grow and create keeps beauty alive, while refusing leaves only aging and an empty future.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
Thy bosom is endeared with all hearts,
Which I by lacking have supposed dead;
And there reigns Love, and all Love’s loving parts,
And all those friends which I thought buried.
summary: I feel everyone I ever loved and thought I lost is still alive inside you.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
All days are nights to see till I see thee,
And nights bright days when dreams do show thee me.
summary: I feel like my days are dark without you and only my dreams of you bring light.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
O, no! thy love, though much, is not so great:
It is my love that keeps mine eye awake:
Mine own true love that doth my rest defeat,
To play the watchman ever for thy sake:
summary: I stay awake all night not because you love me but because my love watches over you.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
How heavy do I journey on the way,
When what I seek, my weary travel’s end,
Doth teach that ease and that repose to say,
‘Thus far the miles are measured from thy friend!’
summary: I feel exhausted traveling because every rest stop just reminds me how far I am from you.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
Not mine own fears, nor the prophetic soul
Of the wide world dreaming on things to come,
Can yet the lease of my true love control,
Supposed as forfeit to a confin’d doom.
summary: I refuse to let my fears or dark predictions shorten the time I will keep loving you.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
So long as men can breathe, or eyes can see,
So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.
summary: True love can live on through words as long as people are alive to read them.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
Tir’d with all these, from these would I be gone,
Save that, to die, I leave my love alone.
summary: I feel exhausted with life and want to disappear, but I stay because I cannot abandon you.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
Save that my soul’s imaginary sight
Presents thy shadow to my sightless view,
Which, like a jewel hung in ghastly night,
Makes black night beauteous, and her old face new.
summary: I picture you in the dark and the image makes my lonely night feel beautiful and new.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
Such is my love, to thee I so belong,
That for thy right, myself will bear all wrong.
summary: I love you so completely that I belong to you and will take the blame to protect you.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
But when my glass shows me myself indeed
Beated and chopp’d with tanned antiquity,
Mine own self-love quite contrary I read;
Self so self-loving were iniquity.
summary: I look in the mirror and see how old I have gotten, and I cannot love what I see anymore.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
O! that you were your self; but, love you are
No longer yours, than you yourself here live:
Against this coming end you should prepare,
And your sweet semblance to some other give:
summary: You need to think about the future and have a child who carries part of you forward.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
So I return rebuk’d to my content,
And gain by ill thrice more than I have spent.
summary: I came back humbled to what I have and feel I learned far more from the pain than it cost me.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
Nor dare I question with my jealous thought
Where you may be, or your affairs suppose,
But, like a sad slave, stay and think of nought
Save, where you are, how happy you make those.
summary: I am afraid to ask where you are, so I just wait sadly picturing how happy you make the people around you.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
In our two loves there is but one respect,
Though in our lives a separable spite,
Which though it alter not love’s sole effect,
Yet doth it steal sweet hours from love’s delight.
summary: We still love each other deeply, but something keeps us apart and robs us of happy time together.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
Love is too young to know what conscience is,
Yet who knows not conscience is born of love?
Then, gentle cheater, urge not my amiss,
Lest guilty of my faults thy sweet self prove:
summary: I feel guilty about my desires in love, but I tell myself true love should not judge me harshly.

author: William Shakespeare
summary: I am who I am, and people who criticize me are really revealing their own twisted thinking.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
Then others, for the breath of words respect,
Me for my dumb thoughts, speaking in effect.
summary: While others get praised for talking a lot, I stay quiet and let my actions speak for me.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
That you were once unkind befriends me now,
And for that sorrow, which I then did feel,
Needs must I under my transgression bow,
Unless my nerves were brass or hammer’d steel.
summary: Because you once hurt me, I now understand your pain and feel ashamed of how I treated you.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
But here’s the joy; my friend and I are one;
Sweet flattery! then she loves but me alone.
summary: I feel close to my best friend and tell myself his lover loving him means loving me too.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
And all in war with Time for love of you,
As he takes from you, I engraft you new.
summary: I will fight aging and time to keep you alive through my love and care.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
Sometime all full with feasting on your sight,
And by and by clean starved for a look;
Possessing or pursuing no delight,
Save what is had, or must from you be took.
summary: I feel full when I see you and empty when I cannot.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
Lo! thus, by day my limbs, by night my mind,
For thee, and for myself, no quiet find.
summary: I cannot rest day or night because I cannot stop thinking about you and us.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
So then I am not lame, poor, nor despis’d,
Whilst that this shadow doth such substance give
That I in thy abundance am suffic’d,
And by a part of all thy glory live.
summary: I feel whole and worthy because being connected to you lets me share your success.

author: William Shakespeare
text: Be wary then, best safety lies in fear. Youth to itself rebels, though none else near.
summary: I need to stay careful and a little afraid because youth makes me reckless even when no one is around.

author: William Shakespeare
text: I could interpret between you and your love, if I could see the puppets dallying.
summary: I joke that I could narrate for you and your lover if I watched you flirt together.

author: William Shakespeare
text: OPHELIA. You must sing ‘Down a-down, and you call him a-down-a.’ O, how the wheel becomes it!
summary: She sings a nonsense folk song out loud while unraveling from grief and confusion.

author: William Shakespeare
text: Ay, so, God b’ wi’ ye. Now I am alone. O what a rogue and peasant slave am I!
summary: I am finally alone and I hate myself for being a cowardly failure who does nothing.

author: William Shakespeare
text: I am satisfied in nature, Whose motive in this case should stir me most To my revenge.
summary: I feel in my gut that I have every personal reason to go after revenge now.

author: William Shakespeare
text: He is far gone, far gone. And truly in my youth I suffered much extremity for love; very near this.
summary: I see someone lovesick now and remember how intensely I suffered for love when I was young.

author: William Shakespeare
text: Then there’s hope a great man’s memory may outlive his life half a year.
summary: People forget even great people so quickly that being remembered for six months feels hopeful.

author: William Shakespeare
text: I am myself indifferent honest; but yet I could accuse me of such things that it were better my mother had not borne me.
summary: I am not really a good person and sometimes I feel so guilty I wish I had never been born.

author: William Shakespeare
text: Truly, and I hold ambition of so airy and light a quality that it is but a shadow’s shadow.
summary: I think chasing success is so empty and weightless that it feels like nothing at all.

author: William Shakespeare
text: I do not fear it. I have seen you both; But since he is better’d, we have therefore odds.
summary: I am not scared about the contest because I have watched us both and think I still have a chance.

author: William Shakespeare
text: Why, look you there! look how it steals away! My father, in his habit as he liv’d!
summary: I swear I just saw my dad standing there and now he is fading away before my eyes.

author: William Shakespeare
text: You should not have believed me; for virtue cannot so inoculate our old stock but we shall relish of it. I loved you not.
summary: I feel like I am too broken to be good for you and I never really loved you anyway.

author: William Shakespeare
text: You lie out on’t, sir, and therefore ’tis not yours. For my part, I do not lie in’t, yet it is mine.
summary: I am joking around with someone about who is lying and insisting that I am telling the truth.

author: William Shakespeare
text: But in my terms of honour I stand aloof, and will no reconcilement Till by some elder masters of known honour I have a voice and precedent of peace To keep my name ungor’d.
summary: I refuse to make peace and protect my reputation until respected elders say it is honorable.

author: William Shakespeare
text: How chances it they travel? Their residence, both in reputation and profit, was better both ways.
summary: Someone wonders why those performers are touring when staying home was better for fame and money.

author: William Shakespeare
text: Now what my love is, proof hath made you know, And as my love is siz’d, my fear is so.
summary: I love you deeply, so I worry just as much about what might happen to you.

author: William Shakespeare
text: OPHELIA. There’s fennel for you, and columbines. There’s rue for you; and here’s some for me. We may call it herb of grace o’ Sundays.
summary: I am handing out keepsakes while grieving and trying to make sense of my sorrow.

author: William Shakespeare
text: GHOST. Pity me not, but lend thy serious hearing To what I shall unfold.
summary: I need you to stop feeling sorry and really listen to what I have to tell you.

author: William Shakespeare
text: Nothing but to show you how a king may go a progress through the guts of a beggar.
summary: Even powerful people end up in the same humiliating decay as everyone else.

author: William Shakespeare
text: Hear you, sir; What is the reason that you use me thus? I lov’d you ever. But it is no matter.
summary: I do not understand why you treat me this way after I have always loved you, but never mind.

author: William Shakespeare
text: Lo, where it comes again! I’ll cross it, though it blast me. Stay, illusion!
summary: I see something frightening again and force myself to confront it even though it might destroy me.

author: William Shakespeare
text: A happiness that often madness hits on, which reason and sanity could not so prosperously be delivered of. I will leave him and suddenly contrive the means of meeting between him and my daughter.
summary: I realized crazy talk sometimes reveals truths that logic misses, so I will arrange for those two to meet.

author: William Shakespeare
text: What it should be, More than his father’s death, that thus hath put him So much from th’understanding of himself, I cannot dream of.
summary: I cannot understand what besides losing his father has made him seem like a stranger to himself.

author: William Shakespeare
text: Nature is fine in love, and where ’tis fine, It sends some precious instance of itself After the thing it loves.
summary: When people truly love, they send the best part of themselves to follow the person they love.

author: William Shakespeare
text: I do believe you think what now you speak; But what we do determine, oft we break.
summary: I trust you mean what you say right now, but I know we often fail to keep our own promises.

author: William Shakespeare
text: And this, I take it, Is the main motive of our preparations, The source of this our watch, and the chief head Of this post-haste and rummage in the land.
summary: I think all this frantic activity and late-night worry comes down to one underlying cause.

author: William Shakespeare
text: My tables. Meet it is I set it down, That one may smile, and smile, and be a villain!
summary: I need to write down this painful lesson that friendly smiling people can still betray you completely.

author: William Shakespeare
text: If your mind dislike anything, obey it. I will forestall their repair hither, and say you are not fit.
summary: I trust your gut feeling and I will cover for you by saying you are not feeling well.

author: William Shakespeare
text: I am very proud, revengeful, ambitious, with more offences at my beck than I have thoughts to put them in, imagination to give them shape, or time to act them in.
summary: I know I am arrogant and angry and driven, guilty of more wrong impulses than I could ever act on.

author: William Shakespeare
text: And now, good friends, As you are friends, scholars, and soldiers, Give me one poor request.
summary: I am asking you as trusted friends and capable people to do one small favor for me.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: There are those among you who seek the talkative through fear of being alone.
summary: Some people fill silence with chatter because they are afraid to sit alone with themselves.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: And if it is for your comfort to pour your darkness into space, it is also for your delight to pour forth the dawning of your heart.
summary: You feel relief sharing your struggles, and real joy when you share your hope too.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: And if it is a fear you would dispel, the seat of that fear is in your heart and not in the hand of the feared.
summary: What scares you is not out there; the real fear lives inside your own heart.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: Verily all things move within your being in constant half embrace, the desired and the dreaded, the repugnant and the cherished, the pursued and that which you would escape.
summary: You carry opposite feelings together, wanting and fearing different parts of life at once.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: Or have you only comfort, and the lust for comfort, that stealthy thing that enters the house a guest, and then becomes a host, and then a master?
summary: You wonder if chasing comfort has taken over until it controls your whole life.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: It is to build a house with affection, even as if your beloved were to dwell in that house.
summary: Putting care into work feels like building a home for someone deeply loved.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: For without words, in friendship, all thoughts, all desires, all expectations are born and shared, with joy that is unacclaimed.
summary: True friends understand each other without talking and share quiet happiness together every day.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: And when one of you falls down he falls for those behind him, a caution against the stumbling stone.
summary: When someone fails, their stumble becomes a warning that helps others behind them avoid it.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: Much have we loved you. But speechless was our love, and with veils has it been veiled.
summary: We loved you deeply but never said it openly and kept our feelings hidden away.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: See first that you yourself deserve to be a giver, and an instrument of giving.
summary: A person must first feel worthy of giving before they can truly help others.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: And my heart bled within me; for you can only be free when even the desire of seeking freedom becomes a harness to you, and when you cease to speak of freedom as a goal and a fulfilment.
summary: I feel heartbroken realizing true freedom means letting go of even obsessing over being free.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: And when you work with love you bind yourself to yourself, and to one another, and to God.
summary: When you work with love you feel connected to yourself and others in a deeper way.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: Long were the days of pain I have spent within its walls, and long were the nights of aloneness; and who can depart from his pain and his aloneness without regret?
summary: I spent so many painful lonely days here that leaving it behind still feels strangely sad.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: Oftentimes in denying yourself pleasure you do but store the desire in the recesses of your being.
summary: When you deny yourself pleasure, the wanting does not disappear but hides deeper inside you.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: That you, alone and unguarded, commit a wrong unto others and therefore unto yourself.
summary: When you are alone and unguarded, hurting others ends up hurting yourself as well.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: Yet was it not your loving mindfulness of my days and my nights that made food sweet to my mouth and girdled my sleep with visions?
summary: Your constant care for me made everyday life sweeter and filled my dreams with hope.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: And though death may hide me, and the greater silence enfold me, yet again will I seek your understanding.
summary: Even if death takes me away, I will still try to reach you and be understood.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: It is thy urge in us that would turn our nights, which are thine, into days which are thine also.
summary: I feel a higher power inside us trying to turn our darkness into light.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: Your fear of death is but the trembling of the shepherd when he stands before the king whose hand is to be laid upon him in honour.
summary: Your fear of dying is like nervous awe before receiving a great honor.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: And yet who does not feel that very love, though boundless, encompassed within the centre of his being, and moving not from love thought to love thought, nor from love deeds to other love deeds?
summary: Everyone feels boundless love held at their core rather than moving between thoughts and actions.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: But how shall I, unless you yourselves be also the peacemakers, nay, the lovers of all your elements?
summary: I cannot bring you peace unless you learn to accept and love every part of yourself.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: It makes mock of your sound senses, and lays them in thistledown like fragile vessels.
summary: Something powerful overwhelms my clear thinking and leaves me feeling delicate and exposed.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: In your longing for your giant self lies your goodness: and that longing is in all of you.
summary: Wanting to become my best self is what makes me good, and everyone shares that same yearning.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: But now our sleep has fled and our dream is over, and it is no longer dawn.
summary: We have woken up from a hopeful time and now face a harsher reality together.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: Where shall you seek beauty, and how shall you find her unless she herself be your way and your guide?
summary: You cannot find beauty somewhere else unless you let it guide how you live each day.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: And the selfsame well from which your laughter rises was oftentimes filled with your tears.
summary: Your greatest joy and your deepest sorrow seem to come from the same place inside you.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: Would that I could be the peacemaker in your soul, that I might turn the discord and the rivalry of your elements into oneness and melody.
summary: I wish I could calm the conflict inside you and help everything in you feel harmonious.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: And then to sleep with a prayer for the beloved in your heart and a song of praise upon your lips.
summary: You fall asleep thinking lovingly of the person you love and feeling thankful.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: Some of your youth seek pleasure as if it were all, and they are judged and rebuked.
summary: Some young people chase only fun and get harshly criticized for it by others.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: Now therefore disclose us to ourselves, and tell us all that has been shown you of that which is between birth and death.
summary: We want you to show us who we really are and what life truly means.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: But I’m only interested in being able to love the world, not to despise it, not to hate it and me, to be able to look upon it and me and all beings with love and admiration and great respect.”
summary: I just want to love the world and myself instead of judging everything with hate and contempt.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: How I hated myself, have deprived, poisoned, tortured myself, have made myself old and evil!
summary: I hate myself for how I have damaged and poisoned my own life over time.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: These people are rare who know how to listen. And I did not meet a single one who knew it as well as you did.
summary: I finally met someone who truly listens better than anyone else I have ever known.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: Never I’ll stop searching, this seems to be my destiny. You too, so it seems to me, have been searching.
summary: I feel like I will always be searching for more, and I can tell you are searching too.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: There, where I ran away from, there everything smelled of ointments, of spices, of wine, of excess, of sloth. How I hated this world of the rich, of those who revel in fine food, of the gamblers! How I hated myself for staying in this terrible world for so long!
summary: I ran away from a greedy wealthy lifestyle that disgusted me and I hate myself for staying so long.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: This is what makes them so dear and worthy of veneration for me: they are like me. Therefore, I can love them.
summary: I finally feel close to other people because I see myself in them and that lets me love them.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: Even bad people, even thieves and robbers have children and love them, and are being loved by them, all except for me.”
summary: I feel like everyone else gets to be loved by their family except me, no matter how flawed they are.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: I had to spend many years losing my spirit, to unlearn thinking again, to forget the oneness.
summary: I wasted years shutting down my inner life and forgetting what once made everything feel connected and clear.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: Time is not real, Govinda, I have experienced this often and often again. And if time is not real, then the gap which seems to be between the world and the eternity, between suffering and blissfulness, between evil and good, is also a deception.”
summary: I keep realizing time is an illusion, so the distance between pain and peace and bad and good is not real.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: You’ve changed a lot, my friend.—And so you’ve now become a ferryman?”
summary: Seeing an old friend after a long time and being surprised by how much their life has changed.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: But I was not able to overcome it, could only deceive it, could only flee from it, only hide from it.
summary: I cannot face my problem head on and just keep avoiding it and hiding from it.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: Sometimes, for an hour or for an entire day, I have felt knowledge in me, as one would feel life in one’s heart.
summary: I sometimes feel a deep understanding inside me that feels as alive as my own heartbeat.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: I had to sin, to be able to live again. Where else might my path lead me to?
summary: I feel like I had to mess everything up just to feel alive and wonder where I go next.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: And yet, this path has been very good; and yet, the bird in my chest has not died. But what a path has this been! I had to pass through so much stupidity, through so much vice, through so many errors, through so much disgust and disappointments and woe, just to become a child again and to be able to start over. But it was right so, my heart says “Yes” to it, my eyes smile to it.
summary: I went through many stupid mistakes and pain, but I am grateful because it let me start fresh.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: Behold, now you’ve turned into a man and are choosing your path for yourself.
summary: You have grown up and are now choosing your own path in life.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: Dead to himself, not to be a self any more, to find tranquility with an emptied heart, to be open to miracles in unselfish thoughts, that was his goal.
summary: He wants to let go of his ego completely and find peace by thinking only of others.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: Therefore, I can love them. And this is now a teaching you will laugh about: love, oh Govinda, seems to me to be the most important thing of all. To thoroughly understand the world, to explain it, to despise it, may be the thing great thinkers do.
summary: I have realized that loving people matters more than trying to analyze or judge the world.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: You have renounced your home and your parents, renounced your birth and possessions, renounced your free will, renounced all friendship. This is what the teachings require, this is what the exalted one wants. This is what you wanted for yourself.
summary: You gave up your home, family, belongings, freedom, and friendships to follow a spiritual path you chose.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: For more than three years, I have been without possessions, and have never thought about of what I should live.”
summary: I have lived with almost nothing for years and never worried about how I would get by.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: To be honest, I also have no high opinion of thoughts. I have a better opinion of things.
summary: I do not trust abstract ideas much anymore and prefer to focus on real things I can experience.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: But what will become of you? Aren’t you able to do anything else but thinking, fasting, making poetry?”
summary: I worry that you only think and create and have no practical skills for your future life.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: No longer, I want to begin my thoughts and my life with Atman and with the suffering of the world.
summary: I want to restart my life by facing deep truth and the pain everyone carries.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: Let the things be illusions or not, after all I would then also be an illusion, and thus they are always like me.
summary: I wonder if everything is unreal, then I must be unreal too, so we are the same.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: Stay with me, Siddhartha, my friend. I used to have a wife, her bed was next to mine, but she has died a long time ago, for a long time, I have lived alone.
summary: I am an old widower who has lived alone for years and I am asking you to stay with me.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: It is unlikely for one of us to see the other again in this incarnation. I see, beloved, that you have found peace. I confess that I haven’t found it.
summary: I know we will probably never meet again and I see you have found peace that I still lack.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: I came to tell you that it is my longing to leave your house tomorrow and go to the ascetics.
summary: I finally want to leave this comfortable home tomorrow to pursue a simpler spiritual life.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: And then, so it seems, I have fallen asleep myself, I who wanted to guard your sleep.
summary: I feel guilty because I fell asleep myself when I had promised to stay awake and watch over you.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: It has come to you in the course of your own search, on your own path, through thoughts, through meditation, through realizations, through enlightenment.
summary: You finally found clarity on your own by thinking deeply and following your personal journey.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: How shouldn’t I reach that goal, which I have set for myself yesterday: to be your friend and to learn the joys of love from you!
summary: I feel hopeful I can become closer to you and finally learn what real love feels like.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: Light and shadow ran through his eyes, stars and moon ran through his heart.
summary: He feels overwhelmed with emotion as light and darkness move through him all at once.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I only mean to say that I have a feeling that it never was intended I should live long.
summary: I have a quiet feeling that I am not meant to live a long life.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I want to be great, or nothing. I won’t be a common-place dauber, so I don’t intend to try any more.”
summary: I would rather be amazing than average, so I feel like quitting altogether.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: You can go through the world with your elbows out and your nose in the air, and call it independence, if you like. That’s not my way.”
summary: I think your cold independence is not real strength and I choose kindness instead.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: Then your father came, and I was so happy that I found it easy to be good.
summary: I felt so happy when he came home that being good felt easy.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: You are not like your old self a bit, and seem ever so far away from me. I don’t mean to plague you and will bear it like a man, but I do wish it was all settled.
summary: I feel you have changed and grown distant, and I just want things resolved between us.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I have no fears for you, yet I am anxious that you should take this trouble rightly. Don’t grieve and fret when I am gone, or think that you can be idle and comfort yourselves by being idle and trying to forget.
summary: I trust you completely but I worry how you will handle this hard time after I leave.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: My rooms are always open to you, and your own shall be as comfortable as I can make it. There are some pleasant people in the house if you feel sociable, and your evenings are always free.
summary: I want you to feel at home here and know you can join others or have quiet time.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I never wanted to go away, and the hard part now is the leaving you all.
summary: I did not want to leave, and saying goodbye to everyone I love hurts the most.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I, too, have seen them all, and heartily believe in the sincerity of your resolution, since it begins to bear fruit. Go on, dear, patiently and bravely, and always believe that no one sympathizes more tenderly with you than your loving...
summary: I see how hard you are trying to change and I fully support you to keep going.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: It was getting late, and I was afraid if it wasn’t done right away that I shouldn’t have it done at all, and you know when I start to do a thing, I hate to give it up.
summary: I stayed up late to finish because I knew I would quit if I waited and I hate quitting.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I begin to feel quite young already, for somehow all my troubles seemed to fly away when you came.
summary: I feel young and light again because just having you here makes all my worries disappear.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: All about people you know, and such fun! You ought to hear it, and I’ve been aching to tell it this long time.
summary: I have such a funny story about people we both know and I cannot wait to tell you everything.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I asked for splendid things, to be sure, but in my heart I knew I should be satisfied, if I had a little home, and John, and some dear children like these.
summary: I dreamed of big impressive things but I know I would be happy with a small home and a loving family.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: If you’d remember that, and practice it, you’d be better liked than I am, because there is more of you.”
summary: You have so much potential that if you keep practicing kindness you will be loved even more than me.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I want to know so much, for I can’t go to work with any heart until I learn whether I am to have my reward in the end or not.”
summary: I need answers so badly because I cannot focus on my work until I know if it will pay off.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: The happy old times can’t come back, and we mustn’t expect it. We are man and woman now, with sober work to do, for playtime is over, and we must give up frolicking. I’m sure you feel this.
summary: I know our carefree childhood is over and now we have to grow up and face adult responsibilities together.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I’m not afraid, but it seems as if I should be homesick for you even in heaven.”
summary: I am not scared of dying but I know I will miss you terribly no matter where I end up.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: Make this home happy, so that you may be fit for homes of your own, if they are offered you, and contented here if they are not. One thing remember, my girls.
summary: Learning to create happiness at home now prepares you for whatever future family life brings.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I’m sure you feel this. I see the change in you, and you’ll find it in me. I shall miss my boy, but I shall love the man as much, and admire him more, because he means to be what I hoped he would.
summary: I can see you have grown up and I miss who you were but I admire the adult you are becoming.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: For I felt a great many in my heart. We have such funny times, and now I can enjoy them, for everyone is so desperately good, it’s like living in a nest of turtledoves.
summary: I feel so much love inside because life with these kind people is joyful and funny every day.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: Now put on all your best things, and I’ll tell you how to behave at each place, so that you will make a good impression. I want people to like you, and they would if you’d only try to be a little more agreeable.
summary: I want you to look your best and act friendly so people will like you.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I’m cross and have been out of sorts all day. I like to have you tell me my faults and be sisterly, so don’t mind if I am grumpy sometimes. I thank you all the same.”
summary: I have been grumpy all day but I still want your honest feedback and appreciate your support.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I only came here because I don’t know many people and felt rather strange at first, you know.”
summary: I only showed up because I barely know anyone and I felt awkward and out of place at first.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I want to do something splendid before I go into my castle, something heroic or wonderful that won’t be forgotten after I’m dead. I don’t know what, but I’m on the watch for it, and mean to astonish you all some day.
summary: I want to do something amazing and unforgettable with my life before I settle down.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: While Hannah and I did your work, you got on pretty well, though I don’t think you were very happy or amiable. So I thought, as a little lesson, I would show you what happens when everyone thinks only of herself.
summary: I did your work to show you how unhappy everyone is when we only think of ourselves.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: It is so pleasant to be out in this great room and creep around as I please!
summary: I finally feel free and happy to move around this big space however I want.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: Life is very much more exciting now than it used to be. You see I have something more to expect, to look forward to, to watch.
summary: My life feels exciting again because I finally have something interesting to anticipate and follow.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: At night in any kind of light, in twilight, candlelight, lamplight, and worst of all by moonlight, it becomes bars!
summary: At night the familiar pattern changes and starts looking like cold prison bars.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: I don’t want to go out, and I don’t want to have anybody come in, till John comes.
summary: I want to stay alone in my room and see no one until the person I trust returns.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: It is getting to be a great effort for me to think straight. Just this nervous weakness, I suppose.
summary: I feel so mentally exhausted lately that even thinking clearly takes real effort.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I never can write it again, and I’ll never forgive you as long as I live.”
summary: I am so furious about what you destroyed that I know I can never redo it or forgive you.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I felt I ought to do it, for life is uncertain and I don’t want any ill feeling over my tomb.”
summary: I feel I should make peace now because life feels fragile and I want no grudges left behind me.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: You can do your part out West, I can do mine here, and both be happy hoping for the best, and leaving the future to be as God wills.”
summary: I am learning to accept living apart and staying hopeful while we each do our best where we are.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I’m to be a famous musician myself, and all creation is to rush to hear me. And I’m never to be bothered about money or business, but just enjoy myself and live for what I like.
summary: I dream of becoming a famous musician with crowds adoring me and no worries about money ever again.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: You get everything you want out of people. I don’t know how you do it, but you are a born wheedler.”
summary: I am amused at how you always charm people into giving you exactly what you want.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: I thought it was a good time to talk, so I told him that I really was not gaining here, and that I wished he would take me away.
summary: I finally spoke up to say this place is not helping me and I want to leave.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: Of course I don’t when John is here, or anybody else, but when I am alone.
summary: I act normal around other people but do things differently when I am completely alone.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: But John says if I feel so I shall neglect proper self-control; so I take pains to control myself,—before him, at least,—and that makes me very tired.
summary: I force myself to act composed around him even though pretending all the time leaves me exhausted.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: In this damp weather it is awful. I wake up in the night and find it hanging over me.
summary: I wake up at night feeling anxious and overwhelmed by something looming over me in this gloomy place.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: There is nothing so dangerous, so fascinating, to a temperament like yours.
summary: Someone with your sensitive personality can find certain things both dangerous and completely captivating.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: So now she is gone, and the servants are gone, and the things are gone, and there is nothing left but that great bedstead nailed down, with the canvas mattress we found on it.
summary: Everyone has left and I am alone in an empty room with only heavy old furniture remaining.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: Personally, I believe that congenial work, with excitement and change, would do me good.
summary: I feel I would feel better if I had meaningful work that brings excitement and variety.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: But I don’t want to go there at all. I had a friend who was in his hands once, and she says he is just like John and my brother, only more so!
summary: I really do not want to see that specialist because I hear he is controlling just like the men in my family.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: Why, I wouldn’t have a child of mine, an impressionable little thing, live in such a room for worlds.
summary: I would never let my young child stay in a creepy room like this for anything.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: Else, why should it be let so cheaply? And why have stood so long untenanted?
summary: Something feels wrong about this cheap place that has been empty for so long.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: It strikes me occasionally, just as a scientific hypothesis, that perhaps it is the paper!
summary: I keep wondering if this wallpaper in my room is actually what is making me feel so unwell.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: That spoils my ghostliness, I am afraid; but I don’t care—there is something strange about the house—I can feel it.
summary: I feel silly for being spooked, but I cannot shake the sense that something is off in this house.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: I sometimes fancy that in my condition if I had less opposition and more society and stimulus—but John says the very worst thing I can do is to think about my condition, and I confess it always makes me feel bad.
summary: I think I would feel better with more support and company, but I am told not to dwell on how I feel.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: I always lock the door when I creep by daylight. I can’t do it at night, for I know John would suspect something at once.
summary: I lock my door during the day to hide what I am doing because I am afraid of getting caught.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: It is very seldom that mere ordinary people like John and myself secure ancestral halls for the summer.
summary: I feel lucky and a little out of place renting such a grand historic house for the summer.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: I’m feeling ever so much better! I don’t sleep much at night, for it is so interesting to watch developments; but I sleep a good deal in the daytime.
summary: I finally feel better and stay up at night fascinated by what is happening, then sleep all day.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: But I said it was so quiet and empty and clean now that I believed I would lie down again and sleep all I could; and not to wake me even for dinner—I would call when I woke.
summary: I told them everything feels calm and clear now so I just want to be left alone to sleep.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: Nobody would believe what an effort it is to do what little I am able—to dress and entertain, and order things.
summary: No one understands how exhausting it is for me just to get dressed and handle basic daily tasks.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: He says no one but myself can help me out of it, that I must use my will and self-control and not let any silly fancies run away with me.
summary: I was told that only I can fix myself by trying harder and not letting my imagination get out of control.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: It is quite alone, standing well back from the road, quite three miles from the village.
summary: The house sits completely isolated far back from the road miles outside town.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: There I live, and there I hear from day to day the low hum of restful life. In winter’s twilight, when the red sun glows, I can see the dark figures pass between the halls to the music of the night-bell.
summary: I feel at peace watching people head home across campus as the sun sets in winter.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: As I lingered there in the joy and pain of meeting old school-friends, there swept over me a sudden longing to pass again beyond the blue hill, and to see the homes and the school of other days, and to learn how life had gone with my school-children; and I went.
summary: I felt happy and sad seeing old friends and suddenly needed to revisit my old school and check on everyone.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: Love-songs are scarce and fall into two categories—the frivolous and light, and the sad.
summary: Most love songs feel either shallow and fun or deeply sad with little in between.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: I saw much of this family afterwards, and grew to love them for their honest efforts to be decent and comfortable, and for their knowledge of their own ignorance.
summary: I got to know a struggling family over time and came to love their honesty and humility.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: Then it dawned upon me with a certain suddenness that I was different from the others; or like, mayhap, in heart and life and longing, but shut out from their world by a vast veil.
summary: I suddenly realized I was just like everyone else inside but still shut out from their world.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: She didn’t know I was in the room, and when I asked her in a quiet, a very quiet voice, with the most restrained manner possible, what she was doing with the paper she turned around as if she had been caught stealing, and looked quite angry—asked me why I should frighten her so!
summary: I tried to ask calmly what she was doing and she snapped at me like I had caught her doing something wrong.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: He said I was his darling and his comfort and all he had, and that I must take care of myself for his sake, and keep well.
summary: He tells me I mean everything to him and asks me to stay healthy for his sake.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: It is so discouraging not to have any advice and companionship about my work.
summary: I feel discouraged working alone with no one to guide me or share ideas with.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: I tried to lift and push it until I was lame, and then I got so angry I bit off a little piece at one corner—but it hurt my teeth.
summary: I strained to move something heavy until I got furious and hurt myself trying to bite it.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: I never thought of it before, but it is lucky that John kept me here after all. I can stand it so much easier than a baby, you see.
summary: I am starting to think it is good I stayed here because I can handle this better than a child could.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: I long for work. I pant for a life full of striving. I am no coward, to shrink before the rugged rush of the storm, nor even quail before the awful shadow of the Veil. But hearken, O Death!
summary: I want hard meaningful work and a life of effort, and I am not afraid to face hardship head on.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: Alas, with the years all this fine contempt began to fade; for the words I longed for, and all their dazzling opportunities, were theirs, not mine.
summary: I slowly realized the exciting future and language I wanted actually belonged to other people, not me.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: Freedom, too, the long-sought, we still seek,—the freedom of life and limb, the freedom to work and think, the freedom to love and aspire.
summary: We are still chasing real freedom to live safely, work, think, love, and dream big.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: Ever since I was a child these songs have stirred me strangely. They came out of the South unknown to me, one by one, and yet at once I knew them as of me and of mine.
summary: Songs I heard growing up moved me deeply because they felt like part of who I am.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
