text: Nothing new, no time-saving devices,—simply old time-glorified methods of delving for Truth, and searching out the hidden beauties of life, and learning the good of living.
summary: The best learning still comes from slow traditional ways of finding truth and appreciating life.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: Nor can we pause here. We are training not isolated men but a living group of men,—nay, a group within a group. And the final product of our training must be neither a psychologist nor a brickmason, but a man.
summary: We should educate whole people rooted in community, not just train them for jobs.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: Some of these thoughts of mine have seen the light before in other guise.
summary: I feel like I have shared some of these ideas before in different forms.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: I remembered the broken, blighted family that used to live there. The strong, hard face of the mother, with its wilderness of hair, rose before me. She had driven her husband away, and while I taught school a strange man lived there, big and jovial, and people talked.
summary: I still picture that struggling household nearby and remember how neighbors gossiped about the mother.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: And now that he is gone, I sweep the Veil away and cry, Lo! the soul to whose dear memory I bring this little tribute.
summary: Now that he has passed, I want to honor his spirit openly with this memorial.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: I did not love it then; it seemed a ludicrous thing to love; but her I loved, my girl-mother, she whom now I saw unfolding like the glory of the morning—the transfigured woman.
summary: I did not appreciate that place at the time, but I loved my young mother and now see her strength clearly.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: The wretched of my race that line the alleys of the nation sit fatherless and unmothered; but Love sat beside his cradle, and in his ear Wisdom waited to speak.
summary: I see so many of my people feeling abandoned, yet I remember one child raised with deep love and wisdom.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: Why may I not rest me from this restlessness and sleep from this wide waking?
summary: I feel constantly restless and awake and just want to finally rest and sleep peacefully.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: All this I have ended with a tale twice told but seldom written, and a chapter of song.
summary: I am finishing my story with an old tale people rarely write down and some music.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: We cannot settle this problem by diplomacy and suaveness, by “policy” alone.
summary: We cannot fix this deep problem with polite talk and official policies alone.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: And yet it seemed a ghostly unreal day,—the wraith of Life. We seemed to rumble down an unknown street behind a little white bundle of posies, with the shadow of a song in our ears.
summary: We felt numb on a surreal day, following a small flower-covered coffin while music haunted our minds.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: How hard a thing is life to the lowly, and yet how human and real! And all this life and love and strife and failure,—is it the twilight of nightfall or the flush of some faint-dawning day?
summary: Life is brutally hard for struggling people yet deeply real, leaving wonder whether this is an ending or a beginning.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: The soul, long pent up and dwarfed, suddenly expands in new-found freedom. What wonder that every tendency is to excess,—radical complaint, radical remedies, bitter denunciation or angry silence. Some sink, some rise.
summary: After being held down for so long, finally feeling free can feel overwhelming, and some people cope while others fall apart.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: Patience, humility, and adroitness must, in these growing black youth, replace impulse, manliness, and courage. With this sacrifice there is an economic opening, and perhaps peace and some prosperity.
summary: Young people are told to stay quiet and obedient to get jobs and stay safe, giving up pride for security.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: It is a keen, hard struggle for living here, and few have time to talk.
summary: Life here is such a hard daily grind for survival that nobody has energy left to connect.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: Here is one now,—Shepherd’s, they call it,—a great whitewashed barn of a thing, perched on stilts of stone, and looking for all the world as though it were just resting here a moment and might be expected to waddle off down the road at almost any time.
summary: A big awkward white building sits oddly balanced on stones, looking like it could wander away down the road.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: But the loneliness overcame me. There I was in the midst of thousands, and yet a perfect stranger; without home and without friends, in the midst of thousands of my own brethren—children of a common Father, and yet I dared not to unfold to any one of them my sad condition.
summary: I felt completely alone in a huge crowd with no home or friends I could trust.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: But in spite of him, and even in spite of myself, I continued to think, and to think about the injustice of my enslavement, and the means of escape.
summary: I could not stop thinking about how unfair my situation was and how I might get out.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: I was at work for myself and newly-married wife. It was to me the starting-point of a new existence.
summary: I am finally working for myself and my new spouse and starting a whole new life.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: The love of them was my tender point, and shook my decision more than all things else. Besides the pain of separation, the dread and apprehension of a failure exceeded what I had experienced at my first attempt. The appalling defeat I then sustained returned to torment me. I felt assured that, if I failed in this attempt, my case would be a hopeless one—it would seal my fate as a slave forever.
summary: I am torn because I love them but I am scared another failed escape will trap me forever.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: I spent this in a sort of beast-like stupor, between sleep and wake, under some large tree. At times I would rise up, a flash of energetic freedom would dart through my soul, accompanied with a faint beam of hope, that flickered for a moment, and then vanished.
summary: I lay half asleep under a tree feeling numb, with brief flashes of hope for freedom that quickly faded.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: I had now been absent from it almost, if not quite, five years. I, however, remembered the place very well.
summary: I had been away for almost five years, but I still remembered the place clearly.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: I loved them with a love stronger than any thing I have experienced since.
summary: I loved those people more deeply than I have ever loved anyone since then.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: As the time drew near for our departure, our anxiety became more and more intense. It was truly a matter of life and death with us.
summary: We grew more anxious every day as leaving approached because everything felt at stake.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: My mother was dead, my grandmother lived far off, so that I seldom saw her.
summary: I had lost my mother and rarely saw my distant grandmother, so I felt alone.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: I was all alone, and within the walls of a stone prison. But a few days before, and I was full of hope.
summary: I felt completely alone locked up, even though I had been full of hope just days before.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: In any community or nation it is these little things which are most elusive to the grasp and yet most essential to any clear conception of the group life taken as a whole.
summary: I realize that small everyday details are hardest to explain but matter most for understanding a community.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: Was not the world’s alembic, Time, in his young hands, and is not my time waning?
summary: I feel my own time running out while a younger person still holds endless possibility ahead.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: And with all this change, so curiously parallel to that of the Other-world, goes too the same inevitable change in ideals.
summary: I notice my community's values are shifting just like the outside world's values are shifting too.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: And to make men, we must have ideals, broad, pure, and inspiring ends of living,—not sordid money-getting, not apples of gold. The worker must work for the glory of his handiwork, not simply for pay; the thinker must think for truth, not for fame.
summary: I believe we need inspiring purpose in life and work for pride and truth, not just money or fame.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: Here there can be none of that social going down to the people,—the opening of heart and hand of the best to the worst, in generous acknowledgment of a common humanity and a common destiny.
summary: I live where privileged and struggling people stay apart instead of recognizing our shared humanity and future.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: I have observed this in my experience of slavery,—that whenever my condition was improved, instead of its increasing my contentment, it only increased my desire to be free, and set me to thinking of plans to gain my freedom.
summary: Whenever my situation gets a little better, I just want full freedom even more and start planning for it.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: I have been frequently asked how I felt when I found myself in a free State.
summary: People often ask me how it felt when I finally reached a place where I was free.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: I had not gone far before my little strength again failed me. I could go no farther.
summary: I had barely started walking when my body gave out and I could not take another step.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: Here I was perplexed. I did not dare to ask any one about its meaning, for I was satisfied that it was something they wanted me to know very little about.
summary: I was confused but afraid to ask questions because I knew they were hiding the truth from me.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: I prefer to be true to myself, even at the hazard of incurring the ridicule of others, rather than to be false, and incur my own abhorrence.
summary: I would rather stay honest with myself and face judgment than lie and feel ashamed of myself.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: My cart was upset and shattered, my oxen were entangled among the young trees, and there was none to help me.
summary: I messed up badly with my work and I am stuck alone with no one to help me.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: My home was charmless; it was not home to me; on parting from it, I could not feel that I was leaving any thing which I could have enjoyed by staying.
summary: I am leaving a place that never felt like home and I feel no sadness about going.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: I had a number of warmhearted friends in Baltimore,—friends that I loved almost as I did my life,—and the thought of being separated from them forever was painful beyond expression.
summary: I love my close friends deeply and the thought of never seeing them again breaks my heart.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: I suffered more anxiety than most of my fellow-slaves. I had known what it was to be kindly treated; they had known nothing of the kind.
summary: I feel more anxious than those around me because I once knew what kindness felt like.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: I often found myself regretting my own existence, and wishing myself dead; and but for the hope of being free, I have no doubt but that I should have killed myself, or done something for which I should have been killed.
summary: I sometimes wish I were dead and only my hope for freedom keeps me from giving up.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: Now he is gone. Gone a second time, and I have lost him now for ever ... and he will not love me the littlest bit ever any more—only hate me!...
summary: I feel crushed because the man I love has left me for good and now hates me.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: I became another woman, filled full of new life from you. How could I be the early one?
summary: I feel completely changed by loving you and I can never go back to who I was before.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: It frightens me! Having begun to love you, I love you for ever—in all changes, in all disgraces, because you are yourself.
summary: I am scared by how deeply I love you and I will stay with you no matter what happens.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: My religious mania, or whatever it was, is over. But I retain a little good nature; I hope I do. Now, Tess, by all that’s tender and strong between man and woman, trust me! I have enough and more than enough to put you out of anxiety, both for yourself and your parents and sisters.
summary: I have moved past my intense phase and I want you to trust that I can take care of you and your family.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: My life looks as if it had been wasted for want of chances! When I see what you know, what you have read, and seen, and thought, I feel what a nothing I am!
summary: I feel like I wasted my life without opportunities and I seem worthless next to everything you know.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: This state of mind, however, very soon subsided; and I was again seized with a feeling of great insecurity and loneliness.
summary: I felt briefly better, then insecurity and loneliness hit me all over again.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: I sank down again, mourning over my wretched condition. I was sometimes prompted to take my life, and that of Covey, but was prevented by a combination of hope and fear.
summary: I collapsed feeling hopeless about my life and had dark thoughts, held back only by mixed hope and fear.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: When I could get no calking to do, I did nothing. During these leisure times, those old notions about freedom would steal over me again.
summary: When I had no work to do, I just sat idle and started dreaming about being free again.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: My discontent grew upon me. I was ever on the look-out for means of escape; and, finding no direct means, I determined to try to hire my time, with a view of getting money with which to make my escape.
summary: I grew more unhappy and kept looking for a way out, planning to earn money to escape.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: If, however, I found in my new home hardship, hunger, whipping, and nakedness, I had the consolation that I should not have escaped any one of them by staying.
summary: Even though my new place brought suffering and hunger, I knew staying would have been just as bad.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: I have lost my mother since you were at Trantridge, and the place is my own.
summary: I lost my mom recently and now I am on my own with the house.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: But I knew your mind all the same, and I thought as you thought—not from any reasons of my own, but because you thought so.
summary: I just went along with what you believed because I trusted you more than myself.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: But the loss of my mother hit me most; and by degrees I was brought to see daylight.
summary: Losing my mom broke me, but slowly I started to feel like myself again.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: But I intend to sell it, and devote myself to missionary work in Africa. A devil of a poor hand I shall make at the trade, no doubt. However, what I want to ask you is, will you put it in my power to do my duty—to make the only reparation I can make for the trick played you: that is, will you be my wife, and go with me?...
summary: I want to make up for hurting you by marrying you and starting a new life together abroad.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: But you have a friend, and I have determined that you shall be comfortable in spite of yourself.
summary: I will make sure you are okay even if you resist my help.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: It was a new and strange sight to me, brightening up my pathway with the light of happiness.
summary: I saw something new and unexpected that suddenly made my life feel brighter and happier.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: From that moment, I understood the pathway from slavery to freedom. It was just what I wanted, and I got it at a time when I the least expected it.
summary: I finally saw how I could get free, and it came when I least expected it.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: I have ever regarded it as the first plain manifestation of that kind providence which has ever since attended me, and marked my life with so many favors. I regarded the selection of myself as being somewhat remarkable.
summary: I still see that lucky break as the first sign that life was looking out for me.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: We tried to conceal our feelings as much as possible; and I think we succeeded very well.
summary: We tried hard to hide how we felt and think we pulled it off.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: But I must deprive myself of this pleasure, and the curious of the gratification which such a statement would afford.
summary: I have to hold back details I would enjoy sharing even though others really want to hear them.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: I was born bad, and I have lived bad, and I shall die bad in all probability.
summary: I feel like I have always been a bad person and I probably never will change.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: You are as weak as a bled calf, you know you are; and yet you need have done nothing since I arrived. How could you be so obstinate?
summary: You seem completely exhausted yet you stubbornly refuse to stop and rest a while.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: Now, permit me to put it in this way. You belong to me already, you know; your heart, I mean.
summary: I feel like your heart is already mine and you truly belong with me.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: But it strikes me that there is a want of harmony between your present mood of self-sacrifice and your past mood of self-preservation.”
summary: I notice your selfless attitude now does not match how self protective you were before.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: I think I should love you more, if that were possible, if you could bring yourself to do it, since there’s no other way of escape for ’ee.
summary: I would love you even more if you would do this hard thing to save us.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: Then I should not have wasted my time as I have done—I should have had so much longer happiness!”
summary: I feel I wasted so much time and missed out on happiness I could have had.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: I have thought it sad—especially since coming here, and knowing that many of the hills and fields I see once belonged to my father’s people.
summary: I feel sad looking at this land around me because it once belonged to my family.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: The best is not to remember that your nature and your past doings have been just like thousands’ and thousands’, and that your coming life and doings ’ll be like thousands’ and thousands’.”
summary: You find comfort in forgetting that your life is as ordinary as everyone else.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: The daylight has nothing to show me, since you are not here, and I don’t like to see the rooks and starlings in the field, because I grieve and grieve to miss you who used to see them with me.
summary: I miss you so much that everyday sights feel empty without you beside me.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: And if I can bring myself to bear it—if it is desirable, possible—I will come to you.
summary: I want to come to you if I can find the strength and if you still want me.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: D’Urberville was struck mute. “I knew nothing of this till now!” he next murmured.
summary: He was speechless after hearing shocking news he claims he never knew before.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: I am so exposed to temptation, Angel. I fear to say who it is, and I do not like to write about it at all.
summary: I feel vulnerable around someone tempting and I am too scared and ashamed to explain it in writing.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: You know that nobody wished to hinder your going. And how unnecessary it has been for you to toil along on foot, and encumber yourself with this heavy load! I have followed like a madman, simply to drive you the rest of the distance, if you won’t come back.”
summary: I chased after you on foot because I hated watching you struggle alone with a heavy load.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: Perhaps—perhaps you are a little better and kinder than I have been thinking you were. Whatever is meant as kindness I am grateful for; whatever is meant in any other way I am angered at.
summary: I am starting to think you might be kinder than I thought, and I appreciate real kindness but resent anything else.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: “I will leave something to show that I did it myself—on account of my shame.
summary: I want to leave proof that I acted alone because I feel too ashamed to let others take the blame.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: There are many questions that I am tempted to ask, but I will not do so, of course, in opposition to your wishes.
summary: I have so many questions I want to ask you but I will respect your boundaries and stay quiet.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: Why did you go away—why did you—when I loved you so? I can’t think why you did it.
summary: I still do not understand why you left me when I loved you so deeply.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: What I am in worldly estate, she is. What I become, she must become. What I cannot be, she cannot be.
summary: I feel like my partner shares my social standing and future completely, for better or worse.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: If it is I you do love, O how can it be that you look and speak so? It frightens me!
summary: I am scared because if you really love me I cannot understand why you act so cold.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: I am, as I say, worried, pressed to do what I will not do. It cannot be that I shall yield one inch, yet I am in terror as to what an accident might lead to, and I so defenceless on account of my first error. I cannot say more about this—it makes me too miserable. But if I break down by falling into some fearful snare, my last state will be worse than my first.
summary: I feel pressured to do something wrong and I am terrified my past mistake leaves me vulnerable to ruin.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: So many lives depending on my attention, you see, my man, that I can’t give so much thought as I would like to other things.”
summary: I feel stretched thin by everyone counting on me and cannot focus on what I actually care about.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: I wish we hadn’t come! The place gives me the horrors: it seems so unnatural as the climax of our love! I wish it had been at church, if it had to be at all.
summary: I regret coming here with you because this cold place feels like the wrong way to celebrate our love.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: I have always regretted that feint of ours in going away and pretending to come back legally married, to save appearances. I loved you, and you loved me; and we closed with each other; and that made the marriage.
summary: I wish we had not lied about being married because our mutual love already made us truly committed.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: I may feel as well as you that I have a perfect right to live with you as you thought—from this moment.
summary: I believe starting now I have every right to live with you just as you expected.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: That’s unfortunate. I have hardly any other friend. I have, indeed, one very old friend here somewhere, but I don’t quite like to call on him just yet.
summary: I feel alone here with almost no friends and I am not ready to reach out to the one I know.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: Self-renunciation—that’s everything! I cannot humiliate myself too much.
summary: I feel like giving up everything about myself is the only right thing to do.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: I should never have noticed their being in love, if you hadn’t said so.”
summary: I would never have realized those two people liked each other if you had not pointed it out.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: I think it will be better both for you and for me. I wish some things had never begun! I was much to blame, I know.
summary: I think ending this is best for us both and I blame myself for letting it start at all.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: So I am not a bit frightened about losing you, now I really am yours and you really are mine.
summary: I feel completely secure with you now because we truly belong to each other.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: I daresay you think me eccentric, or super-sensitive, or something absurd. Well—why should I suffer for what I was born to be, if it doesn’t hurt other people?”
summary: I know you think I am strange and oversensitive, but why should I apologize for how I am.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: But I have an uncomfortable feeling that my freedom has been obtained under false pretences!”
summary: I feel guilty that the freedom I finally have might be based on a lie.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: Why should we faint, and fear to live alone, Since all alone, so Heaven has will’d, we die?
summary: I remind myself not to fear being alone in life since we all face death alone.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: The life suits us, certainly; but if we could get away to a place where we are unknown, we should be lighter hearted, and have a better chance. And so I am afraid we must break it up here, however awkward for you, poor dear!”
summary: I love our life here but I think we need to move somewhere fresh where nobody knows us.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: You think you are the stronger; and so you are, in a physical sense, now. You could push me over like a nine-pin. You did not send that letter the other day, and I could not resent your conduct. But I am not so weak in another way as you think.
summary: I may be physically weaker than you, but I am stronger inside than you realize.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: But I can’t say any more—it breaks my heart—it will be undoing all I have begun!
summary: I have to stop talking because it hurts too much and threatens everything I have started.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: Let them go! Let me help you, even if I do love you, and even if you…”
summary: I want to let go of everything else and stay to support you even though I love you

author: Thomas Hardy
text: And there is no reason to wish it. We gave up all ambition, and were never so happy in our lives till his illness came.”
summary: We gave up chasing success and were truly happy together until sickness changed everything for us

author: Thomas Hardy
text: “I never heard anything of you, or I don’t know that I should have come here.
summary: I had no news about you for so long that I wonder why I even came back here

author: Thomas Hardy
text: Be kind to me—even though I have not been kind to you! I will go away, go abroad, anywhere, and never trouble you.
summary: Please treat me gently despite how I hurt you, and I promise to leave you alone

author: Thomas Hardy
text: But I have always striven to do what has pleased me. I well deserved the scourging I have got! I wish something would take the evil right out of me, and all my monstrous errors, and all my sinful ways!”
summary: I have always lived selfishly and I hate myself for it and desperately want to change

author: Thomas Hardy
text: It is a thing I never thought o’, wi’ all my experience! I never thought beyond bringing about the real thing—not that one could sham it!”
summary: I never imagined with all my experience that someone could fake something I thought was always real.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: I have thought that we have been selfish, careless, even impious, in our courses, you and I. Our life has been a vain attempt at self-delight. But self-abnegation is the higher road.
summary: I feel our relationship has been selfish and empty, and I now believe putting others first is the better path.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: It amazes me when I think of it! I have not been conscious of it, or of any wrongdoing towards you, whom I love more than myself.
summary: I am shocked looking back because I never meant to hurt you, and I love you more than myself.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: I can’t help being as I am, I am convinced I am right—that I see the light at last.
summary: I cannot change who I am, and I finally feel clear and confident that I am on the right path.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: I have hopelessly ruined my prospects because of my decision as to what was best for us, though she does not know it; I see only dire poverty ahead from my feet to the grave; for I can be accepted as teacher no more.
summary: I ruined my career by choosing what I thought was best for us, and now I only see poverty ahead.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: I haven’t been alone one minute since it happened--and I want to be. I want to be quite silent and quiet and try to realize it.
summary: I just need some time alone in silence to process what just happened to me.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: You see, I’ve never had a real home since I can remember. It gives me that pleasant ache again just to think of coming to a really truly home.
summary: I have never really had a home and dreaming about finally belonging somewhere hurts in a good way.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: I’ve always been afraid of it, and now I know it is so. Well, I suppose I shall just have to resign myself to it.”
summary: I always feared this would happen and now that it has I am trying to accept it.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: And it’s so hard to keep from loving things, isn’t it? That was why I was so glad when I thought I was going to live here. I thought I’d have so many things to love and nothing to hinder me.
summary: I fall in love with everything so easily and I thought moving here would finally let me love freely.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: I couldn’t have Diana stay, she’s good and kind and sweet--but it’s not her sorrow--she’s outside of it and she couldn’t come close enough to my heart to help me. It’s our sorrow--yours and mine.
summary: I need to grieve privately with someone who truly shares this loss because others cannot reach my pain.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: All that’s best and noblest in me loves you, and your freedom from everything that’s gross has elevated me, and enabled me to do what I should never have dreamt myself capable of, or any man, a year or two ago.
summary: I love you deeply because you bring out the best in me and help me become someone better.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: I made up my mind that a man confined to his room by inflammation of the lungs, a fellow who had only two wishes left in the world, to see a particular woman, and then to die, could neatly accomplish those two wishes at one stroke by taking this journey in the rain. That I’ve done. I have seen her for the last time, and I’ve finished myself—put an end to a feverish life which ought never to have been begun!”
summary: I was so sick and heartbroken that I risked my health for one last visit, feeling ready to give up.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: I saw that schools were admitted in the afternoons, and thought you might come; but I got so deeply interested that I didn’t remember where I was.
summary: I hoped you would show up where I was visiting, but I got so absorbed I lost track of time.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: You had got my promise a long time before that, remember. Then, as time went on, I regretted I had promised you, and was trying to see an honourable way to break it off.
summary: I had promised you something long ago, but later I regretted it and wanted a decent way out.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: You have been my social salvation. Stay with me for humanity’s sake! You know what a weak fellow I am.
summary: You saved me socially and I feel too weak to manage alone, so I am begging you to stay.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: It makes me feel so sorrowful--just as I feel when I look at any ugly thing.
summary: I feel really sad about this, the same heavy way ugly things make me feel.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: But I can understand your feeling. I think we all experience the same thing.
summary: I totally get how you feel because I think everyone goes through that same thing sometimes.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: I mean to devote all my energies to being good after this and I shall never try to be beautiful again. Of course it’s better to be good. I know it is, but it’s sometimes so hard to believe a thing even when you know it.
summary: I want to focus on being a good person instead of looks, even though that truth is hard to really feel.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: I suppose people of that kind serve some useful purpose in society, but I must say I don’t know what it is any more than I know the use of thistles.
summary: I guess certain annoying people must be good for something, but I honestly cannot figure out what it is.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: I feel it’s a great responsibility because I have only the one chance. If I don’t grow up right I can’t go back and begin over again. I’ve grown two inches this summer, Marilla.
summary: I feel huge pressure to grow up right since I only get one chance, and I notice I am changing fast.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: And I’m afraid I’ll never be able to think out another one as good. Somehow, things never are so good when they’re thought out a second time.
summary: I worry I peaked with one good idea and trying to redo it will never feel as good.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: It’s at times like this I’m sorry I’m not a model little girl; and I always resolve that I will be in future. But somehow it’s hard to carry out your resolutions when irresistible temptations come.
summary: I feel bad for messing up and promise to be better, but it is hard when temptation hits.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: I just let my thoughts run and I thought of the most surprising things.”
summary: I let my mind wander freely and ended up amazed by where my imagination went.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: I know I talk too much, but I am really trying to overcome it, and although I say far too much, yet if you only knew how many things I want to say and don’t, you’d give me some credit for it.
summary: I know I talk too much and I am trying to hold back more than anyone realizes.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: I’d go crazy with trouble and loneliness. And my sight would go--I know it would.”
summary: I feel like stress and being alone would break me and even affect my health.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: I’m sorry you won’t have a home to come to in your vacations, that’s all, but I suppose you’ll manage somehow.”
summary: I feel bad that you have nowhere welcoming to return to for the holidays.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: Last night I was horribly lonesome all alone in my room and wished so much you were with me.
summary: I felt so lonely alone in my room last night and just wanted you here with me.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: But I feel very sad. I’ve just been imagining that it was really me you wanted after all and that I was to stay here for ever and ever. It was a great comfort while it lasted.
summary: I feel sad after pretending you actually chose me and I could stay here forever.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: I’ve tried to be patient all the morning, but I really feel that I cannot bear not knowing any longer. It’s a dreadful feeling.
summary: I tried to stay patient all morning but I cannot stand waiting without answers anymore.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: I feel sure I was born under an unlucky star. Everything I do gets me or my dearest friends into a scrape.
summary: I feel like I was born unlucky because everything I do causes trouble for me and my friends.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: Why, Diana, I didn’t think anybody could love me. Nobody ever has loved me since I can remember.
summary: I finally feel loved for the first time and I am shocked that someone actually cares about me.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: I felt like I do when I look up to the stars. Tears came into my eyes, but, oh, they were such happy tears.
summary: I was so overwhelmed with wonder and happiness that I started crying happy tears like looking at stars.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: Oh, it seems so wonderful that I’m going to live with you and belong to you.
summary: I am so happy that I finally have a home and I truly belong with people who want me.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: Oh, I can’t tell you how I felt. But it seemed to me that it could never be hard to be good any more.
summary: I felt so inspired and hopeful that being a good person suddenly felt easy and natural to me.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: It shows our club is doing some good in the world. Mrs. Allan says that ought to be our object in everything. I do really try to make it my object but I forget so often when I’m having fun.
summary: I am proud our group is helping others, and I try to stay focused on that even when fun distracts me.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: I feel just now that I may grow up to be sensible yet. But perhaps that is only because I’m tired.
summary: I am so exhausted right now that I finally feel calm and sensible, though it might not last.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: I thought when it happened I could never laugh again. And it somehow seems as if I oughtn’t to.”
summary: After what happened I thought I would never laugh again and I still feel guilty when I do.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: But just now I feel as if it were joy enough to sit here and look at you. I’m tired, I think--tired of being studious and ambitious.
summary: I am exhausted from pushing myself so hard and right now just being near you feels like enough.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: Mine was that I would marry a dark-complected man who was very wealthy, and I would go across water to live. I looked carefully at all the dark men I saw after that, but I didn’t care much for any of them, and anyhow I suppose it’s too early to be looking out for him yet. Oh, it was a never-to-be-forgotten day, Marilla. I was so tired I couldn’t sleep at night.
summary: I spent the day daydreaming about my exciting future marriage and was too wired to sleep that night.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: I feel irresistibly tempted to do it. Now, what do you think is the reason I feel like that? Do you think it’s because I’m really bad and unregenerate?”
summary: I feel strongly tempted to misbehave and I keep wondering if that means I am a bad person.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: You won’t see much because it’s a dark night, but you can see something.”
summary: It is too dark to see clearly tonight, but I can still make out a little.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: You’ll have to play about and look after yourself. You’ll be told what rooms you can go into and what rooms you’re to keep out of. There’s gardens enough. But when you’re in the house don’t go wandering and poking about.
summary: I feel unwelcome in this house where I have to entertain myself and avoid certain rooms.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: I can’t stand lying still and pretending, and besides I look too different.
summary: I am tired of pretending to be sick and still because I have clearly changed.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: I dare say it will frighten them nearly into fits when they see me—but I am never going to get into the chair again.
summary: I know they will be shocked to see me walking, but I refuse to use my wheelchair anymore.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: I skip and run—and I look about to see if things are beginning to stick up out of the earth. I don’t do any harm.”
summary: I run around outside happily watching for new sprouts, and I am not hurting anything.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: It is very sad, now the poor beautiful thing is gone, to remember that many people never even knew that she had a child at all.”
summary: It feels heartbreaking that after she died most people never knew she was a mother.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: Sometimes I have been taken to places at the seaside, but I won’t stay because people stare at me.
summary: I avoid going on trips because I hate how strangers stare at me.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: But I am not as queer as I was before I began to like people and before I found the garden.”
summary: I feel less strange now that I have opened up to people and found my own peaceful place.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: I am going to make the scientific experiment of trying to get some and put it in myself and make it push and draw me and make me strong. I don’t know how to do it but I think that if you keep thinking about it and calling it perhaps it will come.
summary: I want to try focusing my thoughts to make myself stronger even though I am unsure how it works.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: The Magic in this garden has made me stand up and know I am going to live to be a man.
summary: I feel healed by this special place and now believe I will grow up strong and live fully.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: I feel—I feel as if I want to shout out something—something thankful, joyful!”
summary: I feel so full of happiness and gratitude that I just want to shout it out loud.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: But, strange as it seemed to him, there were minutes—sometimes half-hours—when, without his knowing why, the black burden seemed to lift itself again and he knew he was a living man and not a dead one.
summary: For brief moments his heavy sadness lifts and he suddenly feels alive again after feeling numb.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: Play out of doors as much as you like. It’s a big place and you may go where you like and amuse yourself as you like.
summary: Someone kindly tells me I am free to explore outside and enjoy myself anywhere I want.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: At first they thought I was too little to understand and now they think I don’t hear. But I do. My doctor is my father’s cousin.
summary: I feel ignored because adults assume I am too young to understand what they say around me.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: You are too sensitive about things. You must not undo the good which has been done.”
summary: Someone tells me I am overreacting and risking the progress I have already made.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: I’m going to see everything grow here. I’m going to grow here myself.”
summary: I feel hopeful watching new life around me because I finally feel myself starting to grow too.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: I wakened when it was bright moonlight two nights ago and felt as if the Magic was filling the room and making everything so splendid that I couldn’t lie still. I got up and looked out of the window.
summary: I woke up to bright moonlight feeling full of wonder and too restless and amazed to stay in bed.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: This room and the next are where you’ll live—and you must keep to them.
summary: I feel trapped because I am told I must stay inside my small rooms alone.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: I had never watched things before and it made me feel very curious. Scientific people are always curious and I am going to be scientific. I keep saying to myself, ‘What is it?
summary: I am noticing the world closely for the first time and feel curious to learn how everything works.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: If they died I should feel as if I’d been a bad lad and somehow treated them heartless.”
summary: I worry that if those I care for died I would feel guilty for not treating them kindly enough.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: I should have to give up my place in time, for fear of doing my muscles an injury.”
summary: I worry I will have to quit what I love because I am afraid of hurting my body again.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: Nobody wants it, nobody cares for it, nobody ever goes into it. Perhaps everything is dead in it already. I don’t know.”
summary: I feel sad looking at something abandoned that no one loves and wondering if anything alive remains inside it.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: I’m always thinking about it—but we couldn’t go on like this much longer.
summary: I cannot stop worrying about my situation and I know I cannot keep living this way much longer.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: I can always send the nurse out of the room and say that I want to be by myself.
summary: I know I can ask my caregiver to leave so I can finally have some quiet time alone.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: And my father would not have hated to look at me. I dare say I should have had a strong back.
summary: I wish my body had been stronger so my own parent could have looked at me with love.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: This inscrutable man never felt more alone than when surrounded by his dogs.
summary: He feels most lonely even when surrounded by companions who should keep him company.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: She was one of the kind that likes to grow up. In the end she grew up of her own free will a day quicker than other girls.
summary: She embraces getting older and chooses to mature a little faster than everyone around her.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: On the other hand, if they are not in time, I solemnly promise that it will all come right in the end.
summary: I reassure others that even if help arrives late, everything will still work out fine.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: It was not really a light; it made this light by flashing about so quickly, but when it came to rest for a second you saw it was a fairy, no longer than your hand, but still growing.
summary: A tiny flashing light turns out to be a small fairy that is still growing bigger.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: But there was one who did not fear him: there was one prepared to enter that circle.
summary: One brave person is unafraid and ready to step into a frightening situation alone.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: She had been beginning to think it would be, but now she had changed her mind entirely.
summary: She thought things were going one way but now she completely changed her mind about it.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: In a few days he was in Yorkshire again, and on his long railroad journey he found himself thinking of his boy as he had never thought in all the ten years past. During those years he had only wished to forget him.
summary: On a long train ride home he finally thinks about his son after years of trying to forget him.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: Do you know that when I waken in the morning, Mary, when it’s quite early and the birds are just shouting outside and everything seems just shouting for joy—even the trees and things we can’t really hear—I feel as if I must jump out of bed and shout myself.
summary: I wake up early to birds singing and feel so happy and alive that I want to shout too.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: “If I were to live, this place would sometime belong to me. They all know that.
summary: I am sick and thinking that if I survive, this house will one day be mine.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: Anyone is selfish who doesn’t do what they want. You’re more selfish than I am.
summary: I tell you that everyone is selfish and you are even more selfish than me.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: So great indeed was their faith in a mother’s love that they felt they could afford to be callous for a bit longer.
summary: They trust their mom will always forgive them, so they keep putting off going home a little longer.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: I said, ‘Thank you, kind parents, for giving me bottles to make me well.’”
summary: I feel grateful to the caring adults looking after me and thank them for helping me get better.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: Instead of watching the ship, however, we must now return to that desolate home from which three of our characters had taken heartless flight so long ago.
summary: I am turning my attention back to the empty house the kids left behind long ago.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: In the bitterness of his remorse he swore that he would never leave the kennel until his children came back.
summary: Feeling guilty for his mistakes, he refuses to leave his makeshift punishment spot until his kids return home.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: I think all were gone when a group of savage boys surrounded Hook, who seemed to have a charmed life, as he kept them at bay in that circle of fire. They had done for his dogs, but this man alone seemed to be a match for them all.
summary: I watched one outnumbered man hold off a whole group of attackers and could not believe he survived.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: All knew that what was about to happen concerned him alone, and that from being actors they were suddenly become spectators.
summary: They all suddenly realized this moment was only about him and they could only watch.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: In they went; I don’t know how there was room for them, but you can squeeze very tight in the Neverland.
summary: I watched everyone crowd into a tiny magical space where we somehow all fit together.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: Everything just as it should be, you see. Off we skip like the most heartless things in the world, which is what children are, but so attractive; and we have an entirely selfish time, and then when we have need of special attention we nobly return for it, confident that we shall be rewarded instead of smacked.
summary: We act selfish and carefree as kids, then come home expecting love instead of punishment.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: However, as we are here we may as well stay and look on. That is all we are, lookers-on. Nobody really wants us.
summary: We feel unwanted and invisible, just staying to watch because nobody really needs us here.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: Oh dear no! I am only the breadwinner, why should I be coddled—why, why, why!”
summary: I feel like I only matter for the money I earn and nobody cares about comforting me.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: Travel, change, interest, excitement! The whole world before you, and a horizon that’s always changing!
summary: I feel thrilled by the chance to travel somewhere new with endless possibilities ahead.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: Independence is all very well, but we animals never allow our friends to make fools of themselves beyond a certain limit; and that limit you’ve reached. Now, you’re a good fellow in many respects, and I don’t want to be too hard on you.
summary: I care about you, so I have to tell you honestly that you have gone too far this time.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: And it’s not such a very bad house, is it? You know you rather like it yourself. Now, look here.
summary: Someone tries to convince a friend that their home is actually pretty good after all.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: You know how kind they always are. And they made things as jolly for me as ever they could, right up to the moment I left. But I felt a brute all the time, as it was clear to me they were very unhappy, though they tried to hide it.
summary: I felt guilty leaving kind people who tried to stay cheerful even though I could tell they were hurting.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: And they got very cocky, and went about saying you were done for this time! You would never come back again, never, never!”
summary: People arrogantly assumed someone was gone for good and would never manage to return home.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: Take care lest an adventure is now offered you, which, if accepted, will plunge you in deepest woe.
summary: Be careful because this exciting opportunity could lead you into deep sadness and lasting pain.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: You don’t think I would send her away all by herself when she is frightened!”
summary: I would never leave someone I love alone when they are scared and need me nearby.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: It is to listen to the stories. O Wendy, your mother was telling you such a lovely story.”
summary: Listening to a comforting family story told with love feels warm and safe.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: All the beds are aired, and she never leaves the house, and observe, the window is open. For all the use we are to her, we might well go back to the ship.
summary: We keep everything ready at home but feel useless and ignored, so we might as well leave.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: You will never carry the bottle in your mouth again, Nana, and it is all my fault.”
summary: I feel guilty because my mistake means you can never do that important job again.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: The extraordinary upshot of this adventure was—but we have not decided yet that this is the adventure we are to narrate. Perhaps a better one would be the night attack by the redskins on the house under the ground, when several of them stuck in the hollow trees and had to be pulled out like corks.
summary: I cannot decide which funny story to tell first because they all seem exciting in different ways.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: When their voices died away there came cold silence over the lagoon, and then a feeble cry.
summary: Everything goes suddenly quiet and then a weak cry makes the silence feel scary.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: “Because I am grown up, dearest. When people grow up they forget the way.”
summary: I feel sad because growing up made me forget how to find joy like I used to.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: I expect he was right, for fairies don’t live long, but they are so little that a short time seems a good while to them.
summary: I remind myself that a short time can still feel full and meaningful to someone small.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: In the old days at home the Neverland had always begun to look a little dark and threatening by bedtime. Then unexplored patches arose in it and spread, black shadows moved about in them, the roar of the beasts of prey was quite different now, and above all, you lost the certainty that you would win. You were quite glad that the night-lights were on.
summary: At bedtime your imagination turns dark and frightening and you feel less sure you will be okay.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: She died of old age, and at the end she had been rather difficult to get on with; being very firmly convinced that no one knew how to look after children except herself.
summary: An elderly caregiver passed away after becoming stubborn about being the only one who could care properly.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: They were already the only persons in the street, and all the stars were watching them.
summary: They walked alone together late at night feeling like the whole universe was quietly noticing their moment.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: Usually it is done quite easily, as by your wearing too many garments or too few, but if you are bumpy in awkward places or the only available tree is an odd shape, Peter does some things to you, and after that you fit.
summary: You have to awkwardly adjust your clothes and body to squeeze through a strange tight space.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: Once you fitted, you drew in your breath at the top, and down you went at exactly the right speed, while to ascend you drew in and let out alternately, and so wriggled up. Of course, when you have mastered the action you are able to do these things without thinking of them, and nothing can be more graceful.
summary: You learn to control your breathing to slide down smoothly and climb back up feeling completely graceful.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: “What is gay and innocent and heartless? I do wish I were gay and innocent and heartless.”
summary: I wish I could be carefree and innocent again without feeling hurt or responsible for others.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: It’s my world, and I don’t want any other. What it hasn’t got is not worth having, and what it doesn’t know is not worth knowing. Lord! the times we’ve had together! Whether in winter or summer, spring or autumn, it’s always got its fun and its excitements.
summary: I love my life exactly as it is and feel grateful for all the fun we have had together year-round.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: But do not trouble about me. I hate being a burden to my friends, and I do not expect to be one much longer.
summary: I do not want my friends to worry because I hate feeling like a burden and think this will end soon.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: “People come—they stay for a while, they flourish, they build—and they go. It is their way. But we remain.
summary: People move in and out of life while those rooted here quietly stay and endure.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: By this time they were all three talking at once, at the top of their voices, and the noise was simply deafening, when a thin, dry voice made itself heard, saying, “Be quiet at once, all of you!” and instantly every one was silent.
summary: Everyone was shouting over each other until a stern voice cut through the noise and silenced the whole room.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: Last year it was house-boating, and we all had to go and stay with him in his house-boat, and pretend we liked it. He was going to spend the rest of his life in a house-boat.
summary: We all went along with his houseboat obsession last year even though none of us enjoyed it.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: When we’ve converted you to a proper point of view we may quit, but not before.
summary: I will keep pushing you until you finally see things my way.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: Why this craving for change? Why not stay on quietly here, like us, and be jolly?
summary: I do not understand why you chase change when staying here with us feels happy.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: I had everything I could want—everything I had any right to expect of life, and more; and here I am!
summary: I had more than I ever deserved in life, yet I still ended up lost and unhappy.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: It’s my home, my old home! I’ve just come across the smell of it, and it’s close by here, really quite close.
summary: I just caught the familiar smell of my old home and realized it is right near me.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: And the sight of an animal in tears always makes me feel queer and softhearted.
summary: I always feel tender and strange inside when I see someone crying.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: But to want to talk about it, or even think about it, till you really need——”
summary: Putting off thinking about a stressful thing until there is no choice left.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: The first thing we want is a good fire; I’ll see to that—I always know where to find things.
summary: I want to get us warmed up first because I know how to sort things out here.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: Been in prison—got out of it, of course! Been thrown into a canal—swam ashore! Stole a horse—sold him for a large sum of money! Humbugged everybody—made ’em all do exactly what I wanted!
summary: I survived jail and drowning and scams and I am bragging about outsmarting everyone.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: I am, unfortunately, thrown into a canal by a woman fat of body and very evil-minded.
summary: I was humiliated when someone cruel pushed me into the water without warning.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: I’ll just take a look outside and see if everything’s quiet, and then we really must be off.”
summary: I need to check that it is safe outside before we finally leave this place.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: Little was visible but squares of a dusky orange-red on either side of the street, where the firelight or lamplight of each cottage overflowed through the casements into the dark world without.
summary: Warm light glows from houses into a dark empty street at night.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: We are an enduring lot, and we may move out for a time, but we wait, and are patient, and back we come.
summary: We always come back eventually no matter how long we stay away from home.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: Everything seems asleep, and yet going on all the time. It is a goodly life that you lead, friend; no doubt the best in the world, if only you are strong enough to lead it!”
summary: I admire how you live a quiet steady life that looks peaceful but takes real strength.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: I know everybody there, and their ways just suit me. I spent many jolly weeks in the island, staying with friends up country.
summary: I feel completely at home where I know everyone and I have spent many happy weeks with friends.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: No; I feel as if I had been through something very exciting and rather terrible, and it was just over; and yet nothing particular has happened.”
summary: I feel shaky and relieved after something intense and scary, even though nothing actually happened to me.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: Conversation was impossible for a long time; and when it was slowly resumed, it was that regrettable sort of conversation that results from talking with your mouth full.
summary: People are so busy eating they cannot talk, then mumble awkwardly with their mouths still full.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: But it was from one little window, with its blind drawn down, a mere blank transparency on the night, that the sense of home and the little curtained world within walls—the larger stressful world of outside Nature shut out and forgotten—most pulsated.
summary: Seeing a lit window at night gives a cozy feeling of safe home apart from the stressful outside world.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: All very true, no doubt the others always reply; we quite envy you—and some other year perhaps—but just now we have engagements—and there’s the bus at the door—our time is up! So they depart, with a smile and a nod, and we miss them, and feel resentful.
summary: People always say they envy my free time but are too busy to join me, then leave and I feel left behind and bitter.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: ‘Run away?’ says I; ‘it won’t be me that’ll be running away, in a very short time from now!’”
summary: I am standing my ground and telling myself I will not be the one to back down soon.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: You see, I understand my work thoroughly, and attend to it all myself.
summary: I know exactly what I am doing at work and I handle every part of it myself.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: This is my share in the advantages my country shall reap from the possession of such a magnificent dependency. The mere wealth I leave to others.
summary: I feel proud to help my country succeed and I do not care about getting rich myself.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: I—I have mourned so long in silence—in silence.... You were with him—to the last? I think of his loneliness.
summary: I have grieved quietly for so long and I keep wondering if he felt alone at the end.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: The night was very clear; a dark blue space, sparkling with dew and starlight, in which black things stood very still. I thought I could see a kind of motion ahead of me. I was strangely cocksure of everything that night.
summary: I walked outside on a clear starry night feeling oddly confident while watching for movement in the dark.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: For a time I would feel I belonged still to a world of straightforward facts; but the feeling would not last long. Something would turn up to scare it away.
summary: I sometimes feel connected to normal reality but then something unsettling quickly makes that comfort disappear.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: I am a simple man. He thought it would scare you away—that you would give it up, thinking him dead. I could not stop him.
summary: I am an ordinary person and I could not prevent him from pushing you away with lies.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: ‘You will be lost,’ I said—‘utterly lost.’ One gets sometimes such a flash of inspiration, you know.
summary: I suddenly realized someone I care about was heading toward disaster and warned them they would be completely lost.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: When you have to attend to things of that sort, to the mere incidents of the surface, the reality—the reality, I tell you—fades. The inner truth is hidden—luckily, luckily.
summary: I get so busy handling daily surface details that deeper reality fades, which honestly feels like a relief.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: I always went my own road and on my own legs where I had a mind to go. I wouldn’t have believed it of myself; but, then—you see—I felt somehow I must get there by hook or by crook.
summary: I have always done things my own way, but now I am surprisingly determined to reach this goal no matter what it takes.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: I have no great thoughts. I want nothing from anybody. How can you compare me to...?’
summary: I feel ordinary and want nothing from anyone, so I do not understand why you would compare me to others.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: Then I began to look for a ship—I should think the hardest work on earth. But the ships wouldn’t even look at me. And I got tired of that game, too.
summary: I tried exhaustingly hard to find work but kept getting ignored, and eventually I just got tired of trying.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: I felt I was becoming scientifically interesting. However, all that is to no purpose.
summary: I feel like people only find me interesting as a strange case and none of it matters.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: When I had a chance I begged him to try and leave while there was time; I offered to go back with him. And he would say yes, and then he would remain; go off on another ivory hunt; disappear for weeks; forget himself amongst these people—forget himself—you know.’
summary: I kept urging someone I cared about to walk away before it was too late, but he kept staying and losing himself.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: I had rather be alone than have the kind of men you can dispose of with me.” It was more than a year ago.
summary: I would rather be completely on my own than stuck with people I cannot trust or respect.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: They were intruders whose knowledge of life was to me an irritating pretence, because I felt so sure they could not possibly know the things I knew.
summary: I get annoyed by outsiders acting like they understand life when they have no idea what I have been through.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: At that time there were many blank spaces on the earth, and when I saw one that looked particularly inviting on a map (but they all look that) I would put my finger on it and say, ‘When I grow up I will go there.’
summary: As a kid I used to stare at maps and dream about growing up and traveling to faraway unknown places.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: ‘You show them you have in you something that is really profitable, and then there will be no limits to the recognition of your ability,’ he would say. ‘Of course you must take care of the motives—right motives—always.’
summary: If I prove I can make money for them, they will finally respect my talent if my intentions stay good.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: I am a simple man. I have no great thoughts. I want nothing from anybody.
summary: I see myself as an ordinary person with no big ideas and no need to ask others for anything.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: We are too late; he has vanished—the gift has vanished, by means of some spear, arrow, or club. I will never hear that chap speak after all’—and my sorrow had a startling extravagance of emotion, even such as I had noticed in the howling sorrow of these savages in the bush. I couldn’t have felt more of lonely desolation somehow, had I been robbed of a belief or had missed my destiny in life....
summary: I arrived too late to meet someone important and felt gutted like I had lost my purpose in life.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: There was a lamp in there—light, don’t you know—and outside it was so beastly, beastly dark.
summary: One small warm light feels safe while everything outside feels overwhelmingly dark and threatening.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: The most you can hope from it is some knowledge of yourself—that comes too late—a crop of unextinguishable regrets. I have wrestled with death.
summary: I have faced death and learned that self understanding only brings lasting regrets when it arrives too late.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: I had cut him off cleverly; but when actually confronting him I seemed to come to my senses, I saw the danger in its right proportion.
summary: I thought I was clever to corner him, but face to face I finally understood how risky it really was.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: Well, you see, the notion drove me. I had an aunt, a dear enthusiastic soul. She wrote: ‘It will be delightful. I am ready to do anything, anything for you.
summary: I was obsessed with an idea, and my supportive aunt promised to do everything she could to help me.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: ‘I went a little farther,’ he said, ‘then still a little farther—till I had gone so far that I don’t know how I’ll ever get back. Never mind. Plenty time.
summary: I kept going further and further until I felt lost about getting back, but I brushed it off.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: ‘Do you know what you are doing?’ I whispered. ‘Perfectly,’ he answered, raising his voice for that single word: it sounded to me far off and yet loud, like a hail through a speaking-trumpet.
summary: I anxiously asked if he understood what he was doing, and his loud confident answer sounded strange and distant to me.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: It made you feel very small, very lost, and yet it was not altogether depressing, that feeling.
summary: Something vast makes you feel tiny and lost, but in a way that is not entirely sad.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: I thought I would never get back to the steamer, and imagined myself living alone and unarmed in the woods to an advanced age.
summary: I felt completely lost and started imagining growing old alone stranded far from help.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: To tell you the truth, I was morbidly anxious to change my shoes and socks.
summary: I felt gross and on edge and all I could think about was getting into dry shoes and socks.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: I asked. ‘Oh, I never see them,’ he remarked; ‘and, moreover, the changes take place inside, you know.’ He smiled, as if at some quiet joke. ‘So you are going out there.
summary: I asked someone a question and got a cryptic smiling answer about inner change before I left.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: I am proud to know I understood him better than any one on earth—he told me so himself.
summary: I feel proud that I knew someone more deeply than anyone else ever did.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: How can you compare me to...?’ His feelings were too much for speech, and suddenly he broke down. ‘I don’t understand,’ he groaned. ‘I’ve been doing my best to keep him alive, and that’s enough.
summary: He breaks down upset at being compared and insists he did his best to keep someone alive.

author: Jack London
text: This lost mine was steeped in tragedy and shrouded in mystery. No one knew of the first man.
summary: There is a place haunted by old loss that no one fully understands or can explain.

author: Jack London
text: You’ve learned your place, and I know mine. Be a good dog and all ’ll go well and the goose hang high. Be a bad dog, and I’ll whale the stuffin’ outa you.
summary: I have made the rules clear and expect obedience, with rewards for cooperation and punishment for defiance.

author: Jack London
text: Throw away that tent, and all those dishes,—who’s going to wash them, anyway? Good Lord, do you think you’re travelling on a Pullman?”
summary: You need to pack much lighter and stop expecting comfort while traveling rough.

author: Jack London
text: Yet it was a secret growth. His newborn cunning gave him poise and control. He was too busy adjusting himself to the new life to feel at ease, and not only did he not pick fights, but he avoided them whenever possible.
summary: He is quietly learning how to survive a new life and avoids conflict while he adjusts.

author: Jack London
text: About his body there was a peculiar springiness, or resiliency, almost catlike, and a quick alertness as of one who lived in perpetual fear of things seen and unseen.
summary: His body stays tense and alert all the time because he expects danger from everywhere.

author: Jack London
text: And such is the paradox of living, this ecstasy comes when one is most alive, and it comes as a complete forgetfulness that one is alive.
summary: A person feels most alive and joyful when completely forgetting themselves in the moment.

author: Jack London
text: Each day the sun rose earlier and set later. It was dawn by three in the morning, and twilight lingered till nine at night. The whole long day was a blaze of sunshine. The ghostly winter silence had given way to the great spring murmur of awakening life.
summary: After a long dark winter, the lengthening sunny days feel full of new energy and hope.

author: Jack London
text: Over the whiteness and silence brooded a ghostly calm. There was not the faintest whisper of air—nothing moved, not a leaf quivered, the visible breaths of the dogs rising slowly and lingering in the frosty air.
summary: Everything feels completely still and frozen on a silent winter morning when even breath hangs in the air.

author: Jack London
text: By this time all the amenities and gentlenesses of the Southland had fallen away from the three people.
summary: After a hard time away from home, people lose their soft manners and become harsh.

author: Jack London
text: They were alert and active, anxious that the work should go well, and fiercely irritable with whatever, by delay or confusion, retarded that work.
summary: A team becomes tense and easily annoyed when focused on getting an important job done right.

author: Jack London
text: The toil of the traces seemed the supreme expression of their being, and all that they lived for and the only thing in which they took delight.
summary: Hard work has become the only thing that gives my life purpose and real happiness.

author: Jack London
text: He wanted, not to escape a clubbing, but to have the leadership. It was his by right. He had earned it, and he would not be content with less.
summary: I am done just surviving and now I want the leadership role I know I have earned.

author: Jack London
text: No lazy, sun-kissed life was this, with nothing to do but loaf and be bored.
summary: My life now is busy and hard, not easy and boring like just lying around.

author: Jack London
text: There was nothing lively about it, no snap or go in him and his fellows.
summary: Everyone around me feels tired and flat, with no energy or excitement left in us.

author: Jack London
text: For to play a system requires money, while the wages of a gardener’s helper do not lap over the needs of a wife and numerous progeny.
summary: I cannot afford to gamble because my low pay barely covers what my large family needs.

author: Jack London
text: Nothing daunted him. It was because nothing daunted him that he had been chosen for government courier.
summary: He never lets fear stop him, which is why he earned an important trusted job.

author: Jack London
text: There is an ecstasy that marks the summit of life, and beyond which life cannot rise.
summary: I feel pure joy at the peak of living, knowing nothing could ever feel better than this.

author: Jack London
text: Driving snow, a wind that cut like a white-hot knife, and darkness had forced them to grope for a camping place. They could hardly have fared worse.
summary: We are stuck in brutal snow and darkness, struggling to find shelter on the worst night imaginable.

author: Jack London
text: Every night, regularly, at nine, at twelve, at three, they lifted a nocturnal song, a weird and eerie chant, in which it was Buck’s delight to join.
summary: Every night they howl together at set hours, and he loves joining their strange beautiful chorus.

author: Jack London
text: There was life abroad in it different from the life which had been there throughout the summer.
summary: The world around me feels alive in a new way that was missing all summer long.

author: Jack London
text: Even in the night, in his dreams, he was haunted by this fear. At such times he would shake off sleep and creep through the chill to the flap of the tent, where he would stand and listen to the sound of his master’s breathing.
summary: He is so afraid of losing someone he loves that he wakes at night just to hear them breathing.

author: Jack London
text: So greatly had he suffered, and so far gone was he, that the blows did not hurt much. And as they continued to fall upon him, the spark of life within flickered and went down.
summary: He has been hurt so long that he feels numb as the last bit of strength leaves his body.

author: Jack London
text: So that was the way. No fair play. Once down, that was the end of you.
summary: He realizes life is unfair and that falling down even once can mean losing everything.

author: Jack London
text: The old awe departed, and they grew equal to challenging his authority.
summary: They no longer respect him and now feel bold enough to question his control over them.

author: Jack London
text: They were a new kind of men to Buck (of which he was destined to see many more), and while he developed no affection for them, he none the less grew honestly to respect them.
summary: He meets a different kind of people he does not love but learns to genuinely respect.

author: Jack London
text: In the excess of their own misery they were callous to the suffering of their animals.
summary: When people are overwhelmed by their own pain, they stop caring about the hurt they cause others.

author: Jack London
