text: They’re lazy, I tell you, and you’ve got to whip them to get anything out of them. That’s their way. You ask any one.
summary: I feel frustrated with people I see as lazy and believe harsh pressure is the only way to motivate them.

author: Jack London
text: To Buck it was boundless delight, this hunting, fishing, and indefinite wandering through strange places.
summary: He feels pure happiness spending his days exploring outdoors, fishing and wandering freely without any fixed plans.

author: Jack London
text: The driver examined him, but could find nothing. All the drivers became interested in his case.
summary: They look him over for what is wrong but find nothing, and soon everyone around becomes curious about his situation.

author: Jack London
text: He, alone among men, could put a pack upon Buck’s back in the summer travelling.
summary: He is the only person trusted enough to handle the difficult work that no one else is allowed to do.

author: Virginia Woolf

summary: I stopped visiting after their accident because I felt awkward and then life got in the way.

author: Edith Wharton
text: And the sweetness of Mattie’s avowal, the wild wonder of knowing at last that all that had happened to him had happened to her too, made the other vision more abhorrent, the other life more intolerable to return to....
summary: Realizing she loves him back makes going back to his unhappy everyday life feel impossible.

author: Edith Wharton
text: I don’t blame you, nor I don’t blame myself. Maybe both of us will do better separate.
summary: I hold no hard feelings and think we might both be happier if we go our separate ways.

author: Edith Wharton
text: But this new doctor has scared her about herself. You know she believes all they say the first time she sees them. And this one’s told her she won’t get well unless she lays up and don’t do a thing about the house—not for months—”
summary: She is frightened by a new doctor who told her to stop all housework for months to recover.

author: Edith Wharton
text: His father’s death, and the misfortunes following it, had put a premature end to Ethan’s studies; but though they had not gone far enough to be of much practical use they had fed his fancy and made him aware of huge cloudy meanings behind the daily face of things.
summary: After his father died he had to quit school, but learning left him sensing deeper meaning in ordinary life.

author: Edith Wharton
text: I chafed at first, and then, under the hypnotising effect of routine, gradually began to find a grim satisfaction in the life.
summary: I hated my routine at first, but eventually the repetition numbed me into a dark kind of contentment.

author: Edith Wharton
text: It’s the way your father begun, and I was warned of it when I took you, and I tried to keep my things where you couldn’t get at ’em—and now you’ve took from me the one I cared for most of all—” She broke off in a short spasm of sobs that passed and left her more than ever like a shape of stone.
summary: She accuses someone of stealing what matters most to her, then breaks down crying and goes numb.

author: Edith Wharton
text: I want to do for you and care for you. I want to be there when you’re sick and when you’re lonesome.”
summary: I want to take care of you and stay close especially when you feel sick or lonely.

author: Edith Wharton
text: To prolong and intensify the feeling he added: “I guess we’re well enough here.”
summary: He says they are fine where they are because he wants to hold onto a happy moment together.

author: Edith Wharton
text: You said you could. So ’t we’d never have to leave each other any more.”
summary: You promised we could stay together forever and never have to be apart again.

author: Edith Wharton
text: To have them was in itself a distinction, though it was also, in most cases, a death-warrant.
summary: Earning this rare recognition feels like an honor that will ultimately ruin him.

author: Edith Wharton
text: I don’t believe but what you’re the only stranger has set foot in that house for over twenty years.
summary: I realize no outsider has entered that isolated home in twenty years.

author: Edith Wharton
text: And there’ll be that strange girl in the house ... and she’ll sleep in my bed, where I used to lay nights and listen to hear you come up the stairs....”
summary: I feel replaced imagining another woman sleeping in my bed and waiting for you.

author: Edith Wharton
text: Far off above us a square of light trembled through the screen of snow. Staggering along in Frome’s wake I floundered toward it, and in the darkness almost fell into one of the deep drifts against the front of the house.
summary: I struggle through deep snow toward a distant lit window trying not to fall.

author: Edith Wharton
text: I felt myself to blame for having accepted Frome’s offer, and after a short discussion I persuaded him to let me get out of the sleigh and walk along through the snow at the bay’s side.
summary: I feel guilty for accepting his ride so I get out to walk beside him.

author: Edith Wharton
text: His hard day’s work in the keen air made him feel at once lazy and light of mood, and he had a confused sense of being in another world, where all was warmth and harmony and time could bring no change.
summary: After a hard day outside he feels relaxed and happy, as if he has entered a warm world that will never change.

author: Edith Wharton
text: He used to think that fifty years sounded like a long time to live together; but now it seemed to him that they might pass in a flash.
summary: He realizes that fifty years with someone he loves could fly by instead of feeling long at all.

author: Edith Wharton
text: He was never so happy with her as when he abandoned himself to these dreams.
summary: He feels happiest just imagining a life with her rather than living their actual reality together.

author: Edith Wharton
text: I won’t let you! She’s always had her way, but I mean to have mine now—”
summary: I am finally standing up for myself after letting someone else control everything for too long.

author: Edith Wharton
text: Despair seized him at the thought of her setting out alone to renew the weary quest for work.
summary: He feels hopeless imagining her heading off alone to face another exhausting search for work.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: Now it’s time to be living. I don’t want to frighten you, but I would like to make you understand the import of what you think of attempting.
summary: I want to tell you this moment matters and what you are about to do is serious.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: When father went to sleep I leaned out of the window and thought of the life I had led.
summary: I stayed up late after everyone slept and stared outside thinking about my past choices.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: I don’t know what I shall do. I just want to go away and look at people and think.”
summary: I feel lost about my future and just want to travel alone to watch others and clear my head.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: Everyone stands around and laughs and they talk but they say nothing to me. Then I feel so queer that I can’t talk either. I go away.
summary: I feel invisible when everyone chats around me, so I shut down and walk away alone.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: It hurt me to do what I did and made everything strange. That’s why I did it. I’m glad, too. It taught me something, that’s it, that’s what I wanted.
summary: I did something painful that changed everything, but I am glad because it taught me what I needed.

author: Edith Wharton
text: He had foreseen an immediate demand for money, but not a permanent drain on his scant resources.
summary: He expected a one-time expense but now fears it will drain his limited money for good.

author: Edith Wharton
text: But the thought of a definite rupture had never come to him, and even now could not lodge itself in his mind.
summary: He cannot even imagine a final breakup, even though the idea is now right in front of him.

author: Edith Wharton
text: Beneath their wondering exclamations I felt a secret curiosity to know what impressions I had received from my night in the Frome household, and divined that the best way of breaking down their reserve was to let them try to penetrate mine.
summary: I could tell they wanted to hear about my night there, so I let them draw it out of me.

author: Edith Wharton
text: Everybody but you could see it. And everybody in Bettsbridge knows about Dr. Buck.
summary: You are the only one who cannot see what everyone else already knows about him.

author: Edith Wharton
text: His dread was so strong that, man-like, he sought to postpone certainty.
summary: He was so afraid of the truth that he kept putting off finding out for sure.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: She was so grown up, you see. She was a woman. I thought she would be bigger than I was there in that room.”
summary: I felt small and intimidated standing next to someone who seemed so much more mature than me.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: I’ve been going to come to your house and tell you of some of my ideas.
summary: I have been meaning to visit you because I really want to share what I have been thinking about lately.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: Perhaps I am trying to conceal my identity and don’t want to be very definite.
summary: I think I am hiding who I really am because I am afraid to be clear about myself.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: I don’t know. I guess I don’t care much. I just want to work and keep quiet. That’s all I’ve got in my mind.”
summary: I do not really care about much right now and just want to keep working quietly alone.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: He had always thought of himself as a successful man, although nothing he had ever done had turned out successfully.
summary: He keeps seeing himself as successful even though everything he tries seems to fail.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: I must get myself into touch with something orderly and big that swings through the night like a star.
summary: I feel lost and want to connect with something steady and larger than my life.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: It’s different with me. I don’t belong. I’ll not make a fuss about it, but I’m going to get out of here.”
summary: I finally admit I do not fit in here so I will quietly leave.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: I wanted to get out of town, out of my clothes, out of my marriage, out of my body, out of everything.
summary: I feel trapped in my life and want to escape everything including my own skin.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: One shudders at the thought of the meaninglessness of life while at the same instant, and if the people of the town are his people, one loves life so intensely that tears come into the eyes.
summary: Someone feels life is pointless yet loves their own people so much it makes them cry.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: When she had gone I cried like a silly boy. Pretty soon I had a chance to sell the house and I sent that money to her.”
summary: After she left I broke down crying and later sent her money from selling my house.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: By remembering it I have been able to understand many people and things that I was never able to understand before.
summary: Looking back on that memory helped me finally understand people I never got before.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: Soon we’d regain all we had lost. Mind, I don’t say the new things would be the same as the old. They wouldn’t. Maybe they’d be better, maybe not so good.
summary: I keep telling myself we will rebuild after loss, even if things turn out differently.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: ‘No, no,’ I said to myself, but I got up and opened the door just the same.
summary: I told myself not to do it, but I got up and did it anyway.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: I wanted to run away from everything but I wanted to run towards something too.
summary: I feel stuck and want to escape my life while also chasing something better.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: He loved the woman with a love as absorbing as the hatred he later felt for all women.
summary: He loved one woman completely, then ended up hating women after it fell apart.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: Sadness swept over her. Dropping to her knees, she tried to pray, but instead of prayers words of protest came to her lips. “It is not going to come to me. I will never find happiness.
summary: She kneels trying to pray but feels certain happiness will never come to her.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: In the last fifty years a vast change has taken place in the lives of our people.
summary: I feel like life for people like me has completely changed over recent decades.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: I was sick of living alone and wanted her back. The longer I waited the more raw and tender I became.
summary: I am tired of being alone and miss her so much that waiting only makes me feel more vulnerable.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: I might keep still and get more credit in your eyes. I have a desire to make you admire me, that’s a fact. I don’t know why.
summary: I want to impress you and earn your admiration even though I do not understand why I care so much.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: It makes no difference to me. I am a man of distinction, you see. Why should I concern myself with what I eat.”
summary: I tell myself I am too important to care about something as ordinary as what I eat each day.

author: James Joyce
text: Night after night I had passed the house (it was vacation time) and studied the lighted square of window: and night after night I had found it lighted in the same way, faintly and evenly.
summary: I keep walking past the same house every night, drawn to its softly lit window.

author: James Joyce
text: Our path through life is strewn with many such sad memories: and were we to brood upon them always we could not find the heart to go on bravely with our work among the living.
summary: I carry sad memories but I have to keep showing up for life.

author: James Joyce
text: My eyes were often full of tears (I could not tell why) and at times a flood from my heart seemed to pour itself out into my bosom. I thought little of the future.
summary: I often feel like crying for no reason as overwhelming emotion washes over me.

author: James Joyce
text: He could not feel her near him in the darkness nor her voice touch his ear. He waited for some minutes listening. He could hear nothing: the night was perfectly silent. He listened again: perfectly silent.
summary: He waits in the dark for someone who is gone and hears only silence.

author: James Joyce
text: The high cold empty gloomy rooms liberated me and I went from room to room singing. From the front window I saw my companions playing below in the street.
summary: I feel free wandering alone through a big empty house, singing while friends play outside.

author: James Joyce
text: I wished to annihilate the tedious intervening days. I chafed against the work of school.
summary: I am so impatient for something exciting that school and waiting feel unbearable.

author: James Joyce
text: We banded ourselves together, some boldly, some in jest and some almost in fear: and of the number of these latter, the reluctant Indians who were afraid to seem studious or lacking in robustness, I was one.
summary: I joined my friends on a risky adventure even though I was scared to look weak if I backed out.

author: James Joyce
text: She arranged in her mind all she was going to do and thought how much better it was to be independent and to have your own money in your pocket.
summary: She feels excited planning her future and proud to support herself with her own money.

author: James Joyce
text: Some would say, perhaps, that with us it is rather a failing than anything to be boasted of. But granted even that, it is, to my mind, a princely failing, and one that I trust will long be cultivated among us. Of one thing, at least, I am sure.
summary: I feel proud of our generous flaw and hope our people keep it alive for years.

author: James Joyce
text: “A new generation is growing up in our midst, a generation actuated by new ideas and new principles. It is serious and enthusiastic for these new ideas and its enthusiasm, even when it is misdirected, is, I believe, in the main sincere.
summary: I see young people with new passionate ideas and I trust their energy is mostly genuine.

author: James Joyce
text: You can’t help having a certain feeling for it. That’s human nature....
summary: I cannot help feeling attached to it because that is just human

author: James Joyce
text: His father, who had begun life as an advanced Nationalist, had modified his views early.
summary: His father started out with strong political beliefs but softened them early in life

author: James Joyce
text: Sometimes he caught himself listening to the sound of his own voice. He thought that in her eyes he would ascend to an angelical stature; and, as he attached the fervent nature of his companion more and more closely to him, he heard the strange impersonal voice which he recognised as his own, insisting on the soul’s incurable loneliness. We cannot give ourselves, it said: we are our own.
summary: He tries to impress someone he likes but realizes deep down that everyone remains fundamentally alone

author: James Joyce
text: I will not attempt to choose between them. The task would be an invidious one and one beyond my poor powers.
summary: I refuse to pick a favorite because the choice feels unfair and beyond what I can do

author: James Joyce
text: You’re the very same serious person that used to lecture me on Sunday mornings when I had a sore head and a fur on my tongue.
summary: I tease you for still being the serious one who lectured me during my hungover Sunday mornings

author: James Joyce
text: “They believe in enjoying life—and don’t you think they’re right? If you want to enjoy yourself properly you must go to Paris.
summary: I feel like some people really know how to live and I should travel somewhere exciting to truly enjoy myself.

author: James Joyce
text: Some distant lamp or lighted window gleamed below me. I was thankful that I could see so little.
summary: I feel relieved to barely see anything in the dark because keeping my distance feels safer right now.

author: James Joyce
text: His life would be lonely too until he, too, died, ceased to exist, became a memory—if anyone remembered him.
summary: He worries his life will stay lonely until he dies and is eventually forgotten by everyone.

author: James Joyce
text: I could not call my wandering thoughts together. I had hardly any patience with the serious work of life which, now that it stood between me and my desire, seemed to me child’s play, ugly monotonous child’s play.
summary: I cannot focus at all because my responsibilities feel pointless and boring compared to what I really want.

author: James Joyce
text: I found myself in a big hall girdled at half its height by a gallery. Nearly all the stalls were closed and the greater part of the hall was in darkness. I recognised a silence like that which pervades a church after a service.
summary: I walked into a huge empty place that felt dark and silent like an abandoned church service.

author: James Joyce
text: But real adventures, I reflected, do not happen to people who remain at home: they must be sought abroad.
summary: I feel like nothing exciting will ever happen if I just stay home all the time.

author: James Joyce
text: There was no doubt about it: if you wanted to succeed you had to go away.
summary: Sometimes it feels like you have to leave home to ever succeed in life.

author: James Joyce
text: It filled me with fear, and yet I longed to be nearer to it and to look upon its deadly work.
summary: I feel terrified by something dark but I still want to get closer and watch it happen.

author: James Joyce
text: He said that there was nothing in this world he would like so well as that.
summary: He feels like there is nothing in life he wants more than that one thing.

author: James Joyce
text: We have all of us living duties and living affections which claim, and rightly claim, our strenuous endeavours.
summary: We all have real responsibilities and people we love who deserve our full effort every day.

author: James Joyce
text: Here we are gathered together for a brief moment from the bustle and rush of our everyday routine.
summary: We finally paused our busy daily lives to spend a little time together.

author: James Joyce
text: Every morning I lay on the floor in the front parlour watching her door. The blind was pulled down to within an inch of the sash so that I could not be seen. When she came out on the doorstep my heart leaped.
summary: I secretly watched for my crush every morning and felt thrilled whenever she appeared outside.

author: James Joyce
text: At night in my bedroom and by day in the classroom her image came between me and the page I strove to read.
summary: I could not focus on anything because I kept picturing the girl I liked day and night.

author: James Joyce
text: For the first time in his life he felt himself superior to the people he passed.
summary: He walked past strangers feeling confident and better than them for the first time ever.

author: James Joyce
text: I wondered at this for, as my uncle had said the night before, he had taught me a great deal.
summary: I felt surprised that my uncle had really taught me so much useful stuff.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: It was pitch dark almost. Once or twice I stopped by the way under a bush to redden my pipe and only for the dew was thick I’d have stretched out there and slept. At last, after a bend of the road, I spied a little cottage with a light in the window.
summary: I was walking alone exhausted in the dark and felt relieved to finally see a lit house ahead.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: It might be difficult for you to live here now. But is it that makes you go?
summary: Someone wonders if hardship at home is really why I am leaving.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: Then, in that case, all the rest, all that I thought I thought and all that I felt I felt, all the rest before now, in fact... O, give it up, old chap! Sleep it off!
summary: I feel like everything I believed about myself was fake and I just want to sleep it off.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: You were brought up religiously by your parents. You had the sacraments and grace and indulgences of the church to aid you.
summary: Someone reminds me that my religious upbringing gave me every spiritual advantage growing up.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: Be therefore ready every moment, seeing that you may die at any moment.
summary: I try to stay ready for anything because I know life could end without warning.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: But I will tell you also what I do not fear. I do not fear to be alone or to be spurned for another or to leave whatever I have to leave. And I am not afraid to make a mistake, even a great mistake, a lifelong mistake, and perhaps as long as eternity too.
summary: I am ready to be alone and risk a huge lifelong mistake to live honestly.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: Faintly, under the heavy night, through the silence of the city which has turned from dreams to dreamless sleep as a weary lover whom no caresses move, the sound of hoofs upon the road. Not so faintly now as they come near the bridge; and in a moment, as they pass the darkened windows, the silence is cloven by alarm as by an arrow.
summary: A quiet sleeping city is suddenly startled by loud approaching sounds in the dark night.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: But I am curious to know are you trying to make a convert of me or a pervert of yourself?
summary: I wonder if you are trying to change my beliefs or just questioning your own.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: I fear him. I fear his redrimmed horny eyes. It is with him I must struggle all through this night till day come, till he or I lie dead, gripping him by the sinewy throat till...
summary: I am terrified of someone and feel I must fight him all night until one of us breaks.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: Time is, time was, but time shall be no more. At the last blast the souls of universal humanity throng towards the valley of Jehosaphat, rich and poor, gentle and simple, wise and foolish, good and wicked.
summary: At the end of time all kinds of people from everywhere gather together for final judgment.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: All else is worthless. One thing alone is needful, the salvation of one’s soul.
summary: Nothing else matters except protecting the soul and focusing on what truly counts.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: When I was a young fellow I tell you I enjoyed myself. I mixed with fine decent fellows. Everyone of us could do something.
summary: I miss when I was young and having fun with good friends who were all talented.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: So be it. Welcome, O life! I go to encounter for the millionth time the reality of experience and to forge in the smithy of my soul the uncreated conscience of my race.
summary: I am ready to embrace life and face real experience to create something meaningful and true.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: Set that before you as your first aim. Then, little by little, you will see your way. I mean in every sense, your way in life and in thinking. It may be uphill pedalling at first.
summary: You need to keep your main goal in mind and trust that your path will slowly become clear.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: To discover the mode of life or of art whereby your spirit could express itself in unfettered freedom.
summary: You want to find a way of living and creating that lets you be completely free.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: Banish from your minds all worldly thoughts and think only of the last things, death, judgement, hell and heaven.
summary: I should stop worrying about daily life and face what death and judgment really mean.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: But, O, the road there between the trees was dark! You would be lost in the dark.
summary: I am scared to walk down that dark path alone because I know I will get lost.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: But why in the square? You went there when you wanted to do something.
summary: I keep wondering why I chose that familiar spot whenever I needed to get something done.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: You implore now a moment of earthly life wherein to repent: in vain. That time is gone: gone for ever.
summary: I am begging for one more chance to fix my mistakes but that time has passed forever.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: But was your father what is called well-to-do? I mean, when you were growing up?
summary: I want to know if your family had money back when you were a kid growing up.

author: Victor Hugo
text: Formerly I should never have spoken as I have just done; so many misfortunes have happened to me, that I sometimes do not know what I am saying.
summary: I have been through so much that I sometimes blurt things out and barely recognize myself anymore.

author: Victor Hugo
text: On the day when a woman as she passes before you emits light as she walks, you are lost, you love.
summary: The moment someone walks by and lights up everything, I know I am completely falling for them.

author: Victor Hugo
text: What is there in all that for me to think about? I am safe; all is over. I had but one partly open door through which my past might invade my life, and behold that door is walled up forever!
summary: I finally feel safe because the one way my past could hurt me again is closed for good.

author: Victor Hugo
text: I am all alone. I arrange a chamber prettily. If I could have put the good God there I would have done it. My chamber is left on my hands.
summary: I am completely alone and I decorated a room with love, but no one came to fill it.

author: Victor Hugo
text: My heart is full. I could not live on as I was living, and I have come.
summary: My heart is overflowing and I could not keep living like before, so I finally came to you.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: I desire to press in my arms the loveliness which has not yet come into the world.
summary: I ache to hold onto a beautiful future love that I have not met yet.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: You have erred but you are always my children. It is one heart that loves another heart.
summary: Someone who messed up still feels deeply loved and accepted as family.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: That’s quite rightly expressed. And I’m proud that I’m an emotionalist.
summary: I feel proud of how I expressed my feelings and I own being an emotional person.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: Mother is putting my new secondhand clothes in order. She prays now, she says, that I may learn in my own life and away from home and friends what the heart is and what it feels. Amen. So be it.
summary: I am leaving home with used clothes while my mother prays I learn what love really means.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: And remember, my dear boys, that we have been sent into this world for one thing and for one thing alone: to do God’s holy will and to save our immortal souls.
summary: I was taught that our only purpose in life is to obey God and save our souls.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: A fellow was coming out of the bicycle house and I fell and they got broken. I don’t know the fellow’s name.
summary: I fell down when someone came out of a doorway and broke my stuff and I did not even know him.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: It seems now I failed. It is very difficult. I tried to unite my will with the will of God instant by instant. In that I did not always fail.
summary: I feel like I failed at living up to my faith even though I tried hard every moment and sometimes succeeded.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: You have no fear of that. And you know what that word means? Not only to be separate from all others but to have not even one friend.
summary: You are not scared enough of ending up completely alone with no real friends at all.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: But I am as good as you any day. Do you know what I think about you now as compared with myself?
summary: I am tired of feeling less than you and I want you to know I see myself as your equal now.

author: James Joyce
work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
text: But their souls were seen by God; and if their souls were in a state of grace they were radiant to see: and God loved them, seeing them.
summary: People who live in a good and honest way shine brightly and feel deeply loved for who they are.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: Some day when we are married and I can save both his money and my own, we will be rich. Then we can travel together all over the world.”
summary: I dream about getting married someday, saving money together, and traveling the world.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: I’m not afraid. What you say clears things up. If being a newspaper man had put the notion of becoming a writer into your mind that’s all right. Only I guess you’ll have to wake up to do that too, eh?”
summary: I feel reassured by your honesty and I encourage you to fully commit to becoming a writer.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: Thoughts came and I wanted to get away from my thoughts. I began to beat the horse. The black clouds settled down and it began to rain. I wanted to go at a terrible speed, to drive on and on forever.
summary: I was overwhelmed by dark thoughts in the rain and just wanted to drive fast and escape everything forever.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: I didn’t want ever to see her again and I knew, after some of the things I said, that I never would see her again.”
summary: I said things I cannot take back and I know I will never see that person again.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: I tried to keep quiet, to keep myself to myself, but I couldn’t. I felt just as I did about opening the door.
summary: I tried hard to stay quiet and keep to myself but I could not hold back.

author: Victor Hugo
text: You don’t frighten me. I tell you that you shan’t enter this house, because it doesn’t suit me. If you approach, I’ll bark. I told you, I’m the dog, and I don’t care a straw for you.
summary: I am standing my ground at my door and telling an intimidating stranger to back off.

author: Victor Hugo
text: That’s no matter, as I can’t see your face and as I don’t know your name, you are wrong in supposing that I don’t know who you are and what you want.
summary: I cannot see you clearly but I still understand exactly who you are and what you are after.

author: Victor Hugo
text: And I accept this isolation of hatred, without hating any one myself. Now I am eighty-six years old; I am on the point of death.
summary: I have accepted being shut out by others without bitterness as I face dying very old and alone.

author: Victor Hugo
text: I say to you, who are passing by, that you are much more at home here than I am myself.
summary: I feel like a stranger in my own place and tell a passerby they belong here more than I do.

author: Victor Hugo
text: I don’t like all this. If I did not know how good you are, I should be afraid of you.”
summary: I feel uneasy about this situation and admit I would be scared if I did not trust how kind you are.

author: Victor Hugo
text: A passer-by. Ten years ago, I did not know that she was in existence. I love her, it is true. One loves a child whom one has seen when very young, being old oneself.
summary: I love a young girl I only met years ago, the way an older person cherishes a child.

author: Victor Hugo
text: You understand, one conceives an affection for a person; I am a good sort of a beast, I am; I do not reason; I love that little girl; my wife is quick-tempered, but she loves her also.
summary: I cannot explain why I love this little girl so much, but both my wife and I care for her deeply.

author: Victor Hugo
text: As for myself, constrained as I am to do what I have done, and yet abhorring it, I have judged myself also, and you shall soon see to what I have condemned myself.”
summary: I hate what I felt forced to do, so I have judged myself and decided how to punish myself.

author: Victor Hugo
text: But I was perfectly conscious that I was in the way. I gave myself reasons: ‘They do not want you, keep in your own course, one has not the right to cling eternally.’
summary: I knew I was unwanted and kept telling myself to back off and stop clinging to them.

author: Victor Hugo
text: Well, I have made inquiries; you will expose yourselves to no purpose, you see. I swear to you that there is nothing in this house.”
summary: I checked carefully and promise there is nothing here, so you would risk yourselves for no reason.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: I regret leaving before the end, because it was beginning to amuse me.”
summary: I wish I had stayed longer because I was just starting to enjoy myself.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: Those who were beginning to grow old had an air of youth, while there was something mature in the faces of the young.
summary: Older people look surprisingly young while younger people already seem worn and mature.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: A love like ours ought to show itself in the face of heaven. They torture me! I can bear it no longer!
summary: I want our love to be open and proud because hiding it is hurting me too much.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: You were coming confident and fearless, believing in happiness in the future.
summary: You arrived full of confidence and certain that good things were ahead for you.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: I thought I should die. I will tell you about all that and you will see.
summary: I felt like I might not survive what happened and I need to explain everything to you.

author: Victor Hugo
text: It is useless to tell you that which concerns only myself; I keep that to myself. You know the essential points. So I have taken my mystery and have brought it to you.
summary: I am keeping my private struggles to myself and only sharing what you really need to know.

author: Victor Hugo
text: Good God! When I think of what I was on the point of doing, I consider that I am to be envied. Nevertheless, I should have preferred not to have had this occur.”
summary: I feel lucky I stopped myself from doing something terrible, though I wish I had never come that close.

author: Victor Hugo
text: As we have said, at night, its aspect changed. Night is the real element of everything that is dark.
summary: Dark places feel different at night, when darkness finally feels at home.

author: Victor Hugo
text: I no longer see clearly, my children, I had still other things to say, but never mind. Think a little of me. Come still nearer. I die happy.
summary: I am dying peacefully and asking my loved ones to stay close and remember me fondly.

author: Victor Hugo
text: At night I came hither. Do not be afraid, no one sees me. I come to gaze upon your windows near at hand. I walk very softly, so that you may not hear, for you might be alarmed.
summary: I sneak over late at night just to look at your home without wanting to scare you.

author: Victor Hugo
text: I want you to be well, because, in the first place, if you were not well, I should be very unhappy.
summary: I want you to stay healthy because your pain would make me miserable too.

author: Victor Hugo
text: I am a newcomer among you, but I will confess that you amaze me. Where do we stand?
summary: I feel like an outsider here and I am confused about what you all expect from me.

author: Victor Hugo
text: That is the sort of kindness which disorganizes society. Good God! it is very easy to be kind; the difficulty lies in being just. Come! if you had been what I thought you, I should not have been kind to you, not I!
summary: I believe being fair matters more than being nice, and I would not have helped you otherwise.

author: Victor Hugo
text: I am not satisfied: but what more do I want? The goal to which I have aspired for so many years, the dream of my nights, the object of my prayers to Heaven,—security,—I have now attained; it is God who wills it; I can do nothing against the will of God, and why does God will it?
summary: I finally got the safety I prayed for for years, yet I still feel empty and confused.

author: Victor Hugo
text: I have my spouse and my young lady; a very beautiful girl. The journey is long and costly.
summary: I am traveling with my wife and beautiful daughter, but the trip is exhausting and expensive.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: Ah! he was gone, the only charm of her life, the only possible hope of joy.
summary: She feels empty now that the one person who made life joyful has left.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: Always alone! Ah! if I had some aim in life, if I had met some love, if I had found someone!
summary: I feel so alone and wish I had a purpose or a real love in my life.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: At night-every night-I arose; I came hither; I watched your house, its glimmering in the moon, the trees in the garden swaying before your window, and the little lamp, a gleam shining through the window-panes in the darkness.
summary: I spent every night outside your home watching the moonlight and your lit window from the dark.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: No fortune can hold out against waste! I should be ashamed to coddle myself as you do! And yet I am old.
summary: I get frustrated watching you waste money on comforts while I deny myself even in old age.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: It is so sweet, amid all the disenchantments of life, to be able to dwell in thought upon noble characters, pure affections, and pictures of happiness.
summary: When life feels disappointing, imagining kind people and true happiness brings real comfort.

author: Victor Hugo
text: I’m telling you how things stand. I warn you so that you may be prepared.”
summary: I am giving you a heads up about what is happening so you are not caught off guard.

author: Victor Hugo
text: That would not be reasonable. Mon Dieu, in spite of your riches, you have expenses of your own—who has not? I don’t want to ruin you, I am not a greedy fellow, after all.
summary: I do not want to take too much of your money because you have your own bills too.

author: Victor Hugo
text: Youth must amuse itself, and old age must wear out. I have been young, you will be old.
summary: I know what it is to be young and I know aging catches up with us all eventually.

author: Victor Hugo
text: I belong to no family. I do not belong to yours. I do not belong to any family of men. In houses where people are among themselves, I am superfluous.
summary: I feel like an outsider everywhere because I have no family or place where I truly fit in.

author: Victor Hugo
text: In short, I am doing what I can, I suffer with the same universal suffering, and I try to assuage it, I possess only the puny forces of a man, and I cry to all: “Help me!”
summary: I am trying my best to ease the pain we all share but I feel small and need help.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: Oh, no! Besides, you will not go; it is impossible. If you should--listen to me.
summary: I am begging someone not to leave because the thought of them going feels impossible to me.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: When I lost my dear departed, I went into the fields to be quite alone.
summary: After losing someone I loved, I walked out into empty fields just to be alone with my grief.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: With this repeated tinkling the thoughts of the young woman lost themselves in old memories of her youth and school-days.
summary: Hearing a familiar repeating sound, she gets lost remembering her childhood and younger school days.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: But the disparaging of those we love always alienates us from them to some extent.
summary: Criticizing the people I love always creates some distance between us, even when I do not mean it to.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: For the rest, so much the worse! You will see. Good day--for I am not likely to come soon again, as you say, to make scenes.”
summary: I am walking away angry after a fight, telling you not to expect me back anytime soon.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: And yet, why should my heart be so heavy? Is it dread of the unknown? The effect of habits left?
summary: I feel strangely heavy inside and wonder if I am just afraid of what comes next.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: But since it is the lot of all of us, one must not give way altogether, and, because others have died, want to die too.
summary: Death happens to everyone, so grief cannot become a reason to give up on living.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: We shall understand one another by and by. I have always got on with ladies--if I didn’t with my own!”
summary: I am confident we will get along well because I usually connect easily with women.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: You feel the need of confiding the whole of your life, of giving everything, sacrificing everything to this being. There is no need for explanations; they understand one another.
summary: Loving someone makes me want to share everything because we instantly understand each other.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: You do not repulse me! You are good! You understand that I am yours! Let me look at you; let me contemplate you!”
summary: I feel relieved that you accept me because I am completely yours and just want to gaze at you.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: It would be of the utmost importance for our district. But we’ll talk it over later on.
summary: This could really matter for our community, but I do not have time to discuss it right now.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: Or rather--? No; it is the excess of happiness. How weak I am, am I not?
summary: I feel so overwhelmed with happiness that I feel shaky and silly for being this emotional.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: For without me where would you be? What would you be doing? Who provides you with food, education, clothes, and all the means of figuring one day with honour in the ranks of society?
summary: Without everything I give you, you would have nothing and no chance to succeed in life.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: I detest commonplace heroes and moderate sentiments, such as there are in nature.”
summary: I hate boring, ordinary stories and lukewarm feelings and want something more intense and real.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: But for you, and you know it, I might have lived happily. What made you do it?
summary: I could have been happy if not for you, and I need to know why you ruined it.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: I fell at the foot of a tree; I cried; I called on God; I talked nonsense to Him. I wanted to be like the moles that I saw on the branches, their insides swarming with worms, dead, and an end of it.
summary: I collapsed outside crying and praying because I felt so hopeless I just wanted to be dead.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: There are times when I long to see you again, when I am torn by all the anger of love.
summary: I still miss you sometimes and feel ripped apart by frustrated love that will not let go.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: If anyone could take my place, I would accompany you myself. Be quick about it.
summary: I wish I could come with you myself, but since I cannot, please hurry and get it done.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: Sometimes, on Sundays, I go and stay there with a book, watching the sunset.”
summary: On quiet Sundays I like to sit alone somewhere peaceful with a book and watch the sun go down.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: I should certainly have done better to have left you to rot in your poverty and the dirt in which you were born. Oh, you’ll never be fit for anything but to herd animals with horns! You have no aptitude for science! You hardly know how to stick on a label!
summary: I regret ever helping you escape poverty because you are worthless at skilled work and only fit for menial labor.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
53. 1. If I were suddenly to become known, and (put into a position
to) conduct (a government) according to the Great Tao, what I should
be most afraid of would be a boastful display.
summary: If I ever got power and recognition, I would worry most about becoming arrogant and showy.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
Who uses well his light,
Reverting to its (source so) bright,
Will from his body ward all blight,
And hides the unchanging from men's sight.
summary: Staying grounded in inner clarity protects a person from harm and keeps what matters hidden.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
Ordinary men look bright and intelligent, while I alone seem to be
benighted.  They look full of discrimination, while I alone am dull
and confused.  I seem to be carried about as on the sea, drifting as
if I had nowhere to rest.  All men have their spheres of action, while
I alone seem dull and incapable, like a rude borderer.  (Thus) I alone
am different from other men, but I value the nursing-mother (the Tao).
summary: I feel dull and lost while everyone else seems smart and settled, drifting without a place to belong.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
Now it is so; 'twas so of old.
Its name--what passes not away;
So, in their beautiful array,
Things form and never know decay.
summary: Some timeless pattern has always held true, letting life keep unfolding beautifully without fading away.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
Always without desire we must be found,
If its deep mystery we would sound;
But if desire always within us be,
Its outer fringe is all that we shall see.
summary: When I let go of wanting, I see deeper meaning, but craving only shows me the surface.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
2. Let them not thoughtlessly indulge themselves in their ordinary
life; let them not act as if weary of what that life depends on.
summary: People should live simply and respect the basic things that keep daily life going.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
3. In the Way of Heaven, there is no partiality of love; it is always
on the side of the good man.
summary: The universe is fair and eventually rewards people who try to live good and kind lives.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
2. It is the way of Heaven not to strive, and yet it skilfully
overcomes; not to speak, and yet it is skilful in obtaining a reply;
does not call, and yet men come to it of themselves.  Its
demonstrations are quiet, and yet its plans are skilful and effective.
The meshes of the net of Heaven are large; far apart, but letting
nothing escape.
summary: Quiet patience often wins without forcing, and in the end nothing important slips away unnoticed.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
Misery!--happiness is to be found by its side!  Happiness!--misery
lurks beneath it!  Who knows what either will come to in the end?
summary: Good times can hide trouble and hard times can hide hope, so no one knows what comes next.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
The neighbourhood where it prevails
In thriving will abound;
And when 'tis seen throughout the state,
Good fortune will be found.
summary: When kindness spreads through a neighborhood and community, everyone seems to thrive and do well together.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
Simplicity without a name
Is free from all external aim.
With no desire, at rest and still,
All things go right as of their will.
summary: Living simply without chasing goals brings calm and lets life work itself out naturally.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
22. 1. The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty,
full; the worn out, new.  He whose (desires) are few gets them; he
whose (desires) are many goes astray.
summary: Broken things can become whole again, and wanting less leads to more clarity and peace.

author: Lao Tzu
summary: The most important truths feel invisible and quiet, too big to explain in ordinary words.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
2. It is the Way of Heaven to diminish superabundance, and to
supplement deficiency.  It is not so with the way of man.  He takes
away from those who have not enough to add to his own superabundance.
summary: Nature balances by giving to those in need, while people often take from the poor to enrich themselves.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
19. 1. If we could renounce our sageness and discard our wisdom, it
would be better for the people a hundredfold.  If we could renounce
our benevolence and discard our righteousness, the people would again
become filial and kindly.  If we could renounce our artful
contrivances and discard our (scheming for) gain, there would be no
thieves nor robbers.
summary: We would live kinder and safer lives if we let go of clever rules and selfish schemes.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
3. If this transformation became to me an object of desire, I would
express the desire by the nameless simplicity.
summary: I would answer my urge for change with a return to simple and quiet living.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
3. Therefore a sage has said, 'I will do nothing (of purpose), and the
people will be transformed of themselves; I will be fond of keeping
still, and the people will of themselves become correct.  I will take
no trouble about it, and the people will of themselves become rich; I
will manifest no ambition, and the people will of themselves attain to
the primitive simplicity.'
summary: I am learning that stepping back lets people grow and find their own way.

author: Lao Tzu
summary: Real beauty and truth can look plain or strange and turn expectations upside down.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
2. There is no guilt greater than to sanction ambition; no calamity
greater than to be discontented with one's lot; no fault greater than
the wish to be getting.  Therefore the sufficiency of contentment is
an enduring and unchanging sufficiency.
summary: Wanting more and more only brings trouble, while being content brings lasting peace.

author: Lao Tzu
summary: Someone who stays humble despite success becomes a welcoming place others naturally trust.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
56. 1. He who knows (the Tao) does not (care to) speak (about it); he
who is (ever ready to) speak about it does not know it.
summary: Real wisdom stays quiet while loud talk often shows a lack of real understanding.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
What all men fear is indeed to be feared; but how wide and without end
is the range of questions (asking to be discussed)!
summary: Everyone shares the same fears, yet life still feels full of endless questions without answers.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
Profound it is, dark and obscure;
Things' essences all there endure.
Those essences the truth enfold
Of what, when seen, shall then be told.
summary: Something deep and unclear holds the real truth that will make sense once it is finally seen.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
Thus we may see,
Who cleaves to fame
Rejects what is more great;
Who loves large stores
Gives up the richer state.
summary: I see that chasing fame and money makes me lose what truly matters in life.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
3. The people make light of dying because of the greatness of their
labours in seeking for the means of living.  It is this which makes
them think light of dying.  Thus it is that to leave the subject of
living altogether out of view is better than to set a high value on
it.
summary: People stop fearing death when daily survival takes so much exhausting work to stay alive.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
2. All things under heaven sprang from It as existing (and named);
that existence sprang from It as non-existent (and not named).
summary: Everything in the world seems to come from something real, which itself came from something impossible to name.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
2. I do not know its name, and I give it the designation of the Tao
(the Way or Course).  Making an effort (further) to give it a name I
call it The Great.
summary: I cannot fully name this huge force I sense, so I just call it something great to talk about it.

author: Lao Tzu
summary: Everything stable in life only holds together because of some quiet balance, and without it all falls apart.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
47. 1. Without going outside his door, one understands (all that takes
place) under the sky; without looking out from his window, one sees
the Tao of Heaven.  The farther that one goes out (from himself), the
less he knows.
summary: People understand life best by looking inward, and the more they chase outside, the less they truly know.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
4. It produces them and makes no claim to the possession of them; it
carries them through their processes and does not vaunt its ability in
doing so; it brings them to maturity and exercises no control over
them;--this is called its mysterious operation.
summary: True care means helping others grow and supporting them without taking credit or trying to control them.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: For my body liveth by my soul; and my soul by Thee. How then do I seek a happy life, seeing I have it not, until I can say, where I ought to say it, "It is enough"? How seek I it?
summary: I feel incomplete and keep wondering how to find a happiness that finally feels like enough.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: For this is after his kind; because a man is wont to imitate his friend. Be ye (saith he) as I am, for I also am as you are.
summary: People naturally copy their friends and invite each other to meet in the middle.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: O my hope, let not my purpose be confounded. For if times past and to come be, I would know where they be.
summary: I feel unsettled in my goals and keep wondering where the past and future actually exist.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: I name a bodily pain, yet it is not present with me, when nothing aches: yet unless its image were present to my memory, I should not know what to say thereof, nor in discoursing discern pain from pleasure.
summary: I notice I can talk about pain even when I feel fine because I still remember what it felt like.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: It is not so wonderful, if what I myself am not, be far from me. But what is nearer to me than myself?
summary: I am struck that nothing feels stranger than being distant from my own self.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: This is the light, it is one, and all are one, who see and love it. But that corporeal light whereof I spake, it seasoneth the life of this world for her blind lovers, with an enticing and dangerous sweetness.
summary: I feel united with others in a deeper truth while worldly pleasures feel sweet but risky.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: Before them what more foul than I was already, displeasing even such as myself? with innumerable lies deceiving my tutor, my masters, my parents, from love of play, eagerness to see vain shows and restlessness to imitate them!
summary: I feel ashamed looking back at how I constantly lied to my teachers and parents just to goof off.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: Myself verily either way; yet more myself, in that which I approved in myself, than in that which in myself I disapproved. For in this last, it was now for the more part not myself, because in much I rather endured against my will, than acted willingly.
summary: I feel like my true self is the part of me I approve of, not the part I do unwillingly.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: Every vain hope at once became worthless to me; and I longed with an incredibly burning desire for an immortality of wisdom, and began now to arise, that I might return to Thee.
summary: I suddenly stopped caring about shallow goals and desperately wanted lasting wisdom to turn my life around.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: I would also say, O Lord my God, what the following Scripture minds me of; yea, I will say, and not fear.
summary: I feel ready to speak up about what I believe without being afraid of what happens.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: But what I now am, at the very time of making these confessions, divers desire to know, who have or have not known me, who have heard from me or of me; but their ear is not at my heart where I am, whatever I am.
summary: I feel like people are curious about who I really am now but cannot truly hear my heart.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: Whence it seemed to me, that time is nothing else than protraction; but of what, I know not; and I marvel, if it be not of the mind itself?
summary: I keep wondering what time really is and suspect it might just be something stretching inside my own mind.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: For I would not be commended or loved, as actors are (though I myself did commend and love them), but had rather be unknown, than so known; and even hated, than so loved. Where now are the impulses to such various and divers kinds of loves laid up in one soul?
summary: I would rather be unknown or even disliked than famous for something fake, and I wonder why I feel such conflicting desires.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: Then suddenly, filled with a holy love, and a sober shame, in anger with himself cast his eyes upon his friend, saying, "Tell me, I pray thee, what would we attain by all these labours of ours? what aim we at? what serve we for?
summary: He feels ashamed and angry at himself and asks his friend what all their hard work is really for.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: And how was I moved, O my God, who had now learned to be angry at myself for things past, that I might not sin in time to come!
summary: I feel deeply moved because I finally learned to face my past mistakes so I can live better going forward.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: For in those alone found I a little refreshment. But when my soul was withdrawn from them a huge load of misery weighed me down.
summary: I get brief relief when I am with certain things, but I feel crushed by sadness as soon as I leave them.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: How much better then, had I been at once healed; and then, by my friends' and my own, my soul's recovered health had been kept safe in Thy keeping who gavest it. Better truly.
summary: I wish I had healed faster and that my friends and I had protected my recovery better.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: I loved not yet, yet I loved to love, and out of a deep-seated want, I hated myself for wanting not. I sought what I might love, in love with loving, and safety I hated, and a way without snares.
summary: I crave being in love even though I have no one, and I hate myself for feeling so empty and restless.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: Am I not then myself, O Lord my God? And yet there is so much difference betwixt myself and myself, within that moment wherein I pass from waking to sleeping, or return from sleeping to waking!
summary: I feel like a completely different person when I fall asleep and wake up, and it confuses me.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: For what shall I say, when it is clear to me that I remember forgetfulness?
summary: I am confused by the strange fact that I can clearly remember times when I forgot everything.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: Amid increasing anxiety, I was doing my wonted business, and daily sighing unto Thee.
summary: I keep going through my daily routine while feeling more anxious and quietly crying out for help.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: This is the happy life which all desire; this life which alone is happy, all desire; to joy in the truth all desire.
summary: Everyone just wants a truly happy life built on living honestly in the truth.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: But all are gifts of my God: it was not I who gave them me; and good these are, and these together are myself.
summary: I realize everything good in me is a gift I did not give myself.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: And to what purpose? that whosoever reads this, may think out of what depths we are to cry unto Thee.
summary: I want anyone reading this to understand how desperately I needed to cry out for help.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: Here I can stay, but would not; there I would, but cannot; both ways, miserable.
summary: I feel stuck and miserable because I do not want to stay here but cannot reach where I want to be.

author: Homer
text: I can tell you that you will never get back and will have to stay there with the rest of them.
summary: I have to tell you that you will never make it home and are stuck here for good.

author: Homer
text: I will hold the light for all these people. They may stay till morning, but shall not beat me, for I can stand a great deal.”
summary: I will keep showing up for everyone tonight because I know I am tougher than this exhausting situation.

author: Homer
text: Where in the world do you want to go to—you, who are the one hope of the house?
summary: Why would you leave when your whole family is counting on you to hold everything together.

author: Homer
text: You ought to be ashamed of yourself; how can you expect people to come see you any more if you treat them in this way?’
summary: You should feel embarrassed because no one will want to visit you if you keep acting like this.

author: Homer
text: I have nothing of the immortal about me, neither in body nor mind, and most resemble those among you who are the most afflicted.
summary: I feel completely human and broken, just like the most suffering people I know around me.

author: Homer
text: At times I cry aloud for sorrow, but presently I leave off again, for crying is cold comfort and one soon tires of it. Yet grieve for these as I may, I do so for one man more than for them all.
summary: I cry sometimes because I miss everyone, but I miss one person more than all the rest combined.

author: Homer
text: I am flying to escape death at their hands, and am thus doomed to be a wanderer on the face of the earth.
summary: I am running for my life and now I have to wander alone with nowhere safe to go.

author: Homer
text: I should like my future husband to be just such another as he is, if he would only stay here and not want to go away.
summary: I wish the man I marry could be just like him, as long as he would stay with me.

author: Homer
text: I never yet saw any one so beautiful, neither man nor woman, and am lost in admiration as I behold you.
summary: I have never seen anyone as beautiful as you and I am completely amazed just looking at you.

author: Homer
text: We are your own children, yet you show us no mercy in all our misery and afflictions.
summary: We are your own kids and still you watch us suffer without showing any mercy.

author: Homer
text: I am as yet young, and am not strong enough to hold my own if any man attacks me.
summary: I feel too young and weak to defend myself if someone tries to take advantage of me.

author: Homer
text: Nevertheless, I want to get home, and can think of nothing else. If some god wrecks me when I am on the sea, I will bear it and make the best of it.
summary: I miss home so badly that I am willing to risk everything to get back there.

author: Homer
text: I make all my lays myself, and heaven visits me with every kind of inspiration.
summary: I feel proud that my creative work comes from me and feels truly inspired.

author: Homer
text: Now, therefore, have pity upon me and grant that I may find friends and be hospitably received by the Phaeacians.”
summary: I feel vulnerable and alone and just hope strangers will be kind and welcome me.

author: Homer
text: When you were younger you had a greater sense of propriety; now, however, that you are grown up, though a stranger to look at you would take you for the son of a well to do father as far as size and good looks go, your conduct is by no means what it should be.
summary: You look like a grown adult from a good family, but you are acting immature and irresponsible.

author: Homer
text: I suppose you think it better to keep an eye on what the suitors are doing.”
summary: I feel watched and judged while I try to keep track of unwelcome people in my house.

author: Homer
text: I said that after going through much hardship and losing all his men he should come home again in the twentieth year and that no one would know him; and now all this is coming true.”
summary: I predicted after years of loss he would finally return unrecognized, and now I am seeing it happen.

author: Homer
text: Nine days did I drift but in the darkness of the tenth night a great wave bore me on to the Thesprotian coast.
summary: I drifted alone at sea for days until a night wave finally pushed me ashore to safety.

author: Homer
text: Tell me also truly, for I want to know, are you a stranger to this house, or have you been here in my father’s time?
summary: I want an honest answer about whether you are new here or knew my family long ago.

author: Homer
text: I have never slept so soundly from the day my poor husband went to that city with the ill-omened name.
summary: I have not had one good night of sleep since my husband left for a dangerous place.

author: Homer
text: We were driven on to them from the open sea, but I and those who are with me escaped the jaws of death.’
summary: We got pushed into terrible danger at sea but somehow me and my people barely made it out alive.

author: Homer
text: I have trouble enough of my own, and cannot be burdened with other people.
summary: I am already overwhelmed by my own problems and I cannot take on anyone else right now.

author: Homer
text: If I beg and pray you to set me free, then bind me more tightly still.’
summary: If I lose control and beg to be let go, please hold me back even tighter instead.

author: Homer
text: You too, then—for you are a tall smart-looking fellow—show your mettle and make yourself a name in story.”
summary: You look capable, so step up and do something brave that people will remember.

author: Homer
text: Such as I am, it is I, who after long wandering and much hardship have got home in the twentieth year to my own country.
summary: After years of wandering and suffering, I have finally made it back home again.

author: Homer
text: For my own part I should have no more pleasure in life, but had rather die at once.
summary: I feel so hopeless right now that living holds no joy and I would rather be gone.

author: Homer
text: Morning will come in due course, and in the forenoon I care not how much I cry for those that are dead and gone.
summary: I know morning will come and I will allow myself to grieve openly for the people I have lost.

author: Homer
text: Running is the only point in respect of which I am afraid some of the Phaeacians might beat me, for I have been brought down very low at sea; my provisions ran short, and therefore I am still weak.”
summary: I worry I will lose the race because a hard journey left me exhausted and weak.

author: Homer
text: Go in first and leave me here where I am. I am quite used to being beaten and having things thrown at me. I have been so much buffeted about in war and by sea that I am case-hardened, and this too may go with the rest.
summary: I will stay behind alone because I am used to insults and hardship has made me tough enough to endure more.

author: Homer
text: Believe me when I tell you that this man came to my house once when I was in my own country and never yet did any stranger come to me whom I liked better.
summary: I remember a visitor who once came to my home and I have never liked a guest more than him.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: See how the present time, which alone we found could be called long, is abridged to the length scarce of one day.
summary: Even the present moment feels incredibly short, barely lasting a single day.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: And yet these friends I loved for themselves only, and I felt that I was beloved of them again for myself only.
summary: I loved my friends purely for who they were and felt truly loved back the same way.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: What I do here any longer, and to what I am here, I know not, now that my hopes in this world are accomplished.
summary: I feel lost about why I am still here now that everything I hoped for has happened.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: Loving a happy life, I feared it in its own abode, and sought it, by fleeing from it.
summary: I want to be happy but I fear happiness itself and keep running away from what I want.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: For I neither hoped he should return to life nor did I desire this with my tears; but I wept only and grieved. For I was miserable, and had lost my joy.
summary: I was not hoping for a miracle, I just cried because I was miserable and had lost my happiness.

author: Mary Shelley
text: From my earliest remembrance I had been as I then was in height and proportion. I had never yet seen a being resembling me or who claimed any intercourse with me.
summary: I have always felt different from everyone else and never met anyone who truly understands me

author: Jane Austen
text: Your portion is unhappily so small, that it will in all likelihood undo the effects of your loveliness and amiable qualifications. As I must, therefore, conclude that you are not serious in your rejection of me, I shall choose to attribute it to your wish of increasing my love by suspense, according to the usual practice of elegant females.”
summary: An arrogant suitor insults a woman for having little money and assumes her rejection is just flirting

author: Jane Austen
text: I, who have valued myself on my abilities! who have often disdained the generous candour of my sister, and gratified my vanity in useless or blameless distrust.
summary: I realize I was arrogant about my judgment and unfairly looked down on my sister kindness

author: Jane Austen
text: I do assure you that I am not one of those young ladies (if such young ladies there are) who are so daring as to risk their happiness on the chance of being asked a second time. I am perfectly serious in my refusal.
summary: I am firmly rejecting this proposal and I am not playing games hoping you will ask again

author: Jane Austen
text: Your sweetness and disinterestedness are really angelic; I do not know what to say to you.
summary: I am overwhelmed with gratitude by how kind and selfless you are to me

author: Oscar Wilde
text: You remind me of the day I saw you first. You were rather cheeky, very shy, and absolutely extraordinary. You have changed, of course, but not in appearance. I wish you would tell me your secret.
summary: I remember how amazing you were when we first met and I can feel you have changed inside and I want to understand why.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: At present you are a perfect type. Don’t make yourself incomplete. You are quite flawless now. You need not shake your head: you know you are.
summary: You are perfect right now so please do not change anything about yourself.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Youth is the only thing worth having. When I find that I am growing old, I shall kill myself.”
summary: I feel like being young is everything and I am terrified of getting older and losing it.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: If they did believe you, they would like me all the better for it. I know the age better than you do, though you will prate about it so tediously.
summary: I understand how people think today better than you do and your boring opinions would only make them like me more.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Our presence taints the pleasures of others. We are unwelcome when we reappear.
summary: I feel like I ruin the mood for everyone and nobody really wants me to show up again.

author: Charles Dickens
text: Now, I ain’t alone, as you may think I am. There’s a young man hid with me, in comparison with which young man I am a Angel.
summary: I am warning you that I am not alone because someone far more dangerous is hiding nearby.

author: Charles Dickens
text: Indeed, I begin to think we are not much alike in any particular, you and I.”
summary: I am realizing that you and I have almost nothing in common after all.

author: Charles Dickens
text: The confidence is not of my seeking, recollect. Now, you think I may not be right?”
summary: I did not ask for your secret and now I am wondering if you doubt me.

author: Charles Dickens
text: I am not myself. I will speak to you by and by--another time. I will write to you. Don’t speak to me now.
summary: I feel completely overwhelmed right now and need space before I can talk to you.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: I only know myself as a human entity; the scene, so to speak, of thoughts and affections; and am sensible of a certain doubleness by which I can stand as remote from myself as from another.
summary: I notice I can watch my own thoughts from a distance like I am two people.

author: Jane Austen
text: Your person, your disposition, accomplishments, manner; they were all present to me.”
summary: I still remember everything about you, how you looked and acted and carried yourself.

author: Charlotte Brontë
text: And then, after all, I go too fast in my conclusions: for what I yet know, you may be no better than the rest; you may have intolerable defects to counterbalance your few good points.”
summary: I am catching myself for trusting too quickly because you might disappoint me like everyone else has.

author: Emily Brontë
text: I doubt whether I am not altogether as worthless as he calls me, frequently; and then I feel so cross and bitter, I hate everybody!
summary: When someone keeps calling me worthless I start to believe it and then I feel angry at everyone.

author: Charles Dickens
text: As I had grown accustomed to my expectations, I had insensibly begun to notice their effect upon myself and those around me. Their influence on my own character I disguised from my recognition as much as possible, but I knew very well that it was not all good.
summary: I am starting to see how getting what I wanted has changed me for the worse.

author: Charles Dickens
text: I always treated him as a larger species of child, and as no more than my equal.
summary: I always saw him as a big kid and just a regular person like me.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
In all people I see myself, none more and not one a barley-corn less,
And the good or bad I say of myself I say of them.
summary: I see myself in everyone I meet, and whatever I say about myself applies to them too.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
Why what have you thought of yourself?
Is it you then that thought yourself less?
Is it you that thought the President greater than you?
Or the rich better off than you? or the educated wiser than you?
summary: You wonder why you feel smaller than leaders and rich and educated people in your life.

author: Walt Whitman
text:
I dote on myself, there is that lot of me and all so luscious,
Each moment and whatever happens thrills me with joy,
I cannot tell how my ankles bend, nor whence the cause of my faintest wish,
Nor the cause of the friendship I emit, nor the cause of the
friendship I take again.
summary: I love being myself so much that every moment feels thrilling and full of joy.

author: Herman Melville
text: For several hours I lay there broad awake, feeling a great deal worse than I have ever done since, even from the greatest subsequent misfortunes.
summary: I lay awake for hours feeling worse than I ever have, even compared to later hard times.

author: Herman Melville
text: I survived myself; my death and burial were locked up in my chest. I looked round me tranquilly and contentedly, like a quiet ghost with a clean conscience sitting inside the bars of a snug family vault.
summary: I felt calm after facing my own death inside, at peace with myself like a quiet ghost.

author: Herman Melville
text: At last I must have fallen into a troubled nightmare of a doze; and slowly waking from it—half steeped in dreams—I opened my eyes, and the before sun-lit room was now wrapped in outer darkness.
summary: I woke up groggy from a bad nap and realized the bright room had gone completely dark.

author: Herman Melville
text: Oh, lonely death on lonely life! Oh, now I feel my topmost greatness lies in my topmost grief.
summary: I feel completely alone facing death and realize my deepest pain is also my greatest strength.

author: Herman Melville
text: Let me try to explain them. When I was a child, I well remember a somewhat similar circumstance that befell me; whether it was a reality or a dream, I never could entirely settle.
summary: I am trying to describe a strange childhood memory that I still cannot tell was real or imagined.

author: Herman Melville
