text: There he sat, his very indifference speaking a nature in which there lurked no civilized hypocrisies and bland deceits. Wild he was; a very sight of sights to see; yet I began to feel myself mysteriously drawn towards him.
summary: I felt strangely drawn to a wild honest stranger who seemed free of fake polite behavior.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I make a great difference between people. I choose my friends for their good looks, my acquaintances for their good characters, and my enemies for their good intellects.
summary: I pick my friends for looks, my acquaintances for character, and my enemies for intelligence.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Still, in the very fact that people will recognise me wherever I go, and know all about my life, as far as its follies go, I can discern something good for me.
summary: Even though everyone knows about my mistakes, I try to see something positive in being known.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: For half an hour I stood there in the grey November rain surrounded by a jeering mob.
summary: I stood alone in the cold rain for half an hour while a crowd mocked me.

author: Kate Chopin
text: True, I feel at home in the society of these symbols of life’s immutability. In the procession I should feel the crushing feet, the clashing discords, the ruthless hands and stifling breath.
summary: I feel comfortable alone with unchanging things because being in crowds feels crushing and suffocating.

author: Kate Chopin
text: They’re making you a little kinder than usual; but some way I feel as if they were wandering, as if they were not here with me.”
summary: I feel like you are being kinder but your attention is wandering elsewhere.

author: George Eliot
text: I can form an opinion of persons. I know when I like people. But about other matters, do you know, I have often a difficulty in deciding.
summary: I trust my judgment about people I like but I often struggle to make other decisions.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: How mad I am!... But why make you miserable? It’s awful to think that any outsider can shatter our happiness.”
summary: I feel crazy for dragging you down with me and scared that someone else could ruin what we have.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: “Ever since I heard about you, about your refusal, I began.... Of course, I approved of what you did. But there are ways of doing everything.
summary: I heard about how you turned them down and I support your choice but wish you had handled it better.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: And that’s what I wanted to see you for. Your action was just what it should have been. I see that, but you ought not to keep it up.
summary: I came to tell you that you did the right thing at first but you need to stop now.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Don’t imagine I would compare ... I know you, darling. But I could not help remembering....
summary: I am not trying to compare you to anyone else, but I keep thinking about the past anyway.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: Though I don’t look at it as an outsider, for, indeed, it touches me to the heart.... Is it possible, is it possible that you do not feel sick at being here yourself? Evidently habit does wonders! God knows what habit can do with anyone.
summary: It breaks my heart to see you stuck here and I wonder how you got used to a place that makes you feel sick.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: Indeed, I always feel when I meet people that I am lower than all, and that they all take me for a buffoon. So I say, ‘Let me really play the buffoon. I am not afraid of your opinion, for you are every one of you worse than I am.’
summary: I feel like everyone looks down on me so I just lean into acting foolish to hide my hurt.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: You will see great sorrow, and in that sorrow you will be happy. This is my last message to you: in sorrow seek happiness. Work, work unceasingly.
summary: You will face deep sadness but you can find happiness inside it if you keep working.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: But I’ve been longing for you. And what is suffering? I am not afraid of it, even if it were beyond reckoning. I am not afraid of it now.
summary: I have missed you so much that I no longer fear any pain that loving you might bring.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: But I didn’t think about that at all, and I didn’t want to think of it at that moment. I only hated you and longed to revenge myself on you for everything.
summary: I refused to think clearly because I was consumed by hatred and wanted to get back at you.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: I have a longing for life, and I go on living in spite of logic. Though I may not believe in the order of the universe, yet I love the sticky little leaves as they open in spring. I love the blue sky, I love some people, whom one loves you know sometimes without knowing why.
summary: I still want to live for simple joys like spring leaves and blue sky even when life makes no sense.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: But now I don’t think about him. It’s three months since I left home. I’ve forgotten him. I’ve forgotten everything.
summary: I left home months ago and I tell myself I have finally forgotten him and everything else.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: But on the contrary to behold and consider all things according to their true nature, and to carry myself towards everything according to its true worth.
summary: I want to see everything clearly for what it really is and respond to it fairly.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: I have often wondered how it should come to pass, that every man loving himself best, should more regard other men's opinions concerning himself than his own.
summary: I keep wondering why I love myself most yet care more about what others think of me.

author: Epictetus
text: I suppose, you know the measure by which one man is estimated by another. Have you taken pains to learn what is a good man and what is a bad man, and how a man becomes one or the other? Why then are you not good yourself?
summary: You know what makes a person good or bad, so why are you not living up to it.

author: Epictetus
text: Does any man then hinder me from going with smiles and cheerfulness and contentment? Tell me the secret which you possess. I will not, for this is in my power. But I will put you in chains.
summary: I can still choose to stay cheerful and calm because no one can take that freedom from me.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: I see other persons around me of a like nature. I ask them if they are better informed than I am.
summary: I look at people like me and wonder if anyone actually understands life better than I do.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: With you I should spoil all my victories. And many of you would tumble over if ye but heard the loud beating of my drums.
summary: I feel like being around you would cheapen my wins because you could not handle my intensity.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Up to thy height to toss myself—that is MY depth! In thy purity to hide myself—that is MINE innocence!
summary: I want to rise to your level and find shelter in your goodness to feel pure again.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
Since my appeal says I did strive to prove
The constancy and virtue of your love.
summary: I tried hard to show that your love for me has stayed loyal and true.

author: William Shakespeare
text:
Methinks no face so gracious is as mine,
No shape so true, no truth of such account;
And for myself mine own worth do define,
As I all other in all worths surmount.
summary: I catch myself thinking I look better and matter more than everyone else around me.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: To judge you by your failures is to cast blame upon the seasons for their inconstancy.
summary: You should not be judged only by your failures since being inconsistent is just part of being human.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: Your clothes conceal much of your beauty, yet they hide not the unbeautiful.
summary: You cannot cover up what is truly unattractive inside just by dressing well and looking polished outside.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: I have gotten to know people and places, I have received kindness and trust, I have found friendship.
summary: I feel thankful looking back because I have met kind people, earned trust, and built real friendships along the way.

author: Hermann Hesse
text: But let me say this one more thing: I have not doubted in you for a single moment.
summary: I want you to know I have always completely trusted you without ever questioning you for a moment.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: At any rate, you are none the better for it, as far as I can see. I said when we first met that you had improved.
summary: I feel disappointed because you have not actually improved since we first met despite what I had hoped.

author: Epictetus
text: I have leisure, I am tranquil: let us see how we must deal with sophistical arguments; let us see how when a man has accepted an hypothesis he shall not be led away to any thing absurd.” To them such things belong.
summary: I finally have calm free time and I want to use it to think clearly and avoid getting tricked by bad logic.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: Our instinct makes us feel that we must seek our happiness outside ourselves. Our passions impel us outside, even when no objects present themselves to excite them.
summary: I keep chasing happiness in other people and distractions even when nothing is actually pulling me there.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: You have rejected the one, and kept the other. Is it by reason that you love yourself?
summary: You chose one way of living over another and now wonder if loving yourself is even rational.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: We do not content ourselves with the life we have in ourselves and in our own being; we desire to live an imaginary life in the mind of others, and for this purpose we endeavour to shine.
summary: I am never satisfied with just being myself and I constantly perform so other people will admire me.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: But whom wilt thou compare? Thyself, or Me in thee? If it is thyself, it is one who is abominable. If it is I, thou comparest Me to Myself.
summary: You wonder who you are measuring yourself against, your flawed self or something greater living inside you.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: I’m far from it now, but I do my best, and hope in time to be what Mother is.”
summary: I am not there yet but I keep trying because I want to grow into the kind of person my mom is.

author: Louisa May Alcott
text: Forgive me, dear, I can’t help seeing that you are very lonely, and sometimes there is a hungry look in your eyes that goes to my heart.
summary: I can see how lonely you are and it breaks my heart to notice that aching look in your eyes.

author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
text: “Better in body perhaps”—I began, and stopped short, for he sat up straight and looked at me with such a stern, reproachful look that I could not say another word.
summary: I started to say I felt better physically but stopped when his harsh disapproving stare shut me down completely.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: I—yea, all men—are larger and purer by the infinite breadth of that one little life.
summary: I feel like we are all made better and deeper by having known one small precious life.

author: W. E. B. Du Bois
text: Tall, frail, and black he stood, with simple dignity and an unmistakable air of good breeding. I talked with him apart, where the storming of the lusty young orators could not harm us.
summary: I spoke privately with a dignified thin man away from the loud young speakers dominating the room.

author: William Shakespeare
text: I dare not confess that, lest I should compare with him in excellence; but to know a man well were to know himself.
summary: I feel humbled admiring someone so great that truly knowing them feels like understanding myself.

author: William Shakespeare
text: Meet it is I set it down, That one may smile, and smile, and be a villain!
summary: I am shaken realizing that someone can act warm and friendly while secretly being cruel.

author: William Shakespeare
text: That if you be honest and fair, your honesty should admit no discourse to your beauty.
summary: You cannot stay truly honest if you keep using your looks to influence other people.

author: William Shakespeare
text: Tell us where ’tis, that we may take it thence, And bear it to the chapel.
summary: We need to know where it is so we can take it for a proper burial.

author: Kahlil Gibran
text: To measure you by your smallest deed is to reckon the power of ocean by the frailty of its foam.
summary: One small mistake does not define you any more than foam defines the whole ocean.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: My tendency was upward. I was fast approaching manhood, and year after year had passed, and I was still a slave.
summary: I feel I am growing up and meant for more, yet year after year I remain stuck in the same trapped life.

author: Frederick Douglass
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
text: I was afraid that these seemingly good men might use me so; but I nevertheless remembered their advice, and from that time I resolved to run away.
summary: I do not fully trust the people advising me, but their words convinced me it is time to leave for good.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: People still say that I am rather pretty, Angel (handsome is the word they use, since I wish to be truthful).
summary: I feel a little shy telling my partner that other people still think I look good these days.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: Perhaps—perhaps you are a little better and kinder than I have been thinking you were.
summary: I am starting to realize you might be kinder and better than I first thought you were.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: But I felt I should like to treat you with perfect frankness and honour, and I could not do so without telling this.
summary: I want to be completely honest with you out of respect, so I feel I must share this difficult truth.

author: Thomas Hardy
text: I, who love you better than my own self—better—far better—than you have loved me!
summary: I love you far more deeply than I love myself and far more than you ever loved me.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: You’re taller than I am, I declare. And you’re ever so much better-looking than you used to be, too.
summary: I am surprised to see how much taller and better looking you have become.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: I’ll look at myself every time I come to my room and see how ugly I am.
summary: I keep checking the mirror in my room and feeling bad about how unattractive I look.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: But just now I don’t know them and they don’t know me, and probably don’t want to know me particularly.
summary: I feel like an outsider right now because strangers around me do not know me or care to.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: Well, well, we can’t get through this world without our share of trouble. I’ve had a pretty easy life of it so far, but my time has come at last and I suppose I’ll just have to make the best of it.”
summary: I have had an easy life until now, but trouble finally found me and I must face it.

author: L. M. Montgomery
text: Well, if I take you you’ll have to be a good girl, you know--good and smart and respectful. I’ll expect you to earn your keep, and no mistake about that.
summary: I will only take you in if you behave well and work hard to earn your place here.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: The wind wuthered so I couldn’t go to sleep and I heard someone crying and wanted to find out who it was.
summary: I lay awake listening to the wind at night and heard someone crying and needed to know who.

author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
text: We kept it to tell you when you came. I’m well, I can beat Mary in a race. I’m going to be an athlete.”
summary: I feel strong and healthy again and I can outrun anyone and dream of becoming an athlete.

author: J. M. Barrie
text: I have tossed, and the lagoon has won. This almost makes one wish that the gulch or the cake or Tink’s leaf had won.
summary: I left a big choice to chance and now regret the outcome and wish I had picked differently.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: I never stick too long to one ship; one gets narrow-minded and prejudiced.
summary: I move on often because staying in one place too long makes me closed minded and biased.

author: Kenneth Grahame
text: With a great deal of patience, and any quantity of coaching, you may——”
summary: I feel like someone was about to encourage me that with enough help I could improve at something.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: I am a simple man. I have no great thoughts. I want nothing from anybody. How can you compare me to...?’
summary: I am just an ordinary person with no big ideas and I do not understand why anyone would compare me to someone else.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: I! I am a simple man. I have no great thoughts. I want nothing from anybody.
summary: I am just a regular person with no big ambitions and I am not asking for anything from anyone else.

author: Joseph Conrad
text: In the street—I don’t know why—a queer feeling came to me that I was an imposter.
summary: I was walking outside when out of nowhere I suddenly felt like I did not really belong there at all.

author: Jack London
text: He crosses alone from the smiling timber land and comes down into an open space among the trees.
summary: He walks alone out of the woods and into a wide clearing surrounded by trees.

author: Virginia Woolf
text: At last! Half an inch above the elbow; pearl buttons; five and a quarter. My dear slow coach, thought Clarissa, do you think I can sit here the whole morning? Now you'll take twenty-five minutes to bring me my change!
summary: She is getting impatient waiting forever for slow service while trying on clothes.

author: Virginia Woolf
text: From the contagion of the world's slow stain . . . have drunk their cup a round or two before. . . .
summary: She feels worn down watching the world slowly corrupt everything good around her.

author: Virginia Woolf
text: The shopwomen cowered behind the counters. But Clarissa, sitting very up-right, smiled at the other lady.
summary: Everyone panicked in the shop except one calm woman who smiled reassuringly at another customer.

author: Virginia Woolf
text: And Clarissa looked at her arm in the looking glass. The glove hardly came to the elbow. Were there others half an inch longer?
summary: She checks herself in the mirror and wonders if she can find slightly longer gloves instead.

author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
text: Everyone suspects himself of at least one of the cardinal virtues, and this is mine: I am one of the few honest people that I have ever known.
summary: I believe I am one of the few truly honest people I have ever met in my life.

author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
text: We were in the same senior society, and while we were never intimate I always had the impression that he approved of me and wanted me to like him with some harsh, defiant wistfulness of his own.
summary: I was never close with him in college but I could tell he respected me and really wanted me to like him.

author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
text: Sometimes, in my mind, I followed them to their apartments on the corners of hidden streets, and they turned and smiled back at me before they faded through a door into warm darkness.
summary: I sometimes imagine following strangers home and picture them smiling as they disappear into their cozy lives.

author: Edith Wharton
text: The very good people didn't convince me; I felt they'd never been tempted.
summary: I do not trust people who act perfect because I suspect they have never really faced a hard choice.

author: Edith Wharton
text: I was perfectly unconscious at first that people here were shy of me--that they thought I was a dreadful sort of person.
summary: I did not realize at first that people around me were avoiding me because they thought I was awful.

author: Edith Wharton
text: Since you tell me that you're lonely I've no right to keep you from your friends."
summary: I do not want to hold you back from seeing friends when you tell me you feel lonely.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: You want to be like others in town here. You hear them talk and you try to imitate them.”
summary: You try to copy how everyone around you talks because you just want to fit in.

author: Sherwood Anderson
text: It has itched and squirmed with life and now it is night and the life has all gone away. The silence is almost terrifying.
summary: After a busy day full of energy, the night feels empty and the quiet scares me a little.

author: James Joyce
text: You can’t help having a certain feeling for it. That’s human nature.... But tell me something about yourself.
summary: It is natural to care about your roots, but I really want to hear what is going on with you.

author: James Joyce
text: But I disliked the words in his mouth and I wondered why he shivered once or twice as if he feared something or felt a sudden chill.
summary: I did not like how he sounded and I kept wondering why he shivered like something had frightened him.

author: Victor Hugo
text: Speak, I listen, I admire. Oh Cosette! how strange it is and how charming! I am really beside myself.
summary: Please keep talking because I love listening to you and I feel overwhelmed with happy amazement.

author: Edith Wharton
text: For a long time I've hoped this chance would come: that I might tell you how you've helped me, what you've made of me--"
summary: I finally get to thank you for how much you changed me for the better.

author: Edith Wharton
text: No, I wouldn’t be mean enough to tell the other girls. I ain’t as low-down as that.”
summary: I would never gossip about what I know even though other people might expect me to.

author: Edith Wharton
text: You said you had some business there this afternoon. I’ll see you get there.”
summary: I will make sure you get where you need to go this afternoon for your errand.

author: Edith Wharton
text: Everybody said I was lucky to get a girl to come away out here, and I agreed to give her a dollar extry to make sure.
summary: Everyone thought I was fortunate my partner moved out here with me so I paid extra to keep her.

author: Edith Wharton
text: I don’t blame you, nor I don’t blame myself. Maybe both of us will do better separate. I’m going to try my luck West, and you can sell the farm and mill, and keep the money—”
summary: I hold no blame and think separating is best while I leave and you keep everything.

author: Victor Hugo
text: So much for myself; as for the rest of you, you are worth no more than I am. I scoff at your perfections, excellencies, and qualities.
summary: I am done pretending I am worse than everyone else and I reject their claims of being better than me.

author: Gustave Flaubert
text: At any rate, not till you are man yourself and your temperament is formed.”
summary: Someone tells a young person to wait until he is grown and settled before making a big decision.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
33. 1. He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is
intelligent.  He who overcomes others is strong; he who overcomes
himself is mighty.  He who is satisfied with his lot is rich; he who
goes on acting with energy has a (firm) will.
summary: True strength comes from understanding and mastering yourself rather than judging or controlling other people.

summary: Staying humble gives people dignity, just as a whole is more than a list of its separate parts.

author: Lao Tzu
text:
67. 1. All the world says that, while my Tao is great, it yet appears
to be inferior (to other systems of teaching).   Now it is just its
greatness that makes it seem to be inferior.  If it were like any
other (system), for long would its smallness have been known!
summary: I know my path looks unimpressive to others, but its difference is exactly what makes it truly great.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: For even while I dwell in darkness and silence, in my memory I can produce colours, if I will, and discern betwixt black and white, and what others I will: nor yet do sounds break in and disturb the image drawn in by my eyes, which I am reviewing, though they also are there, lying dormant, and laid up, as it were, apart.
summary: Even with my eyes closed in a quiet dark room I can still picture colors clearly in my mind.

author: Augustine of Hippo
text: And yet when dare I say, since so many things of this kind buzz on all sides about our daily life--when dare I say that nothing of this sort engages my attention, or causes in me an idle interest?
summary: I cannot honestly claim that all the noise around me every day never distracts me.

author: Homer
text: And now I do not see how I can find any further shift for getting out of this marriage.
summary: I have run out of excuses and I cannot see any way to avoid this unwanted commitment.
